There are ongoing questions about the appropriate pay for executives in successful and unsuccessful companies.
The Greenbury committee and the Cadbury report provided guidelines on corporate governance and executive pay.
Not all corporate governance rules are mandatory, leading some firms to ignore them.
Leading institutional shareholders like Norwich Union are becoming more active in corporate governance issues.
Anita Skipper from Norwich Union stated that institutional shareholders are paying more attention to remuneration issues due to circumstances.
Skipper emphasized the importance of ensuring that executive pay is justified by company performance.

British yachtsman Tony Bullimore survived for four days in the Southern Ocean.
Bullimore's survival was aided by high-tech safety equipment.
The Emergency Position Indicating Radio Beacon (EPIRB) costs 700 pounds ($1,176).
The EPIRB helped Bullimore's Australian rescuers locate him.
Bullimore's yacht capsized during a solo round-the-world race.
The London International Boat Show featured a Mediterranean marina as its centerpiece.
The smallest vessel at the show, named Tadpole, is six feet (two meters) long and costs 297 pounds.
Around 800 boats were displayed at the show, including 20 in a giant indoor marina.
Visitors to the show had to wear slippers over their shoes to protect the polished decks.
The British boating sector has a turnover of approximately two billion pounds.

Jiang Zemin is the leader of China's Communist Party.
Jiang Zemin is taking actions to strengthen his position after the death of Deng Xiaoping.
Jiang has declared a campaign against corruption, crime, and poverty in China.
Jiang used a recent party plenum to promote ideological puritanism known as spiritual civilisation.
The success of Jiang Zemin in retaining power depends on the upcoming 15th party congress in late 1997.
The Communist Party is considering reviving the post of chairman and creating one or two vice chairman positions.
Premier Li Peng may be appointed to one of the new vice chairman positions.
Li Peng is required to step down as premier in 1998 after serving two terms.
Jiang Zemin aims to avoid the fate of his predecessors Hu Yaobang and Zhao Ziyang, who were removed from power.
A plenum communique emphasized the importance of maintaining both material and spiritual values.

Mou Qizhong is the chairman of the Land Economic Group.
Mou Qizhong is identified as China's second richest man by local media.
Mou Qizhong is facing lawsuits and investigations for alleged irregularities.
Mou Qizhong cannot leave China due to ongoing investigations.
The Land Economic Group owes 200 million yuan in domestic loans and another 200 million yuan in Hong Kong and Russia.
Domestic creditors have demanded repayment of loans from Mou Qizhong.
Mou Qizhong's company plans to repay loans gradually.
Domestic banks have refused to grant new loans to Mou Qizhong.
Mou Qizhong has been cleared of suspicion of tax evasion and unlawful funds but remains under investigation for other irregularities.
Mou Qizhong's passport renewal has been delayed by authorities.

China criticized Taiwan for not banning the formation of the Taiwan Independence Party.
A spokesman for the Taiwan Affairs Office stated that Taiwan's authorities tolerate the party's formation.
The spokesman claimed that Taiwan's anti-independence stance is deceptive.
Beijing considers Taiwan a rebel province since the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949.
A group of Taiwanese activists plans to form the Taiwan Independence Party on December 12.
China has threatened to invade Taiwan if it declares independence.
China conducted missile tests and war games off Taiwan in March prior to Taiwan's presidential elections.
The spokesman described the Taiwan Independence Party as a political organization aimed at splitting the motherland.
Taiwan asserts its commitment to reunification but states it cannot happen overnight and requires China's democratization.
Taiwan has decriminalized advocacy of independence, citing freedom of speech.

Beijing Mayor Li Qiyan is stepping down after the downfall of his mentor, Chen Xitong.
Li Qiyan has been the mayor of Beijing since 1993.
Li Qiyan is expected to become a vice-minister of labour.
Li Qiyan's departure was anticipated after a vice-mayor committed suicide in April 1995.
The suicide of the vice-mayor led to the downfall of Chen Xitong.
Chen Xitong resigned as Beijing's Communist Party boss and was later sacked from the Politburo.
Chen Xitong is under investigation for possible wrongdoing.
The city government was paralyzed following Chen Xitong's disgrace.
Li Qiyan will be replaced by Jia Qinglin, the party secretary of Fujian province.
Jia Qinglin is expected to formally become the mayor after approval from the Beijing People's Congress.

Wang Xianzeng, the father of Chinese dissident Wang Dan, protested his son's innocence before the start of Wang Dan's trial.
Wang Dan is facing a capital charge of plotting to overthrow the government.
The trial is taking place at the Beijing People's Intermediate Court.
The public is effectively barred from the court, which is surrounded by police and roadblocks.
Wang Xianzeng expressed doubt about the trial's outcome and stated the family would appeal.
The court charges against Wang Dan include evidence from his writings in foreign publications.
Wang Lingyun, Wang Dan's mother, expects a harsh sentence despite his not guilty plea.
Wang Dan has been in detention since May 1995 and faces a minimum sentence of 10 years and a maximum penalty of death.
Human Rights Watch stated that the chances of acquittal for Wang Dan are slim due to inadequate defense preparation.
Wang Lingyun, who has no legal background, will attend the trial as one of the defense lawyers.

China announced a restructuring of Capital Iron, also known as Shougang.
Zhou Beifang, the former head of two of Shougang's Hong Kong-listed affiliates, received a suspended death sentence for corruption.
The suspended death sentence was part of China's anti-graft campaign launched last year.
Zhou Beifang is considered a 'princeling', a term for children of the ruling party elite in China.
Zhou Beifang's father, Zhou Guanwu, resigned as chairman of Shougang in February 1995 after his son's detention.
The Zhous have close ties to Deng Xiaoping's family.
Prosecutors filed corruption charges against 30 individuals, including Zhou Beifang and two former Beijing city officials.
Chinese courts often impose the death penalty in major corruption cases, with suspended sentences frequently commuted to life imprisonment after two years.
The restructuring of Shougang aims to clarify property rights, responsibilities, and management between the parent company and its subsidiaries.
Shougang's parent company plans to gradually cut financial subsidies to subsidiaries, which will need to become self-sufficient.

China's exports increased in October due to slow domestic demand and expanded credit to exporters.
Wang Jian, a researcher with the State Planning Commission, stated that the upturn in exports is expected to continue through the first half of 1997.
Exports rose 23.3 percent to $15.22 billion in October compared to the previous year.
China registered its largest monthly trade surplus of the year in October, amounting to $3.9 billion.
The trade surplus in September was $3.2 billion.
Wang Jian noted that slow domestic demand has led manufacturers to seek overseas markets.
The government reduced the export tax rebate on industrial products from 14.0 percent to 9.0 percent on January 1, 1996.
The International Business Daily reported that the government accelerated the payment of export tax rebates and expanded credit to exporters.
Imports increased by 3 percent to $11.31 billion in October compared to October 1995.
In the first 10 months of this year, China's exports totaled $119.22 billion, while imports reached $107.21 billion, a rise of 5.5 percent from the previous year.

China plans to defrock radical monks in Tibet as part of a crackdown that may last up to five years.
The crackdown aims to reduce the influence of the Dalai Lama in Tibet.
A Chinese propaganda official stated that reactionary lamas will be instructed to return to secular life.
The reorganization of monasteries will focus on ideological education.
China has committed to limiting the influence of Buddhism and the Dalai Lama in Tibet.
The Chinese government believes that religion must conform to socialism.
China views religion as feudal superstition but allows a limited degree of religious freedom.
The Tibet Daily reported that monks in Tibet outnumber students and that more funds are allocated to monasteries than to Communist Party buildings.
China has been stationing work teams in Tibetan monasteries to promote patriotism among monks.
The Tibet Daily reported that there were 1,787 temples and 46,000 monks and nuns in Tibet by early 1996.

American movies, hamburgers, and jeans are popular in China.
China and the United States have experienced changing relationships from confrontation to a love-hate dynamic.
Tang Zhenyu is one of the authors of 'China Can Say No', a bestseller that reflects anti-U.S. sentiment.
Tang Zhenyu's view of the United States changed after the U.S. sent aircraft carrier battle groups near Taiwan in March.
The U.S. sent warships to support Taipei during Taiwan's presidential elections.
Some Chinese people felt disillusioned with the United States after Beijing lost its bid to host the 2000 Olympics.
Anti-U.S. sentiment increased after Chinese state media reported perceived unfair treatment of Chinese athletes at the Atlanta Games.
Wang Jisi stated that the perception of the Chinese government being anti-U.S. while the people were pro-U.S. was incorrect.
'China Can Say No' resonated with many Chinese who were frustrated with the United States.
'China Can Say No' has a sequel and has inspired other anti-U.S. books.

Two sons of Chen Xitong, the former Communist Party boss of Beijing, have been detained.
Chen Xitong's sons face possible prosecution for economic crimes.
The fate of Chen Xitong is currently unknown.
Chen Xitong was a powerful figure in China until his fall in April 1995.
Chen Xitong resigned as Beijing's Communist Party boss in April 1995.
Chen Xitong was ousted from the Politburo in September 1995.
Chen Xitong is believed to be under virtual house arrest.
Chen Xitong is officially under investigation for 'serious mistakes'.
Unpublished party documents allege that Chen Xitong abused his office and amassed $24 million in unauthorized funds.
Chen Xitong is reported to have given nine flats to his mistress and her relatives.

China celebrated a diplomatic victory over Taiwan following South Africa's decision to switch recognition from Taipei to Beijing.
South African President Nelson Mandela announced that Pretoria would change diplomatic recognition by the end of 1997.
Beijing welcomed South Africa's decision, stating it was in South Africa's interest.
China and Taiwan have been diplomatic rivals since the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949.
China considers Taiwan a rebel province and seeks to isolate it diplomatically.
Taiwan claims that its 21 million people should have a voice in international affairs.
South Africa is one of only 30 states that recognize Taiwan's exiled Republic of China instead of the People's Republic of China.
The Chinese government asserts that the People's Republic is the sole legitimate government of all China.
Taiwan's Foreign Minister John Chang expressed hope that South Africa's decision would not affect Taiwan's diplomatic relations with other countries.
Taiwan officials plan to review their investments in South Africa, which total over $1.5 billion.

China's parliament aims to improve its image by increasing supervision of the government's executive and judicial branches.
Tian Jiyun, vice-chairman of the National People's Congress, acknowledged that some officials disregard the law.
Tian stated that some officials do not strictly implement the law or investigate legal violations.
Reports of local officials abusing power are frequently published in official media.
Tian claimed that some officials replace the law with their own word.
Some officials suppress the law, and those enforcing the law may also break it.
Tian's remarks are interpreted by some analysts as an effort to enhance the role of parliament in politics.
Tian urged lawmaking bodies to strengthen their supervision of the executive and judicial branches.
Tian described supervision as a weak link in the work of the People's Congress.
Wang Dan's appeal against an 11-year jail term was rejected by a court in 10 minutes.

Rupert Murdoch predicted he would win his legal battle with Ted Turner and Time Warner Inc.
Murdoch stated that News Corp. Ltd. was on track to boost profits by 20 percent this year.
Murdoch expressed that he did not want to buy out John Fairfax Holdings Ltd.
News Corp. publishes major tabloid newspapers in Sydney and Melbourne, including the Courier Mail and The Australian.
News Corp. owns about 5 percent of Fairfax.
Murdoch is confident that News Corp. will win its lawsuit against the $6.7 billion merger of Turner Broadcasting System Inc. and Time Warner.
Turner Broadcasting and Time Warner completed their merger after shareholder approval.
Murdoch is seeking $1 billion in damages from Time Warner and Turner.
Murdoch claimed that Time Warner's decision not to carry News Corp.'s 24-hour Fox News Service stifled competition.
Murdoch confirmed a bullish outlook for News Corp.'s profits, stating a 20 percent rise is attainable if the American and British economies remain stable.

Rupert Murdoch reported that News Corp Ltd performed below expectations in the first quarter.
Murdoch stated that News Corp is still on track for a 20-percent profit rise this year.
Murdoch is the chairman and chief executive of News Corp.
Murdoch announced a more conservative approach to financing new acquisitions.
Murdoch expressed that the first quarter may not meet profit expectations but aims to make up for any shortfall.
Analysts viewed Murdoch's comments as disappointing and expressed skepticism about the 20-percent profit pledge.
Traders on the Australian share market sold News Corp shares, which closed at A$7.20, a decrease of almost two percent.
In the 1995/96 year, News Corp's net profit decreased to A$1.02 billion from A$1.37 billion in the previous year.
Murdoch indicated that revenues at the Fox U.S. television business began slowly due to the Atlanta Olympic Games.
Murdoch stated that Australian newspaper revenues would be flat in 1996/97.

Rupert Murdoch reported that News Corp Ltd had performed below expectations in the first quarter.
Murdoch stated that News Corp is still on track for a 20-percent profit rise this year.
Murdoch is the chairman and chief executive of News Corp.
Murdoch announced a more conservative approach to financing new acquisitions.
Murdoch expressed that the first quarter may not meet expectations but they will strive to make up any shortfall.
Analysts viewed Murdoch's comments as disappointing and expressed skepticism about the 20-percent profit pledge.
Traders on the Australian share market sold News Corp shares, which closed at A$7.20, a decrease of almost two percent.
In the 1995/96 year, News Corp's net profit decreased to A$1.02 billion from A$1.37 billion in 1994/95.
Murdoch indicated that revenues at the Fox U.S. television business had begun slowly due to the Atlanta Olympic Games.
Murdoch stated that Australian newspaper revenues would be flat in 1996/97.

Ridley Corp Ltd forecasted a flat first half year profit due to slow demand and margin pressures.
Ridley Corp Ltd expects a grain price slump to boost profits for the full 1996/97 year.
Ridley Chairman John Keniry stated that overall company after tax earnings for the first half are expected to be in line with last year.
Strong pasture growth reduced demand for stockfeed in some areas.
High wheat prices earlier in the year contributed to lower Australian stockfood earnings in the first quarter.
First quarter earnings from Ridley's AgriProducts division were below budget forecast and last year's results.
Ridley expects good results from its Canadian stock food supplier, Feed-rite, to offset declines in Australia.
Feed-Rite's earnings before interest and tax exceeded both budget and last year's results in the first quarter.
Keniry noted a rapid decline in grain prices could improve margins in Australia later in the year.
Ridley reported an operating profit of A$36.27 million in 1995/96, a 14.3 percent increase from the previous year.

Rupert Murdoch's News Corp Ltd is likely to benefit from the planned US$20 billion merger of MCI Communications Corp and British Telecommunications Plc.
Australian media analysts stated that News Corp's existing partnership with MCI would strengthen its global media interests due to the merger.
The merger will create the world's second largest telecommunications group.
Analysts noted that the BT-MCI merger would stabilize News Corp's partnership with MCI, which had been strained recently.
Concerns existed that MCI might sell its nine percent stake in News Corp within the next year, which had negatively impacted News Corp's shares.
The merger reduces the risk of MCI selling its stake in News Corp for at least the next 12 months.
MCI and News Corp announced a broad alliance in May 1995, where MCI acquired a nine percent stake in News for US$1.35 billion.
MCI and News Corp agreed to jointly establish an American satellite television operation called ASkyB.
Progress with ASkyB has been slow, and other smaller joint ventures have not been successful.
MCI announced it would reduce its stake in ASkyB from 50 percent to 20 percent and indicated no major new launches were expected from the venture.

Burns Philp & Co Ltd announced a net loss of A$61.8 million for the 1995/96 year.
The loss was attributed to a price war in the U.S. and costs associated with Asian expansion.
Burns Philp incurred abnormal losses of A$136.6 million due to rationalisation of U.S. operations and the spice price war with McCormick & Co Inc.
The cost of slotting contracts accounted for A$33.9 million of the abnormal losses.
Burns Philp's managing director Ian Clack stated that market conditions in the U.S. were improving.
Burns Philp increased its U.S. spices market share to 16 percent, while McCormick's share rose to 34 percent.
Burns Philp holds 16 percent of the western world's yeast market and seven percent of its spice market.
Costs from expanding operations in Asia and plant upgrades in China and India contributed to the losses.
Net profit before abnormal items fell to A$74.8 million, down from A$104.1 million in 1994/95.
Burns Philp did not declare a final dividend, which disappointed investors.

Coles Myer Ltd is Australia's largest retailer.
Coles Myer Ltd forecasted a rejuvenation in its profit outlook at its annual meeting.
Shareholders launched a six-hour tirade aimed at Coles' directors during the meeting.
Former executive chairman Solomon Lew was the prime target of the shareholders' criticism.
Solomon Lew was re-elected as a director with the help of proxy votes after the floor rejected his re-election.
Coles Chairman Nobby Clark was jeered when he attempted to cut short the debate on Lew's re-election.
Nobby Clark stated that Coles was experiencing a rejuvenation in its businesses.
Nobby Clark expressed confidence that Coles could improve its performance.
Coles Myer's first quarter performance was running above expectations.
Coles Myer expects its bottom line results to improve in 1996/97 if Christmas trading is reasonable.

An official inquiry into Australia's financial system was established by the conservative government after its March election.
The inquiry will consider recommending a relaxation of rules that prevent big bank mergers and foreign bank takeovers.
The inquiry outlined various options for reform in a discussion paper without stating its own preferences.
The inquiry noted majority industry support for abolishing rules that stop mergers and foreign bank takeovers.
The inquiry prefers an anti-monopolies system that treats the banking sector the same as other sectors.
The government currently has the final say on bank mergers, rather than the anti-monopolies watchdog.
Analysts expect the inquiry's final report to recommend allowing bank mergers and new foreign investment.
Shares in big banks vulnerable to takeover have increased since the beginning of the year.
Possible takeover targets include the Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd and Westpac Banking Corp.
The National Australia Bank Ltd is seen as the main predator in potential bank mergers.

Brambles Industries Ltd is a transport equipment hire and logistics firm based in Australia.
Brambles reported a 15.8 percent profit increase for the 1995/96 year.
The profit increase occurred despite flat economies in Australia and Europe.
Profits from Brambles' U.S. and European CHEP pallet hire joint venture with GKN Plc compensated for slow growth in Australia.
Brambles' net profit rose to A$215.1 million for the year ending June 30, 1997.
The previous year's net profit was A$97.7 million, affected by a large abnormal loss.
Pre-abnormal profits for 1995/96 rose to A$214.8 million.
Pre-tax profits increased by 13 percent from Europe and 30 percent from the United States.
Australian profits rose by eight percent.
Brambles plans to look for further acquisitions outside Australia.

National Foods Ltd is a dairy and fruit juice group.
The company announced that its reforms from July are almost fully completed.
National Foods is poised for above-budget profit growth in the next six to nine months.
Graham Reaney is the outgoing managing director of National Foods.
National Foods reported a 17.3 percent increase in operating profit before tax, totaling A$37.6 million for the year ending June 30.
The company's net profit rose to A$15.05 million from A$10.77 million after an abnormal loss of A$7.89 million.
Net profit before abnormals increased to A$22.7 million from A$19.2 million, which was below analysts' expectations of about A$23 million.
Earnings for July and August were reported to be ahead of budget and last year's figures.
The reforms improved the distribution system for chilled foods and increased sales coverage for National Foods' products.
National Foods completed the sale of non-core assets and is focused on profit growth from existing assets.

Lend Lease Corp and Modern Home Co announced a joint venture to build a markets complex in Northern Bangkok.
The project will cover 160 hectares and cost A$1 billion (US$778 million).
The complex aims to create a new industrial, commercial, and residential hub in Northern Bangkok.
Stage one of the project is 60 percent complete and projected to cost A$700 million.
Stage one is processing 15,000 tonnes of produce a day and has parking for 25,000 vehicles.
The complex, known as the Thai Markets project, will be located about 20 km from the airport.
The project is expected to take four years to complete.
Lend Lease's Asian unit will contribute up to A$100 million for a 10 percent stake in the joint venture.
The second and third stages of the project will cost A$300 million and include factories, retail outlets, and homes.
The project is supported by the Bank for Agriculture and Agricultural Cooperatives and the Thai Ministry of Commerce.

News Corp Ltd must report a stronger second quarter profit to achieve its 20 percent growth target for the 1996/97 year.
Analysts expect News Corp to report a second quarter net profit before abnormals of between A$450 million and A$490 million.
The first half net profits for News Corp are expected to be between A$735 million and A$775 million.
This first half profit would be an increase of 17 percent from the A$663 million posted in the first half of 1995/96.
Strong receipts from the film 'Independence Day' and firm U.S. television revenue are expected to drive the stronger result.
Analysts indicated that News Corp needs a first half profit that is around 15 to 20 percent better to meet its August 1996 forecast.
Rupert Murdoch's group achieved A$1.26 billion in profits in 1995/96.
Analysts expect revenues from Australian newspapers, magazines, and the Ansett airline operation to remain weak in the second quarter.
First Pacific analyst Lachlan Drummond forecasts A$474 million for the second quarter.
News Corp is scheduled to give a presentation to analysts and investors on February 24 in Los Angeles.

Rupert Murdoch's global media group News Corp Ltd reported a lower than expected first half profit.
News Corp Ltd remains confident of a 20 percent profit boost for the full year.
Net profits before abnormals increased by 10.3 percent to A$731 million.
The reported profit was below analysts' expectations of A$735 million to A$775 million.
A senior Sydney analyst expressed disappointment regarding the results.
Andrew Sekely, head of equities at Intersuisse, described the result as moderate.
News' shares fell 16 cents to A$6.60 after the profit announcement.
The company had previously posted a A$1.26 billion net profit for the year to June 30, 1996.
News Corp officials indicated they were still on track for the 20 percent profit growth during a teleconference briefing.
Operating income from News' Fox Filmed Entertainment unit increased to A$202 million for the first half.

Trans World Airlines Inc. is seeking a new chief executive officer.
Jeffrey Erickson will leave his position as CEO in January after two years in the role.
Erickson's departure follows the exit of Chief Financial Officer Robert Peiser four months earlier.
Industry analysts believe the speed of finding a new CEO will impact the airline's financial stability.
TWA reported a $14.3 million loss in the third quarter.
The airline's yield, a measure of fares, decreased in the same quarter.
Analysts suggest TWA's board may be impatient with the turnaround progress after the third-quarter results.
Michael Boyd stated that TWA has significantly improved compared to three years ago.
William Fiala emphasized the need for a proven turnaround manager to regain Wall Street's confidence.

Caterpillar Inc. announced it will impose employment terms on employees represented by the United Auto Workers, effective Oct. 1.
Caterpillar declared an impasse in negotiations with the United Auto Workers regarding the firings of union workers.
The impasse relates to firings that occurred before and during a 17-month strike against Caterpillar that ended in December.
Caterpillar is willing to send firings that occurred after the strike to arbitration, but not those that happened before and during the strike.
The imposed terms include a pledge not to close any facilities except the York, Pa., plant through September 2001, and job guarantees until that time.
Caterpillar operates 31 manufacturing plants in the United States.
Caterpillar plans to increase its supplement of pensions for retirees by 19 percent until they are eligible for Social Security.
Caterpillar's UAW workers have been without a contract since 1991.
The UAW disagrees with Caterpillar's claim of a lawful impasse and views the action as an attempt to undermine collective bargaining.
An analyst stated that Caterpillar's declaration of an impasse appears genuine and does not expect it to impact the company's stock.

McDonnell Douglas Corp. stock fell after the Defence Department removed the company from the competition to build a new generation fighter jet.
The potential value of the fighter jet program could exceed $200 billion.
McDonnell Douglas is the second-largest defence contractor in the United States.
The Pentagon awarded contracts to Boeing Co. and Lockheed Martin Corp. for developing prototype fighter jets.
British and U.S. forces plan to purchase 3,000 joint strike fighter jets, with initial delivery scheduled for 2008.
The fighter jet program could be worth between $200 billion and $500 billion over the coming decades.
McDonnell Douglas stock closed at $52.50, losing $4.25 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Boeing Co. stock rose to $93.25, gaining $1.50, while Lockheed Martin stock rose to $95.625, gaining $1.875.
Analysts suggest McDonnell Douglas may need to pursue mergers or acquisitions to grow its business.
McDonnell Douglas has been rumored to be in talks with Boeing, Rockwell International Corp., and Raytheon Co. regarding potential mergers.

Nine months ago, shareholders and analysts urged H&R Block Inc to spin off its CompuServe unit.
On April 19, H&R Block initiated a public offering of about 20 percent of CompuServe Corp.
Analysts are anticipating the completion of the spinoff.
H&R Block reported a net loss of $74.1 million for the fiscal 1997 second quarter.
The loss of $74.1 million equates to $0.71 a share, compared to a loss of $8.3 million or $0.08 a share a year ago.
The larger loss was primarily attributed to CompuServe's $58 million second quarter loss.
H&R Block still owns 80.1 percent of CompuServe.
In August, H&R Block suspended the remainder of the spinoff due to CompuServe's performance and market conditions.
H&R Block announced a reduction of its quarterly dividend to $0.20 a share from $0.32.
Analysts continue to rate H&R Block stock as a buy, stating there is nothing wrong with the company's core tax business.

Retailers are expected to post solid sales gains for November.
The later Thanksgiving this year may obscure overall sales results.
Sales at stores open at least a year are expected to rise 2.5 percent to 4.0 percent in November.
Clothing is expected to continue being a strong contributor to sales.
Most retailers report November sales on Thursday.
Harry Ikenson, a retail analyst at Rodman & Renshaw Inc., believes most companies will meet or exceed sales plans for November.
Analysts expect profit margins to improve due to managed inventories and discounts being similar or lower than last year.
Dean Ramos at Dain Bosworth Inc. predicts his sales index could rise one to two points higher than last year's 3.1 percent.
Holiday sales are crucial for retailers, who typically earn a significant portion of their annual profits during this season.
Retail consumer spending rose 4.3 percent from a year ago during the post-Thanksgiving weekend, according to TeleCheck Services.

First Chicago NBD Corp chief executive Verne Istock expects more job cuts at the corporate banking unit.
The corporate banking unit has underperformed compared to the rest of the company.
Istock stated that there will likely be a reduced head count and reduced capital allocated to the corporate bank.
The corporate banking unit posted a return on equity of eight percent in the first nine months of the year.
The return on equity for the corporate banking unit was nine percent a year ago.
The corporate banking unit's results were affected by a $12 million trading loss.
Overall, the bank reported a return on equity of 16.9 percent in the first nine months of 1996.
The corporate and institutional banking unit is being restructured to focus on customer relationships.
Istock believes the corporate bank's return on equity can be improved to 15 percent or better.
First Chicago NBD Corp and NBD Bancorp merged a year ago, forming the ninth largest bank holding company in the U.S.

Mercantile Bancorp Inc. agreed to acquire Roosevelt Financial Group Inc. for about $1 billion in cash and stock.
The acquisition will create the largest bank in Missouri.
The acquisition will create the largest locally managed and independently owned financial services organization based in the southern Midwest.
Mercantile will have more than 23 percent of Missouri's deposits after the acquisition.
Mercantile will become the largest bank in St. Louis and Springfield, Missouri.
The acquisition will strengthen Mercantile's presence in major Missouri markets such as Kansas City.
Roosevelt Financial Group has $9 billion in assets and 81 offices and branches in Missouri, Kansas, and Illinois.
Mercantile plans to take a pretax charge of $25 million to $30 million for merger-related costs when the deal closes next year.
The deal is expected to save about $20 million a year in branch costs annually.
Analysts expect about 50 overlapping branches to be closed by 1998.

Rawlings Sporting Goods Inc chief financial officer Paul Martin stated that the company is not for sale.
Paul Martin mentioned that Rawlings recognizes its responsibility to shareholders.
The company does not comment on takeover rumors according to Paul Martin.
Rawlings stock has increased by more than 50 percent since early December.
Market sources have indicated that the stock's increase is related to takeover rumors.
An analyst noted that there are ongoing discussions about a potential takeover.
Timothy Conder, an analyst at A.G. Edwards, expressed skepticism about any current takeover talks.
Timothy Conder stated that the stock has a fair price of 9-1/2 based on fundamentals.
Conder maintained an aggressive rating on Rawlings stock, citing its brand name as an attractive factor for potential acquirers.
Nike Inc is frequently mentioned as a potential acquirer for Rawlings.

Chrysler Corp. introduced new versions of the Chrysler Concorde and Dodge Intrepid sedans.
The introduction is part of a $2.1 billion revamp of the car line.
The new cars will be available in showrooms in the fall.
The price range for the new cars will be about $20,000 to $26,000.
Chrysler's pricing strategy contrasts with Ford Motor Co.'s approach to the redesigned Taurus sedan.
Chrysler Vice Chairman Robert Lutz stated the goal is to keep the new models affordable.
Chrysler introduced the original 'LH' car line in 1992.
The original 'LH' car line was considered by some analysts as Chrysler's 'Last Hope.'
Chrysler did not introduce replacements for the Chrysler LHS luxury car and the Eagle Vision.
The new cars feature improved production processes and new engine technology.

Caterpillar Inc. reported record profits of $1.36 billion for 1996.
Caterpillar's profits for 1996 increased from $1.14 billion in 1995.
Caterpillar's revenues grew 2.8 percent to $16.52 billion in 1996.
Caterpillar's fourth-quarter profits rose to $381 million in 1996.
Caterpillar's fourth-quarter earnings per share were $1.99 in 1996.
Caterpillar's fourth-quarter results exceeded Wall Street analysts' average estimate of $1.88 per share.
Caterpillar's stock fell by $2.125 to $76.375 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Caterpillar expects near flat profits for 1997 compared to 1996.
Caterpillar anticipates slight revenue growth from ongoing operations in 1997.
Caterpillar stated that higher demand in developing regions should offset a weaker market in the U.S. and Japan.

Sears, Roebuck and Co. reported a 24.6 percent increase in earnings for the fourth quarter.
The increase in earnings was attributed to strong sales and improved profit margins during the Christmas selling season.
Sears Chairman Arthur Martinez stated that the fourth-quarter results were impressive compared to last year's results.
December included the company's first back-to-back billion-dollar sales weeks.
Retailers typically earn half or more of their annual profit during the Christmas season.
Analyst Alan Rifkin noted that Sears' sales at comparable stores rose 9.5 percent in December.
Sears' earnings rose to $567 million, or $1.42 a share, in the fourth quarter, up from $455 million, or $1.13 a share, in the previous year.
Sales grew 10.8 percent to $12.04 billion from $10.87 billion.
Sears' earnings exceeded Wall Street forecasts, which averaged $1.38 a share.
Sears' stock fell $2 to $49.125 on the New York Stock Exchange due to profit-taking.

Mercury Finance Co. is facing a lawsuit for violating securities laws.
The lawsuit claims that Mercury inflated its earnings through phony bookkeeping entries.
Mercury fired its chief accountant, James Doyle, who has not been seen since last Thursday.
The stock of Mercury has been halted on the New York Stock Exchange and has not traded since closing at $14.875 on Tuesday.
Traders reported that Mercury's stock was trading at $4.25 overseas, indicating a loss of over $1.8 billion in market value.
The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Chicago, alleges that Mercury and some senior officers misrepresented or omitted crucial information about the company's earnings for the last three years.
The lawsuit states that Doyle sold tens of thousands of shares of Mercury stock at inflated prices, resulting in millions of dollars in illegal profits.
Mercury announced that its 1996 earnings would be restated to $56.7 million from $120.7 million.
Mercury admitted to being in violation of certain provisions of its loan agreements and has formed a special committee to investigate the issues.
Analysts believe that Mercury's planned acquisition of Fidelity Acceptance from BankBoston Corp. is unlikely to be completed.

Canada's six biggest banks are expected to report third-quarter earnings on Tuesday.
An improved interest rate environment, higher investment banking revenues, and better loan quality are anticipated to drive profits.
Analysts expect earnings for the Big Six banks to be 15 percent to 20 percent higher than the same quarter last year.
Bank of Montreal and Bank of Nova Scotia will report earnings on Tuesday.
Toronto-Dominion Bank and National Bank of Canada will report earnings on Thursday.
Royal Bank of Canada and Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce are scheduled to report earnings on Thursday, September 5.
Analysts predict stronger securities earnings compared to last year despite a recent downturn in financial markets.
The banks are expected to benefit from lower loan losses as the industry recovers from past commercial real estate failures.
Bank stocks have remained strong performers despite a stock market correction earlier in the summer.
Lower Canadian interest rates have contributed to bank stock prices reaching all-time highs on the Toronto Stock Exchange.

Shares in Molson Cos. Ltd. decreased on Monday after its Molson Breweries unit lost the rights to brew Coors Light.
Coors Light is Canada's top-selling light beer.
An arbitration panel ruled that Molson relinquished its right to brew and sell Coors products in April 1993.
The ruling was based on Molson breaching its licensing agreement with Coors by allowing Miller Brewing Co. to acquire a stake without Coors' consent.
Molson class A stock closed down C$0.75 at C$20.15 on the Toronto Stock Exchange.
Molson's stock earlier fell to C$19.50, near its 52-week low.
The panel ordered Molson to pay Coors all profits earned from selling Coors beer since 1993.
Coors brands produced by Molson account for 8 percent of its sales volume.
Coors Light commands a 5 to 5.5 percent share of the Canadian beer market.
Molson officials expressed willingness to negotiate a new licensing agreement.

Anti-government protests occurred in Toronto on Friday.
Demonstrators shut down the transit system and disrupted businesses.
Protesters attempted to break into the Toronto Stock Exchange.
Jim Stanford, an economist for the Canadian Auto Workers, spoke to protesters outside the exchange.
Protesters chanted 'Shut it down' while pounding on the glass doors of the stock market.
A man in a mask and combat fatigues was seen trying to break the doors.
Protest organizers later moved the rally away from the stock exchange.
Ontario Finance Minister Ernie Eves commented on the irony of protesting groups having pension funds invested in stocks.
The protests were in response to budget cuts by Ontario's Conservative government.
Subway and bus services were halted, affecting about one million commuters in Toronto.

The Montreal Canadiens are a franchise in the National Hockey League.
There were sale rumors regarding the Montreal Canadiens on Friday.
Molson Cos. Ltd. is the owner of the Montreal Canadiens.
A consortium led by Serge Savard was reportedly assembling a bid for the team.
The Montreal Canadiens have won a record 24 Stanley Cup championships since 1916.
Toronto's Globe and Mail reported that talks with Molson had been ongoing for several days.
Marty York, a sports columnist, suggested there was a good chance of a sale occurring.
Rejean Tremblay, a columnist for La Presse, reported similar sale rumors.
Molson is the sole owner of the Canadiens and the Molson Centre, which cost $150 million.
Analysts speculated that the Canadiens and the arena could be worth up to $300 million.

Fidelity Investments announced that Canadian regulators are investigating trades made by Veronika Hirsch.
Veronika Hirsch is the manager of Fidelity's True North fund.
Hirsch's promotional road show for the True North fund has been postponed due to the regulatory review.
The road show was scheduled to begin on Monday.
A spokesman for Fidelity's Canadian subsidiary stated that Hirsch was contacted by a regulatory agency regarding her personal investments before joining Fidelity.
The British Columbia Securities Commission is reportedly looking into the matter.
Hirsch previously worked at AGF Management Ltd. in Toronto before joining Fidelity.
During her time at AGF, Hirsch purchased 65,000 special warrants of Oliver Gold Corp. through a private placement.
Hirsch paid C$1.53 per warrant for the Oliver Gold shares.
The AGF Growth & Income Fund, managed by Hirsch, later bought 295,000 special warrants at a price of C$3.60 per warrant.

Veronika Hirsch was hired by Fidelity Investments to lead its efforts in the Canadian market.
Hirsch has been removed from her fund while being investigated by Canadian regulators.
Hirsch joined Fidelity three months prior to her removal.
Hirsch is involved in a controversy regarding personal trades made before joining Fidelity.
Hirsch's investments in Oliver Gold Corp. attracted the attention of the British Columbia Securities Commission.
Fidelity has offered clients the option to withdraw their money without penalty.
The fund managed by Hirsch has grown to C$190 million in assets since its launch.
Fidelity's head office in Boston declined to comment on the situation.
Hirsch purchased 65,000 special warrants of Oliver Gold while working at AGF Management Ltd.
Regulators are reviewing whether Hirsch's trades constitute 'front running'.

The Canadian Football League (CFL) is scheduled to hold its 84th Grey Cup championship on Sunday.
The championship will feature the Toronto Argonauts and the Edmonton Eskimos.
The CFL has experienced a chaotic and money-losing season.
All but one of the nine CFL clubs are expected to lose money this season.
The Ottawa Rough Riders franchise folded earlier this month.
The Edmonton Eskimos could not afford to fly players' wives to the Grey Cup game.
CFL Commissioner Larry Smith expressed interest in building a relationship with the National Football League (NFL).
Larry Smith stated that the CFL will not become a Triple A minor league.
Greg Aiello, director of communications for the NFL, mentioned that no agreement has been reached on collaboration with the CFL.
CFL purists are concerned that closer ties with the NFL could threaten the distinctiveness of Canadian-style football.

Bank of Nova Scotia is Canada's fourth largest bank.
The bank reported its first C$1 billion annual profit on Wednesday.
Net income for the year ended October 31 increased by 22 percent to C$1.069 billion.
The bank increased its quarterly dividend by C$0.03 to C$0.37 a share.
Scotiabank was the fourth of Canada's Big Six banks to exceed the C$1 billion profit threshold.
Bank of Montreal reported a record C$1.17 billion profit on Tuesday.
Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce joined the C$1 billion profit club last year.
Return on equity rose to 15.8 percent in 1996 from 14.2 percent the previous year.
Earnings for the fourth quarter increased to C$1.08 a share from C$0.88 a share in the same period in 1995.
Net interest income rose 15 percent to C$3.58 billion in 1996.

Royal Bank of Canada is the largest bank in Canada.
Royal Bank of Canada reported a net income of C$1.43 billion for the year ended Oct. 31.
This net income increased from C$1.26 billion in 1995.
Royal Bank of Canada raised its quarterly dividend by C3 cents to C37 cents a share.
This was the third dividend increase in the past 15 months.
Royal Bank of Canada was the fourth of Canada's Big Six banks to report a third consecutive year of record profits.
The expected earnings from Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce and National Bank of Canada were projected to exceed C$6 billion.
Royal Bank of Canada's provision for credit losses fell to C$440 million in 1996.
Royal Bank of Canada is seeking an acquisition in the United States.
Royal Bank of Canada's fourth-quarter earnings rose to C$1.09 a share.

Ontario Hydro announced a C$2.5 billion ($1.8 billion) charge in 1996 to strengthen its financial structure.
Ontario Hydro's board of directors approved a C$600 million ($440 million) charge against 1997 earnings.
The charges are related to accounting and operational changes.
The Conservative government of Ontario is considering the privatization of Ontario Hydro.
Ontario Hydro reported an estimated net loss of C$1.9 billion ($1.4 billion) for 1996.
Ontario Hydro had previously forecast net income of between C$600 million ($440 million) and C$625 million ($460 million).
Allan Kupcis is the Chief Executive Officer of Ontario Hydro.
Ontario Hydro's debt is estimated at more than C$30 billion ($22 billion).
Ontario Hydro is the largest electricity producer in North America based on installed generating capacity.
Ontario Hydro operates 96 hydro-electric stations, five nuclear plants, and six fossil-fuel stations.

Laidlaw Inc. is a Canadian waste and transportation firm.
Laidlaw Inc.'s stock increased significantly on the Toronto Stock Exchange.
The increase in stock was due to major moves in ambulance services and waste management worth over $2 billion.
CEO James Bullock stated that Laidlaw is poised for strong growth.
Laidlaw plans to acquire American Medical Response Inc. for $1.12 billion in cash.
Laidlaw will merge American Medical Response with its MedTrans ambulance services unit.
Laidlaw signed a letter of intent to sell its Environmental Services unit for $1 billion to Rollins Environmental Services Inc.
After the sale, Laidlaw will own 66 percent of Laidlaw Environmental Services Inc.
Laidlaw completed the sale of its solid waste management business to Allied Waste Industries Inc. for $1.65 billion.
Laidlaw's class B stock closed at a 52-week high of C$18 on the Toronto Stock Exchange.

Icewine enthusiasts harvested icewine in a snow-covered vineyard.
Germany discovered icewine in the late 18th century.
Canada is the world's largest producer of icewine.
Icewine can cost up to C$200 ($150) a bottle in Japan.
Japan is the biggest export market for Canadian icewine.
China and South Korea are developing a taste for icewine.
Most Canadian icewine comes from the Niagara wine region.
In 1995, 24 wineries in Niagara produced 29,700 gallons (112,500 liters) of icewine.
California wineries produce sweet wines that are not considered true icewine.
Icewine is generally amber or golden in color and has a taste similar to honey, apricots, or peaches.

Canada's financial markets reacted positively to Finance Minister Paul Martin's 1997/98 budget.
Analysts expect a modest rally in the markets following the budget announcement.
The Liberal government plans to maintain pressure on the deficit while implementing minor tax cuts and new spending.
Economists believe Martin's assumptions on interest rates and economic growth are prudent.
Bob Boaz, director of research for HSBC James Capel Canada Inc., predicts a flow of funds into the Canadian dollar, bond market, and stock market.
Analysts expect the markets to stabilize quickly due to widely anticipated budget details.
John Anania, an economist at Royal Bank of Canada, stated that there was no significant news in the budget but noted Martin's fiscal resolve.
Martin predicted the deficit for 1996/97 would be no more than C$19 billion, down from a projected C$24.3 billion.
The deficit is expected to decrease to C$17 billion in 1997/98.
The Canadian dollar strengthened slightly to C$1.3534 (US$0.7388) after the budget's release.

The combined profits of the Big Three U.S. automakers reached nearly $2 billion in the third quarter.
This profit figure exceeded the results from the same period a year ago.
Strong demand for light trucks and minivans contributed to the profits of Chrysler Corp and Ford Motor Co.
General Motors Corp's operating earnings were negatively impacted by an increase in U.S. incentives.
In the third quarter of 1995, the three automakers earned a combined total of $1.35 billion.
Analyst Kenneth Blaschke from Dean Witter Reynolds Inc stated that it would be a good quarter overall for the Big Three.
General Motors is expected to report a third quarter net income of about $850 million.
GM's expected results will include an after-tax gain of $250 million from reversing a plant closure decision.
In the year-ago third quarter, GM earned $642 million, including earnings from Electronic Data Systems Corp.
GM's worldwide car and truck production rose 11 percent in the third quarter compared to the previous year.

Second-shift workers at General Motors Corp.'s Cadillac assembly plant will not report to work on Monday due to the Canadian Auto Workers strike.
Thousands more U.S. assembly employees may be laid off this week, according to GM.
The Cadillac plant will operate with only one shift on Monday and Tuesday.
The Cadillac plant is expected to halt production completely unless the strike is resolved.
The Cadillac plant employs more than 3,000 hourly workers represented by the United Auto Workers union.
The Cadillac factory builds Cadillac's DeVille, Seville, and Eldorado luxury cars.
The plant depends on interior trim parts made at a strike-bound plant in Windsor, Ontario.
GM's Canadian workers began an escalating strike on October 3.
The strike shut down all of GM's operations in Canada by late October 9.
GM and the union have been unable to reach an agreement for a new national labor contract for GM's 26,000 CAW members.

Lear Corp. agreed to buy the instrument panel and trim parts unit of Borealis Holding AB.
Lear signed a memorandum of understanding to acquire Borealis Industrier AB for undisclosed terms.
Borealis Industrier is based in Gothenburg, Sweden and manufactures various components for the European car and truck industry.
Borealis Industrier had sales of about $230 million in 1995 and owns five plants in Sweden employing about 1,800 people.
Primary customers of Borealis Industrier include AB Volvo, Saab Automobile AB, and Scania AB.
Borealis Holding is owned by Neste Oy and Statoil AS.
The completion of the transaction is subject to approval by the Swedish competition authority and other conditions.
The acquisition supports Lear's strategy to provide total automotive interior systems, including instrument panels.
Lear previously purchased Masland Corp. for $384 million and Automotive Industries Inc. for $626 million.
Lear's stock was unchanged at $38 a share on the New York Stock Exchange.

General Motors Corp. is in negotiations with the United Auto Workers (UAW) following a 20-day strike by the Canadian Auto Workers.
The UAW negotiations affect approximately 215,000 hourly workers.
The UAW talks were progressing quickly before the Canadian strike began on October 2.
Harley Shaiken, a professor of labor relations at the University of California-Berkeley, stated that the UAW did not want to undermine the Canadian union's negotiating stance.
UAW president Stephen Yokich is directly involved in the negotiations.
Major unresolved issues in the negotiations include the shifting of work to outside suppliers, the sale of parts plants, and job guarantees for 95 percent of GM's workers.
Sources indicate that GM may agree to job guarantees for 95 percent of its workforce, similar to agreements made by Ford Motor Co. and Chrysler Corp.
GM plans to sell a door hardware plant in Flint, Mich., and an interior trim plant in Livonia, Mich., which employ 2,100 UAW members.
Joseph, Littlejohn and Levy, a New York-based investment firm, has been identified as the buyer for the U.S. and Canadian plants.
GM's Delphi Automotive Systems division has about 12 plants it considers 'troubled' and is evaluating restructuring plans for additional parts plants.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) is investigating spontaneous air bag deployments in several General Motors Corp. cars.
NHTSA has received five reports of air bags deploying without a collision in 1996-model GM mid-size sedans.
The spontaneous deployments are attributed to corrosion in the air bag sensing and diagnostic module.
Water was spilled or leaked onto the floor of the vehicle in each case reported.
The investigation involves 395,994 cars, including the 1996 Chevrolet Lumina, Monte Carlo, Buick Regal, Pontiac Grand Prix, and Oldsmobile Cutlass Supreme.
Three of the inappropriate air bag deployments resulted in injuries, but none resulted in death.
Four of the five cars were traveling between 10 and 40 mph when the air bags inflated.
NHTSA has received increasing calls from consumers concerned about child deaths caused by air bags.
Air bags have saved the lives of more than 1,136 adults since 1986, according to NHTSA spokeswoman Liz Neblett.
Air bags have killed 28 children since 1990 due to inflation speeds of up to 200 mph.

General Motors Co. and the United Auto Workers recessed contract negotiations early Monday after their existing contract expired.
Union officials indicated that talks were likely to resume later in the day.
UAW President Stephen Yokich stated that union members continued working despite the impasse.
Bargaining between GM and the UAW recessed around 3 a.m. EST after the contract expired.
The existing contract covers 215,000 UAW members working at GM's U.S. facilities.
Yokich did not mention possible selective strikes at some GM plants during a news conference.
Negotiators talked for about 17 hours on Sunday and early Monday morning in an attempt to reach a new agreement.
GM vice president of personnel Gerald Knechtel described the talks as constructive and stated that significant progress has been made on many issues.
The UAW has reached a new three-year contract with Ford Motor Co. and Chrysler Corp. covering about 171,000 UAW members in the United States.
The UAW is facing challenges in forcing GM to accept job guarantee patterns similar to those agreed upon with Ford and Chrysler.

United Auto Workers (UAW) bargainers reconvened at General Motors Corp.'s headquarters on Tuesday.
UAW workers continued to report to their jobs at GM's U.S. factories despite the expiration of their national labor agreement.
GM spokesman Charles Licari stated that there were no major meetings scheduled on Tuesday.
Key negotiators were communicating in small groups and by telephone.
Licari mentioned that discussions are taking place without a set timetable for negotiations.
A source close to the talks indicated that no significant changes were expected before Saturday.
UAW President Stephen Yokich expressed disappointment with the lack of progress but did not call for a strike.
Yokich noted that some UAW locals may resort to strikes if local negotiations do not improve.
GM is negotiating with over 100 UAW locals for plant-specific agreements in addition to the national contract.
GM Chairman Jack Smith expressed hope that there would be no local strikes during a news conference.

General Motors Corp. has developed the EV1 electric vehicle using exotic materials and sophisticated technology.
GM plans to offer the EV1 only on three-year leases.
Joseph Kennedy is the vice president of sales and marketing for GM's Saturn unit, which will sell the EV1.
The EV1 is the first modern production car designed specifically as an electric vehicle.
The EV1 will be available at Saturn dealerships in the Los Angeles, San Diego, Phoenix, and Tucson areas.
The maximum range of the EV1 is 70 to 90 miles under ideal conditions.
California is expected to provide consumer incentives for the EV1.
Monthly lease payments for the EV1 are expected to be between $400 and $500.
Customers will need to pay an additional $50 a month to lease a 220-volt charging unit.
The cost of electricity to run the EV1 is about one cent per mile.

Local strikes in Wisconsin and Indiana are affecting General Motors Corp.'s truck production.
A walkout at GM's Indianapolis metal stamping plant began on Tuesday.
The Indianapolis walkout has halted shipments of major steel body panels to nine of GM's 11 North American truck assembly plants.
GM will halt production of full-size Chevrolet and GMC pickup trucks at its Fort Wayne, Indiana, assembly plant due to the walkout.
The shutdown of the Janesville plant could cost GM $50 million a week in pre-tax profits.
The Janesville plant employs 4,800 workers and is the sole source for GM's Chevrolet Tahoe, Suburban, and GMC Yukon vehicles.
GM makes about $9,000 in variable profits on each truck produced at the Janesville plant.
GM has 23,158 U.S. workers idled due to shortages of Canadian-made parts.
3,200 workers at GM's Buick City assembly plant in Flint, Michigan, are scheduled to return to work on Thursday.
UAW President Stephen Yokich indicated that local strikes could occur without a national contract.

Negotiators for General Motors Corp. and the United Auto Workers met on Friday to discuss a new national labor contract.
The negotiators did not reach a deal after nearly 32 hours of talks on Thursday night.
The negotiating session on Wednesday and Thursday was the longest since negotiations began in June.
GM spokesman Gerry Holmes stated that the negotiators were working to resolve final issues.
Harley Shaiken, a professor of labor relations at the University of California-Berkeley, noted that talks have faced several setbacks in the past week.
Local strikes in Janesville, Wisconsin, and Indianapolis have caused parts shortages, affecting GM's operations.
GM's compact sport/utility plant in Moraine, Ohio, halted operations, idling 4,000 workers.
Seven other GM truck plants are expected to run out of parts made at the Indianapolis plant in the coming days.
Some states may rule that laid-off workers are not eligible for state unemployment benefits due to the strikes.
The strikes by 2,750 workers in Indianapolis and 4,800 workers in Janesville are aimed at pressuring GM's light truck operations.

Labor negotiations between General Motors Corp. and the United Auto Workers continued into early Saturday morning.
General Motors is facing pressure from production losses related to strikes.
Negotiators at GM's headquarters are discussing a list of plants to exclude from employment guarantees in a three-year national contract.
The national contract covers 215,000 hourly workers.
Ford Motor Co. and Chrysler Corp. have agreed to guarantee jobs for 95 percent of their current hourly workforces.
General Motors wants to exclude several parts plants from job guarantees, including a door hinge plant in Flint, Mich., and an interior trim plant in Livonia, Mich.
A union negotiator stated that the negotiations are not yet complete.
GM spokesman Gerry Holmes did not rule out a settlement early on Saturday but did not provide details on the progress of discussions.
The UAW canceled a Saturday meeting of plant-level leaders, indicating a potential delay in reaching a settlement.
The UAW's 250-member National GM Council is scheduled to meet on Wednesday, Nov. 6, in Chicago if a tentative agreement is reached.

Workers at a General Motors Corp. metal stamping plant in Indianapolis returned to work after ratifying a deal to end a five-day strike.
The strike at the Indianapolis plant threatened to paralyze most of GM's light truck production.
Negotiators at GM's Janesville, Wis., truck assembly plant did not reach a settlement, and a strike by 4,800 workers there entered its sixth day.
The Janesville plant builds GM's Chevrolet Tahoe, Suburban, and GMC Yukon sport/utility vehicles.
The deal for 2,750 workers in Indianapolis includes the hiring of 200 new workers.
The Indianapolis plant has been working heavy overtime due to strong demand for GM's trucks.
GM dropped plans to change job classifications and seniority rules for skilled trades workers.
GM will pay thousands of dollars to workers to settle grievances.
The Indianapolis strike disrupted shipments of parts to nine of GM's North American light truck assembly plants.
The strike caused parts shortages that forced GM to shut down factories in Fort Wayne, Ind., Shreveport, La., Moraine, Ohio, and Linden, N.J.

Imperial Tobacco Group will split from Hanson Plc on October 1.
Imperial Tobacco Group is Britain's second biggest tobacco firm after B.A.T Industries.
Imperial Tobacco Group's brands include Embassy, John Player Special, Superkings cigarettes, Panama, and Castella cigars.
Hanson Plc has reduced Imperial's brands from 150 to 33 and increased productivity by 195 percent since acquiring it.
In 1995, Imperial Tobacco Group reported profits of 348 million pounds on sales of 3.6 billion pounds.
Analysts express concerns that Imperial's shares may struggle once listed in London due to litigation threats against tobacco firms.
Tobacco stocks have recently been affected by new litigation and regulatory measures in the United States.
Analysts believe that litigation risks could hinder potential international takeovers of Imperial Tobacco Group.
Britain accounts for 87 percent of Imperial Tobacco Group's profits.
UBS analysts predict a 20-30 percent price earnings discount for Imperial due to litigation risks and market uncertainties.

Wickes Plc is a British Do-It-Yourself retailer.
Wickes Plc reported accounting irregularities that led to an overstating of profits.
The ex-chairman of Wickes Plc accepted responsibility for the accounting irregularities.
Wickes Plc will write off 51 million pounds due to the overstated profits.
The restatement of accounts will reduce operating profit by 26 million pounds for 1995, 14 million pounds for 1994, and 11 million pounds for earlier years.
Wickes Plc will incur a two million pounds charge against shareholder funds related to European businesses.
Wickes Plc will incur a 10 million pounds charge stemming from property interests.
Wickes Plc recorded an operating loss for the first nine months of the current year.
Michael von Brentano is the new chairman of Wickes Plc.
Wickes Plc plans to finalize a new business plan after negotiations with suppliers.

UK building bosses and health insiders have warned of declining confidence in privately financed health projects.
There is a call for rapid acceleration in the number of contracts awarded in the next few months.
The annual Private Finance Panel conference will be addressed by Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and health secretary Stephen Dorrell.
The government approved a 280 million pounds east London hospital project led by AMEC Plc.
Health has been identified as the biggest issue within the Conservative government's private finance initiative (PFI).
The Treasury set a target of 500 million pounds of health projects for Health Secretary Stephen Dorrell by April.
The likelihood of reaching the 500 million pounds target appeared slim until the announcement of the east London hospital project.
Building firms and NHS leaders have been blaming each other and the government for project delays.
British junior health minister John Horam expressed confidence in reaching the 500 million pounds target.
Some construction industry leaders indicated that around 20 companies may not pursue new bids due to concerns about project delays.

UK leisure group Conrad Plc is expected to finalize its proposed takeover of Sheffield United Football Club in three to four weeks.
Details of the takeover will be sent to shareholders after due diligence is complete.
A senior source close to Conrad Plc provided this information to Reuters.
Conrad confirmed it is in talks with Sheffield United Football Club regarding the acquisition.
The acquisition is expected to take the form of a reversed takeover.
Sheffield United Football Club is expected to float on the London Stock Exchange as part of the takeover.
The source indicated that Conrad will pay a figure approaching 10 million, but it will be under 10 million.

Ecological warfare has emerged in the British construction industry.
Activists are targeting builders' profit margins instead of using peaceful protests.
Some British companies refer to these actions as 'eco-terrorism'.
Companies like Tarmac Plc, Costain Group Plc, and ARC have been targeted by activists.
Activist groups are now viewed as organized and sophisticated by British firms.
David Harding, spokesman at ARC, noted that activists use mobile phones and the Internet to coordinate protests.
A protestor known as Steady Eddie stated that they would aim to drive companies out of business if economic warfare escalates.
Costain's contract for the Newbury bypass has led to violent protests and threats against staff.
Costain has reported various protests at their head office and the homes of executives.
Some underground groups are under police investigation for distributing leaflets on homemade explosives.

Imperial Tobacco Group Plc demerged from Hanson Plc in October.
Imperial Tobacco Group Plc aims to reduce debt levels and invest in export growth.
Gareth Davis is the chief executive of Imperial Tobacco Group Plc.
Davis stated that debt reduction and investment could occur simultaneously due to strong cash generation.
Imperial is in discussions with a Japanese company to enter the Japanese market.
The group is considering a share buyback option in the future.
Imperial inherited approximately 1.1 billion stg of debt from the Hanson family break-up.
Davis indicated that the debt would not hinder plans for distribution deals or joint ventures in overseas cigarette markets.
The company may explore small acquisition deals in the fragmented cigar market.
Davis expressed willingness to raise debt levels for significant acquisition opportunities but prioritized debt reduction.

Sea Launch is a project involving corporate partners from Russia, the U.S., Norway, and Ukraine to develop space technology.
The total cost of the Sea Launch project is 350 million pounds ($583.2 million).
The project is funded by a consortium of four firms: Boeing Commercial Space Co (U.S.), RSC-Energia (Russia), Kvaerner (Norway), and NPO-Yuzhnoye (Ukraine).
Boeing Commercial Space Co holds a 40 percent stake in Sea Launch.
RSC-Energia holds a 25 percent stake in Sea Launch.
Kvaerner holds a 20 percent stake in Sea Launch.
NPO-Yuzhnoye holds a 15 percent stake in Sea Launch.
Kvaerner is the prime contractor responsible for building the mobile sea-borne rocket launch platform and the command ship.
The command ship is under construction in Govan, Scotland, and is expected to be ready for launch next month.
The first rocket launch is scheduled for June 1998.

Eurotunnel Plc is the operator of the Anglo-French Channel Tunnel.
Traffic will be reduced to one third of normal levels due to a fire in one of the main tunnels.
Eight people were injured in the fire that occurred on Monday night.
Services have been terminated until the affected tunnel is cleared.
There is no fixed time for when services will resume or how long the reduced capacity will last.
Eurotunnel's shares fell in both London and Paris following news of the fire.
In London, Eurotunnel shares decreased by 3.5 pence to 88 pence.
In Paris, Eurotunnel shares dropped by around two percent to 7.68 francs per share.
The fire caused damage to overhead powerline cables and steel rails.
The cost of a new train is 25 million pounds, but Eurotunnel does not believe an entire train will need replacing.

Glaxo Wellcome Plc purchased the remaining 50 percent of its Japanese joint venture Nippon Glaxo for 354 million pounds.
The acquisition was made in pursuit of growth in Japan, the world's second largest market.
Shin Nihon Jitsugyo Co Ltd received a payout of 7.7 million pounds in lieu of the 1996 dividend.
Nippon Glaxo develops, produces, and markets prescription medicines in Japan.
As of June 30, Nippon Glaxo had net assets of 30.7 billion yen.
Nippon Glaxo's post-tax profit for the six months ending June 30 was 2.5 billion yen.
Seven percent of Glaxo Wellcome's profits come from Japan, which represents 20 percent of the global market.
The acquisition is expected to enhance earnings slightly as it is financed by debt and Japanese interest rates are low.
Glaxo Wellcome plans to accelerate growth in Japan by launching new products, including respiratory treatments and Valtrex.
Shares in Glaxo Wellcome fell by 3.5 pence to 950 in London following the announcement.

Eurotunnel is awaiting the outcome of insurer investigations into the costs of a fire aboard a freight train.
Union des Assurances De Paris (UAP) stated it is impossible to quantify the cost of the damage from the fire.
There is currently no reliable estimate of the damage caused by the fire on November 18 in the south tunnel.
UAP indicated its maximum residual risk is 75 million francs, equivalent to $14.4 million.
Eurotunnel plans to hold a press conference to update the situation on Wednesday.
The investigating judge has completed his inspection of the fire scene, but investigations by insurers and company engineers are ongoing.
Current restrictions due to fire damage are resulting in a loss of revenue of one million pounds per day for Eurotunnel.
Eurostar's owners, the London and Continental Railways consortium, have provisions for reduced access charges if the tunnel is partially or fully closed.
Eurotunnel's spokeswoman confirmed that the company is fully insured and that insurance should cover various losses.
A source close to Eurotunnel estimated that the cost of fire damage could run to tens of millions of pounds.

Stagecoach is a British bus and rail group.
Stagecoach's share price has grown fivefold in three years.
Stagecoach's stock hit a record high after a 127 percent rise in first half profits.
Stagecoach reported half year pre-tax profits of 47 million pounds ($79 million).
The half year dividend rose 43 percent to three pence a share.
Group turnover increased to 405 million pounds from 198.8 million pounds.
Chairman Brian Souter described the results as excellent.
Shares in Stagecoach rose by 45.5 pence to 629 by 1350 GMT.
UBS analyst Richard Hannah stated that profits were two million above expectations.
Stagecoach upgraded its year forecast by five million to 97 million pounds.

Richard Branson's Virgin Group has secured the CrossCountry passenger rail franchise.
Virgin Group plans to invest an additional 250 million pounds on new trains and increased services.
CrossCountry operates over 100 stations and is based in Birmingham, UK.
CrossCountry is one of the last passenger rail franchises awarded under Britain's rail privatisation programme.
CrossCountry has 842 staff and reported passenger revenues of 108 million pounds for the year ending March 30.
Will Whitehorn, director of Virgin Rail, stated that the company plans to purchase a new fleet as part of the franchise bid.
Train orders for the new fleet will be placed next year, with deliveries expected in 2002.
Virgin Rail will receive a subsidy of 115 million pounds in the first year of the 15-year franchise.
The subsidy amount is 12 million pounds less than the subsidy received in 1996/97.
Virgin Rail will refurbish existing HST 125 diesel trains and increase train miles by 14 percent.

LucasVarity announced a corporate shake-up involving 13 non-core disposals and a plan to cut 3,000 jobs worldwide over two years.
LucasVarity was formed by the merger of Britain's Lucas Industries and Varity Corp of the U.S.
The company expects to achieve operating savings of 120 million pounds, which is double the anticipated amount after the merger.
LucasVarity's shares initially rose to a 12-month high of 263 pence following the announcement.
Comments about the auto industry during a conference call caused the stock to drop by 16.5 pence to close at 234 pence.
LucasVarity expects to incur an additional one-off charge of 130 million pounds, mainly in non-cash items.
The company plans to cut its worldwide headcount by 3,000 as part of its restructuring efforts.
Thirteen companies have been identified for sale following a three-month review after the merger.
Victor Rice, the chief executive, stated that the company is in active negotiations regarding the sale of some of the 13 businesses.
The eight named businesses for sale include small niche firms in Britain, Argentina, and South Africa, with combined sales of 270 million pounds.

SaveSmart Inc. is a start-up company based in Mountain View, Calif.
SaveSmart plans to unveil a credit card-based scheme for consumers to find bargains from various merchants.
Consumers can qualify for automated discounts on items such as groceries, dining, movies, clothing, furniture, and auto repairs.
SaveSmart's special credit card aims to eliminate the inconvenience of paper-based promotional coupons.
Only about 2 percent of paper coupons are redeemed, according to industry figures.
SaveSmart claims its service enhances sales promotions and is cost-effective for merchants.
Bernard David is the executive vice president of business development at SaveSmart.
The interactive promotion service could significantly impact the $120 billion industry, according to advertising analysts.
Mary Doyle is a Web marketing analyst for IDC/Link Resources.
SaveSmart's website offers an online database of personalized merchant promotions.

Computer Associates International Inc. issued its quarterly financial results.
The company's financial results exceeded Wall Street's consensus forecast.
The stock price fell sharply after executives announced plans to accelerate investments in personal computer-based corporate software products.
The company plans to de-emphasize mainframe software sales.
International sales for the company fell about 5 percent in the latest quarter compared to the previous year.
Computer Associates shares lost more than $4 in early trading.
The stock regained some ground later in the day after analysts reaffirmed 'buy' ratings and raised future earnings projections.
The stock closed at $62.875, down $2.75 on the day, on the New York Stock Exchange.
President Sanjay Kumar confirmed plans to increase investments in the PC-related mid-range software business.
Mid-range software accounted for about 31 percent of overall revenue in the latest quarter.

Computer Associates International Inc is set to announce deals to extend its systems management software onto new computer platforms.
The deals are expected to strengthen ties with Microsoft Corp's Windows NT.
Analysts expect CA to announce that its software will run on Novell and Tandem computer systems.
Computer Associates has scheduled press conferences with Microsoft, Intel Corp, and Tandem Computers Inc.
The announcements are expected to be made at the CA World conference starting Sunday in New Orleans.
Chet Geschickter from Hurwitz Consulting Group expects CA and Microsoft to announce tighter integration of CA's Unicenter with Microsoft's BackOffice suite.
CA and Microsoft have a co-marketing pact for CA/Unicenter for Windows NT that was announced in 1995.
Morgan Stanley analyst Chuck Philips speculated that CA and Tandem have agreed to a partnership for CA to port its software to Tandem's transaction computers.
An analyst predicted that CA and Intel would announce a deal for CA to market Intel's LANdesk Novell network management software.
Computer Associates is the world's top mainframe software supplier and the second largest independent software firm after Microsoft.

AT&T Corp named John Walter as heir to Chairman and Chief Executive Robert Allen.
AT&T believes it must take a gamble to prepare for increased competition.
John Walter was previously the chief executive of R.R. Donnelley & Sons Co.
Walter will replace Allen as CEO and chairman in 18 months.
Robert Miles, a corporate turnaround consultant, compared AT&T's challenges to those faced by IBM.
Analysts credited Walter with successfully guiding Donnelley through expansion into marketing services.
Walter has a reputation for understanding business operations and profitability.
At Donnelley, Walter closed underperforming businesses.
Donnelley spun off Metromail Corp and plans to spin off Donnelley Enterprise Solutions Inc.
Financial analysts are skeptical about Walter's ability to manage AT&T's larger scale.

Microsoft Corp. and Fore Systems Inc. plan to announce a deal on Tuesday.
Microsoft will license Fore's high-speed networking technology for future versions of its Windows operating system software.
Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) is an emerging technology for higher speed networks that can handle voice, video, and data simultaneously.
The deal will integrate Fore's ATM emulation software into the Windows operating system.
This integration will allow desktop office computers to use ATM technology without changing existing software.
The deal could open a potential market of millions of PC users to adopt ATM network technology.
The integration will ensure compatibility with older network technologies.
Industry analysts believe Microsoft's support of ATM will increase its legitimacy with corporate network administrators.
Mary Petrosky, a network analyst, stated that connecting PCs to ATM networks will be easier with the new deal.
Existing technologies like Ethernet and Token Ring remain dominant in corporate office networks.

AT&T Corp. is facing competition in its long-distance phone business.
AT&T needs to enter new markets and is undergoing a management transition.
British Telecommunications Plc announced plans to acquire the remaining 80 percent of MCI Communications Inc. that it does not already own.
The acquisition values MCI at more than $20 billion.
AT&T called on U.S. and European regulators to condition approval of the merger on increased competition in the UK market.
British Telecom claims it operates in one of the world's most open markets.
The merger will combine MCI's marketing skills with British Telecom's financial resources to form a new entity called Concert.
Analysts believe the merger will enhance British Telecom's and MCI's global resource pooling and strategy coordination.
AT&T's share of the U.S. long-distance market has decreased from 60 percent to under 55 percent in two years.
MCI is expected to increase its efforts in the local U.S. phone market with British Telecom's financial support.

Leading data networking stocks experienced profit-taking on Tuesday.
Securities analysts reported that profit-taking followed strong price gains in recent weeks.
Cisco Systems Inc opened at a 52-week high of 67.
Cisco Systems Inc's stock retreated to 65-1/8 during the day.
Cabletron Systems Inc began to decline immediately after Tuesday's opening.
Cabletron Systems Inc lost 1-1/8 to 67-3/4 by mid-afternoon.
3Com Corp's stock also fell after the opening.
3Com Corp was down 2 to 70-1/8 by mid-afternoon.

CompuServe Corp investors' fears were allayed by H&R Block Inc's decision to postpone plans to spin off the remaining 80 percent interest in CompuServe.
Analysts noted that the potential market inundation by the 74.2 million CompuServe shares held by H&R Block had negatively impacted the stock's prospects.
