Analyst Peter Krasilovsky of Arlen Communications expressed relief at H&R Block's decision.
CompuServe faces challenges including declining online membership counts and the failure of its new WOW! consumer service.
Other analysts praised H&R Block's decision to postpone a shareholder vote on the spin-off but expressed concerns about the implications for stocks like CompuServe and America Online Inc.
An unnamed analyst stated that the online market is at a crossroads and appears unstable.
CompuServe's issues have negatively affected America Online's stock price.
Analysts indicated that while competition from Internet access providers may have contributed to the slowdown of established online service providers, most of CompuServe's problems are unique.
On Wednesday, CompuServe stock rose to 13-1/2, while H&R Block stock fell to 26-1/4.
America Online stock increased to 31-5/8 by mid-afternoon.

Semiconductor equipment stocks surged on Friday.
Investors reacted positively to signs that the downturn in the chip industry has hit bottom.
Applied Materials Inc. reported lower earnings but indicated that profit margins would remain higher than in prior downturns.
Analysts raised Applied Materials' rating from 'hold' to 'buy' following its report.
Applied Materials stock increased by $6.625 to $38.625 in afternoon trading on Nasdaq.
KLA Instruments Corp. stock rose by $5 to $38.25.
Tencor Instruments stock increased by $5.50 to $26.75.
Lam Research Corp. stock went up by $4.625 to $34.125.
Intel Corp. stock rose by $3.125 to $122.
Sales of personal computers are expected to increase demand for chip-making equipment.

Texas Instruments Inc. established a licensing agreement with Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. that will generate over $1 billion in royalty payments over 10 years.
Both companies agreed to drop pending patent infringement lawsuits against each other as part of the agreement.
The new agreement replaces a previous five-year deal that expired at the end of 1995.
Merrill Lynch analyst Thomas Kurlak stated that the terms of the new agreement appear to be less generous than the previous agreement with Samsung in 1995.
Kurlak assessed that the new agreement's royalty formula is at roughly 40 to 50 percent of the rate of the old agreement.
The new license covers a broad base of patents from both companies, including semiconductors, personal computers, consumer products, and telecommunications equipment.
Texas Instruments expects to receive about $105 million from Samsung in the fourth quarter for catch-up royalties covering the first nine months of 1996.
Analysts indicated that the catch-up payments should significantly boost earnings for the quarter ending in December.
Kurlak estimated that Texas Instruments will see $35 million in additional quarterly royalties from the Samsung deal going forward.
Texas Instruments has nearly completed its 1995 round of patent cross-license agreements with major semiconductor makers.

Flextronics International Inc Chief Executive Michael Marks expects revenues of around $1 billion during fiscal 1998.
This revenue expectation is more than double the $500 million expected in fiscal 1997.
Flextronics' stock price declined by 12-1/4 to 25 after the company announced a restructuring plan.
The restructuring plan is likely to dampen near-term profits.
Marks stated that Flextronics' restructuring is designed to allow the company to gain market share.
Marks anticipates annual earnings growth of 35-40 percent through the year 2000.
Marks claims that Flextronics will be third in the market by revenues next year, rising from its current fourth place position.
Only SCI Systems Inc and Solectron Corp are larger than Flextronics in the market.
Marks attributed the stock price decline to the volatility of the Nasdaq market and the departure of momentum investors.
Flextronics announced that its restructuring would include charges of $5 to $7 million over the December and March quarters.

Technology stocks rose on Wednesday due to increased belief that price-cutting has boosted holiday personal computer sales.
Money managers purchased stocks to enhance their portfolios at year-end.
The rally was influenced by positive comments from Soundview analyst Mark Specker regarding Compaq Computer Corp.
Fears of poor holiday sales for PC manufacturers diminished.
Mark Specker upgraded his short-term rating on Compaq to buy from hold and recommended buying the stock for long-term gains.
Specker's recommendations on technology stocks are influential among institutional investors.
Other PC makers like Dell Computer Corp. also benefited from the rally.
Compaq's stock rose by $6.375 to $78.625 on Nasdaq.
International Business Machines Corp. added $6.75 to $158.625 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Intel Corp. was the most active stock on Nasdaq, gaining $5.75 to $135.75.

Elementary school students with access to the Internet learned more than students without access.
An independent research group conducted a comparative study in seven urban school districts.
The study concluded that online use has positive effects on learning.
Michael Casserly is the executive director of the Council of Great City Schools.
The Council of Great City Schools is an association of 49 large inner city public school districts.
The study was co-sponsored by the Council of Great City Schools and Scholastic Corp.

A company in California can sell a book to a consumer in Canada from a website hosted in England.
Questions about regulations covering consumer protection and taxation are increasing as online sales grow.
Jerry Kaplan runs an Internet site called OnSale that auctions electronic merchandise.
Kaplan states that most commercial law assumes geographical boundaries for actions.
Some states tax transactions originating within their borders, while others collect use taxes from out-of-state purchases.
Laws regarding obscenity, gambling, and alcohol sales differ from state to state and affect some online merchants.
Gary Arlen is the president of Arlen Communications and analyzes online companies.
Arlen believes the federal government should set national standards for online transactions.
Jonathan Rosenoer is an attorney and author of the online 'Cyberlaw' column.
Rosenoer claims more regulation is needed on privacy issues compared to other areas.

Hewlett-Packard Co. unveiled a new plan to boost sales of computer encoding technology.
The plan aims to foster the growth of online commerce while complying with U.S. export laws on encryption products.
Sales of goods and services over the Internet are increasing but still lag behind traditional sales methods.
Some businesses report that consumers are hesitant to send sensitive information over the Internet due to security concerns.
Encryption scrambles information during transmission so that it can only be read by the intended recipient.
Brad Silverberg, senior vice president at Microsoft Corp., stated that unencrypted information is vulnerable to electronic eavesdropping.
Lewis Platt, CEO of Hewlett-Packard, described the plan as the first government-approved encryption framework to enhance Internet security for transactions.
Intel Corp. plans to incorporate encryption into its computer hardware products as part of the effort.
Federal export laws prohibit the sale of strong encryption technology outside the United States.
President Clinton signed an executive order that liberalizes export rules for encryption products under certain conditions.

A U.S. District Court judge barred new federal regulations that allow credit unions to expand their membership beyond workers at one company.
The judge stated that the new regulations would exceed the legal limits of credit unions.
The new rules were adopted by the National Credit Union Administration after an unfavorable court ruling.
The new rules redefined 'a single common bond' for credit union membership.
Judge Thomas Jackson issued an injunction blocking the new rules, stating they were an attempt to circumvent earlier court rulings.
Earlier court rulings limited credit union members to a single company or organization.
The court actions struck down a 1982 NCUA decision that allowed credit unions to draw members from multiple companies.
Under the latest NCUA rules, credit unions could include members from a single trade, industry, or profession even if they worked for different companies.
Judge Jackson criticized the NCUA for acting like a trade association and ordered the agency to rescind 31 approved applications for credit union charters under the new rules.
The case involves the American Bankers Association and the credit union industry, with a lawsuit filed in 1990 against AT&T Family Federal Credit Union.

The Board of Governors of the U.S. Federal Reserve System is expected to vote to expand banks' non-banking activities.
The Fed's vote may increase the push in Congress to completely overhaul U.S. banking regulations.
The Fed is expected to allow banks' section 20 subsidiaries to derive 25 percent of their revenue from non-banking activities.
The current ceiling for non-banking revenue for section 20 subsidiaries is 10 percent.
Comptroller of the Currency Eugene Ludwig announced that his office will approve bank affiliates moving into non-banking businesses.
Robert Litan, director of economic studies at the Brookings Institute, stated that both the Fed's proposal and Ludwig's actions will pressure Congress to scrap the Glass-Steagall Act.
Historically, banks have sought to change the Glass-Steagall Act to enter other businesses, while insurance companies and securities firms opposed these changes.
The financial services industry is converging, with banks, insurance companies, and mutual funds increasingly overlapping in services.
The Fed has required banks to take steps to prevent issues in subsidiaries from affecting the bank and its insured deposits.
Comptroller Ludwig stated that walling off subsidiaries eliminates any form of government subsidy.

An international task force released a draft plan to expand the total number of Internet addresses.
The International Ad Hoc Committee on domain names was formed by the Internet Society in October.
The committee proposed adding seven new top-level domains to the Internet.
Most Internet addresses end with three-letter designations such as 'com', 'gov', and 'edu'.
Network Solutions Inc of Herndon, Va. issues most top-level domain addresses and charges $100 for each registration.
The committee recommended allowing an unlimited number of firms to register new addresses.
Initially, the committee hopes to authorize 20 to 30 new registration services.
Network Solutions will maintain a monopoly on existing domain names but the committee aims for all names to be handled by qualified firms.
Donald Heath is the president of the Internet Society and chair of the committee.
The full text of the recommendations was posted on the Internet at http://www.iahc.org.

The Federal Communications Commission has tentatively decided not to impose fees on Internet service providers for the use of local telephone lines.
The commission issued a notice of proposed rulemaking outlining two plans to reduce the $23 billion a year that long-distance telephone companies pay to local service providers in access fees.
Kevin Werbach, counsel for new technology at the commission, stated that the commission tentatively concluded that Internet service providers should not pay access charges.
Local phone companies advocated for the application of access fees to Internet service companies, arguing that Internet users were utilizing local lines without paying for them.
Internet companies argued that imposing such fees would hinder the growth of the online industry.
Jill Lesser, deputy director of law and public policy at America Online, expressed approval of the FCC's decision, stating it supports the growth of the Internet.
The commission issued a notice of inquiry to gather comments on the issues involved, as both sides presented legitimate concerns.
A notice of inquiry seeks comments but does not grant the commission authority to adopt a rule.
The commission must issue a notice of proposed rulemaking before applying access fees to Internet service providers.
Kevin Werbach described the Internet notice as more forward-looking than the proposed rules for long-distance access fees.

Federal credit unions are involved in a six-year legal battle with the banking industry.
The Supreme Court is expected to decide whether to hear the credit union case.
The banks filed suit to challenge a 1982 policy adopted by the National Credit Union Administration (NCUA).
The 1982 policy relaxed previous membership limits for credit unions.
Lower courts have agreed with banks that membership should be sharply limited at credit unions.
Tim Pryor is the federal regulatory counsel to the National Association of Federal Credit Unions.
Pryor stated that not hearing the case could lead to the dissolution of many credit unions.
Michael Crotty is counsel for the American Bankers Association.
Crotty argued that changes to membership limits should be addressed through legislation, not the courts.
Before 1982, credit unions were limited to members with a single common bond.

The Clinton administration is revising its 1995 proposal to overhaul the U.S. financial services sector.
A faction in the Treasury Department is recommending a more extensive plan for bank reform.
Under Secretary of the Treasury John Hawke is advocating for a plan that would allow commercial companies to own financial companies.
The Hawke plan is currently under review by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin.
There is a consensus among most in the administration and on Capitol Hill that the 60-year-old laws separating banking from other financial activities should be eliminated.
There is significant disagreement regarding the inclusion of outside companies in financial businesses.
House Banking chairman Jim Leach opposes allowing non-financial firms into the financial services sector.
Rep. Marge Roukema supports a bill that would permit financial services companies to derive up to 25 percent of their revenue from non-financial activities.
Sen. Alfonse D'Amato favors removing all limits on ownership, allowing companies like General Electric or Ford to own banks.
Consumer advocates and small banks are alarmed by the prospect of allowing commercial companies into banking.

An international Internet group released a plan to increase the number of available addresses in cyberspace.
The International Ad Hoc Committee proposed seven new top-level domains.
The proposed new top-level domains are 'web', 'store', 'info', 'firm', 'arts', 'rec', and 'nom'.
The new domains will join existing top-level domains such as 'com', 'edu', and 'gov'.
Each new domain reflects a particular type or category of Internet site.
The group received more than 4,000 comments from around the world while drafting the plan.
Donald Heath is the president of the Internet Society and chair of the ad hoc committee.
Heath stated that the plan should be approved by Internet standard setters within a few weeks.
The plan includes provisions to resolve disputes over the use of trademarked names as Internet addresses.
Anyone applying for an Internet address will have to agree to resolve disputes through online mediation.

Several U.S. legislators are planning to introduce measures to relax export restrictions on encryption technology.
Encryption technology is an essential part of global communications and online commerce.
Last year, the Clinton administration relaxed some Cold War era export limits on encryption technology.
Computer companies claimed the Clinton administration's actions did not go far enough.
Rep. Bob Goodlatte plans to reintroduce a bill that would allow computer companies to export products with powerful encryption features.
Goodlatte's bill would permit exports if foreign competitors were selling similar technology.
Senator Conrad Burns is planning to reintroduce his encryption bill known as PRO-CODE.
Burns indicated that he is still making adjustments to the bill to gain more support.
Goodlatte's bill had garnered 54 co-sponsors by Tuesday night.
Senator Patrick Leahy and Rep. Rick White are considering introducing their own bills regarding encryption technology.

Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan urged Congress to modernize U.S. financial laws.
Greenspan warned that some government oversight must be maintained to prevent financial catastrophes.
A top priority of regulators is to prevent systemic risk in the financial system.
Systemic risk can cause problems in one firm or market to spread and undermine the entire economy.
The failure of Drexel Burnham Lambert in the 1980s raised fears of a cascade of failures among large Wall Street firms.
The Federal Reserve has been able to contain previous crises using its authority to oversee banks and provide loans.
Greenspan stated that regulation becomes increasingly obsolete over time.
Congress is considering several bills to reform laws governing banks, which would affect the Federal Reserve.
Legislators have introduced a measure to modernize rules on derivatives.
Greenspan emphasized the importance of Congress periodically reviewing financial laws.

The Czech Republic and Spain are competing in a European group six match as part of the qualifiers for the 1998 World Cup.
This match is the first significant test for the Czech Republic since reaching the Euro 96 final.
Spain is expected to give Raul Gonzalez his first cap in this match.
Both teams won their opening matches against weaker opponents, with Spain winning 6-2 and the Czech Republic winning 6-0.
Yugoslavia and Slovakia have already secured more wins than both the Czech Republic and Spain in the group.
Czech midfielder Karel Poborsky stated that a loss would complicate the situation for either team.
Spain's goalkeeper Andoni Zubizarreta expressed that the team aims to win and is not satisfied with a draw.
Czech coach Dusan Uhrin has named 16 players from the squad that reached the final of the European championship.
Midfielder Patrik Berger scored six goals in ten days for Liverpool prior to this match.
Spain manager Javier Clemente is selecting Raul due to the absence of other players and has faced criticism for previous selections.

Exchanges in Prague, Warsaw, Budapest, Bratislava, and Bucharest gained ground this week.
Zagreb and Sofia traded mixed.
Ljubljana posted slight losses.
The Central European Share Index (CESI) firmed 66.11 points.
The PX50 index on the Prague Stock Exchange edged up 3.6 points to close at 568.6 on Thursday.
SPT Telecom and Komercni Banka were leading trades on the Prague Stock Exchange.
SPT closed on Thursday at 3,340 crowns.
Polish shares rose for the sixth consecutive session on Thursday.
The WIG index closed at 13,597.4 points, up 892.7 points or 7.0 percent from last Friday's close.
Prices rose in Budapest as market participants returned after holidays.

Richard Krajicek lost in the first round of the Czech Indoor Open to David Prinosil with a score of 6-4 6-3.
Wayne Ferreira won against Renzo Furlan with a score of 7-5 4-6 6-3.
Michael Stich defeated Sandon Stolle with a score of 7-6 6-2.
Krajicek struggled with his serve and had seven aces and six double faults during his match.
Krajicek's parents emigrated from Czechoslovakia to the Netherlands when he was a child.
Ferreira committed several unforced errors during his match but managed to win.
Ferreira is currently ranked seventh in the world and holds the eighth spot for the ATP Tour World Championship.
Todd Martin won against Jan Kroslak with a score of 6-3 6-4.
Bohdan Ulihrach defeated Daniel Vacek with a score of 6-2 3-6 7-5.

Boris Becker withdrew from the $475,000 Czech Indoor Open due to a recurring injury to his right wrist.
Becker tore a ligament in his right wrist during a third round match at this year's Wimbledon.
Becker trained on Thursday morning but complained of pain in his wrist afterward.
Becker informed ATP officials that he would not play his second round match against Czech Martin Damm.
ATP Tour Supervisor Gayle Bradshaw stated that Becker's wrist was too sore for him to play.
Becker won his previous match against Frederik Fetterlein with a score of 6-3 6-4.
During the match against Fetterlein, Becker held his wrist several times and appeared to favor it.
Becker left the training court for his hotel after practice on Thursday morning.
Becker has experienced recurring problems with his wrist, leading to his retirement from the first round in Bucharest and withdrawals from Basle and Lyon.
Becker's withdrawal affects his plans to qualify for a record 12th appearance at the ATP Tour Championships.

David Prinosil defeated Tim Henman 6-4 6-3 in the semifinals of the $475,000 Czech Indoor Open.
Petr Korda won against Martin Damm with a score of 4-6 6-3 7-5.
Tim Henman was the seventh seed in the tournament and had not lost a set prior to this match.
Henman struggled with his groundstrokes early in the match but had a strong serve, hitting seven aces in the first set.
Henman's double fault in the 10th game of the match gave Prinosil triple break point.
Henman has reached seven semifinals in his career but has never advanced to a final.
Prinosil was born near Olomouc, Czech Republic, before moving to Germany.
Henman expressed disappointment over his performance and viewed the match as a missed opportunity.
Prinosil stated that he served strongly and focused on maintaining his concentration during the match.
Martin Damm considered his recent performances, including a final appearance at the Beijing Open, as some of the best tennis he has played.

The Czech September trade deficit is expected to be around 14 billion crowns.
The August trade deficit was 14.7 billion crowns.
Czech trade figures for the first nine months will be released by the Czech Statistical Bureau at 0900 local time on Thursday.
Most economists surveyed expect steady growth in the trade deficit.
Boris Gomez, an analyst at ING Barings, stated that it is too early to discuss a period of stabilization in the deficit.
The nine-month trade gap is projected to be a record, with the January-August figure reaching 100.9 billion crowns.
The total trade shortfall for 1995 was 95.7 billion crowns.
The January-September 1995 trade deficit was 62.3 billion crowns.
Analysts expect a September trade gap of 13-15 billion crowns, aligning with trends for an estimated deficit of 150-160 billion crowns.
The foreign exchange and money markets are expected to show little reaction to the trade figures unless they significantly differ from estimates.

The Prague Stock Exchange experienced a significant one-day decline on Friday.
Foreign interest in the Prague Stock Exchange has decreased due to a lack of market transparency.
Four of the five largest issues on the Prague Stock Exchange fell sharply during active trading.
The Reuters RPIX index dropped nearly three percent to 1,052.
Analysts believe that investors, particularly foreigners, are withdrawing from the market due to unmet reform promises.
Jan Sykora of Wood and Company stated that there is a total lack of interest in the market.
The Czech Republic's Securities Act mandates the Securities Registry to provide services related to securities transactions.
The Securities Registry does not disclose transaction details, which has led brokers to prefer its privacy and faster settlement process.
The average daily stock turnover on the Prague Stock Exchange is $4-$6 million, compared to $15 million in Warsaw.
Miroslav Nosal of Patria Finance noted that many foreign investors are dissatisfied with the Czech capital market.

A Czech central bank scheme aims to buy doubtful debts of smaller banks to restore stability to the banking sector.
About 10 banks have expressed interest in the scheme, according to the Czech news agency CTK.
Martin Svehla is a spokesman for the Czech National Bank (CNB).
The CNB outlined the programme in mid-October following the failure of Kreditni Banka in August.
The failure of Kreditni Banka was the 11th bank intervention by the CNB.
The plan is open to small private banks with total paid-in capital of 12.5 billion crowns and total assets of not more than 30 billion crowns.
Konsolidacni Banka will buy the banks' doubtful assets at face value.
Participating banks must follow strict conditions and allow the central bank to make management changes.
Banks must adhere to a three-year stabilisation plan and maintain an eight percent capital adequacy ratio.
The maximum purchase of debt by Konsolidacni can total up to 110 percent of a single bank's paid-in capital.

Czechs had a low voter turnout for the Senate elections on Saturday.
The elections were seen as a key test for Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's minority government.
Early results indicated that Klaus's Civic Democratic Party (ODS) was leading in some constituencies but did not secure a majority.
Foreign Minister Josef Zieleniec expressed caution about the results despite some ODS candidates advancing to the next round.
Turnout figures ranged from 26.36 percent in Most to 29.78 percent in Ostrava.
Ales Kaspar from the Central Electoral Commission predicted that nationwide turnout would be the lowest in four parliamentary elections since 1989.
Optimistic forecasts suggested that turnout could be between 30 and 40 percent.
Opposition Social Democrat leader Milos Zeman criticized voter apathy and predicted higher turnout in the second round.
Zeman stated that non-voters do not have the right to criticize the government.
Share dealers reacted positively to early results indicating a good performance for ODS.

Senate runoff elections on Friday and Saturday are expected to have little impact on Czech capital markets.
Investors are focusing on macroeconomic fundamentals rather than political influences.
Last weekend's first round of voting provided a mild boost to the Czech crown and the Prague Stock Exchange.
Analysts believe that unless the results from the second round of voting vary greatly, no further boost should be expected.
Jay King of Wood and Company stated that the elections will be a non-event for foreign investors.
In the first round of voting, Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's Civic Democratic Party (ODS) received over 36.5 percent of the national vote.
The opposition Social Democrats (CSSD) received 20.3 percent of the vote.
Only 35 percent of the electorate participated in the voting.
The ODS won three outright Senate seats in the first round and has 76 candidates going into the runoff.
The CSSD has 48 candidates going into the runoff.

The three-party coalition of right-wing Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus won a majority of seats in the Senate during run-off elections.
The premier's Civic Democratic Party (ODS) won 32 seats in the Senate.
The Social Democrats, the strongest opposition party, secured 25 seats.
The Christian Democrats, a junior coalition partner, won 13 seats.
The Civic Democratic Alliance, the third party in the government, won seven seats.
The Communists won two seats and two seats went to independents.
The coalition parties secured a total of 52 seats in the Senate.
Voter turnout in the second round was around 30 percent.
The turnout in the first round was 35 percent.
Milos Zeman, chairman of the Social Democrats, expressed satisfaction that the Senate would not be dominated by a single party.

Czech shares rose on Monday after the coalition government's win in Senate elections.
Analysts attributed the rise to a technical correction rather than a change in investor sentiment.
The Prague Stock Exchange's PX50 index increased by 0.82 percent.
Seven of the eight most-capitalised shares contributed to the index's rise.
Brokers expressed limited optimism that the rally would last beyond a few days.
The centre-right government's performance was anticipated and already factored into the market.
Jay King of Wood and Company stated that the rally was technically led and not related to the Senate elections.
A local trader noted that the price increase was driven by year-end anticipation and was domestically motivated.
The minority coalition led by Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus secured 52 of 81 seats in the Senate.
The centre-left opposition Social Democrats won 25 seats in the Senate elections.

Markets in Eastern Europe are experiencing an autumn slump.
Analysts see little potential for improvement in the bearish trend.
Stock exchanges in Warsaw, Prague, Bratislava, Bucharest, Zagreb, and Ljubljana all lost ground this week.
The Budapest Stock Exchange rose slightly but lost momentum by the end of the week.
The PX50 index on the Prague Stock Exchange dipped 0.8 points to close at 509.3.
The centre-right governing coalition in the Czech Republic performed well in Senate elections.
Investors are concerned about poor market regulation in the Czech Republic.
Analysts are divided on the direction of the Warsaw Stock Exchange.
Some analysts believe the Warsaw Stock Exchange could remain in a horizontal trend.
Hungarian shares initially rose due to a government decision to hike energy prices but lost momentum mid-week.

A purge at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell is expected next week for managers responsible for failing to identify irregular dealings by Peter Young.
Deutsche Bank's investment banking arm is completing a preliminary report with Ernst & Young regarding internal issues that led to the suspension of three MGAM funds.
Three Morgan Grenfell Asset Management funds, totaling around 1.4 billion pounds, were temporarily suspended in September but resumed after a 180 million pounds cash injection from Deutsche Bank.
Peter Young's assets have been frozen and his passport impounded as he is under investigation by Britain's Serious Fraud Office.
Young claims he is not guilty of any criminal activity and asserts he is being made a scapegoat for failings.
An investigation into Young's management of two funds, which held a high proportion of unlisted, speculative stocks, has been ongoing since issues arose.
Both MGAM and the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation are conducting inquiries with forensic accountants analyzing the funds' trading history.
IMRO's investigation may result in significant penalties against MGAM and will take longer to conclude.
Keith Percy's position as head of the asset management arm is under review, with conflicting reports about potential actions against him.
Other key managers, including Glyn Owen and Mike Wheatley, are likely to face scrutiny due to their executive responsibilities.

Britain's largest cable operator was formed from the merger of the British operations of Cable & Wireless, NYNEX Corp, and Bell Canada International.
The merger took five weeks to complete.
The merger includes C&W's Mercury, Videotron, Bell Cablemedia, and NYNEX CableComms.
The new company surpasses Telewest as Britain's biggest cable operator.
Richard Brown is the chief executive of C&W and was appointed five months prior to the merger.
C&W replaced BT in a major German alliance with RWE.
The merged company will provide integrated telecommunications, information, and entertainment services.
The merger will give C&W's Mercury access to 18 million business and domestic customers.
30 percent of homes that can take cable have opted for one or more cable services.
The Cable Communications Association stated that the broadband fibre optic network in the UK is the most advanced in the world for delivery to individual homes.

The Big Bang maintained London as one of the world's financial hubs.
Specialised financial boutiques are under pressure from large integrated investment banks.
The Big Bang of 1986 allowed mergers between merchant banks, brokers, and stock jobbers.
Traditional firms such as Wedd Durlacher Mordaunt and Phillips and Drew were absorbed by larger banks.
Investment banking giants have been acquiring smaller firms since the Big Bang.
Corporate financiers believe the trend of smaller firms being acquired by larger firms will continue.
The need for a large broking arm is increasing in corporate finance.
Regulatory demands for capital have reduced opportunities for boutique firms.
European integration poses a threat to corporate finance boutiques due to increased bureaucracy.
Greater research capabilities and legal support are required for advising on takeovers.

Britain's Invesco Plc agreed to merge with AIM Management Group Inc. in a deal valued at $1.6 billion.
The combined entity will be called Amvesco Plc and will manage around $150 billion.
The merger will be financed with approximately $1.1 billion in new stock and the remainder in cash and debt.
Invesco's chief financial officer is Bob McCullough, who stated that the merger is a prototype for future companies.
Invesco Chairman Charles Brady will lead the combined group.
AIM shareholders will own around 45 percent of the merged company.
The merger will involve issuing 290 million new shares to AIM shareholders, valued at about $1.1 billion.
An additional $500 million needed for the merger will come from cash and debt.
Invesco will continue to operate as a 'no-load' house, while AIM will sell its funds through brokers.
The merger is expected to enhance the group's strength in the United States and lead to cost savings.

Top managers in major financial firms need to be highly competent for smooth market operations.
Alistair Darling is a spokesman on treasury affairs for Britain's opposition Labour party.
Darling stated that management sets the ethos of a company.
Darling cited examples of rule-breaking by 'rogue traders' as signs of management failure.
Christine Cumming is a senior vice president at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
Cumming expressed doubts about management's ability to handle regulatory issues.
Cumming stated that the health of an institution depends on its management and directors.
Darling indicated that the British regulatory system would be reformed after the next general election.
Darling emphasized that the reform would not involve dramatic changes.
Angela Knight is Britain's economic secretary to the Treasury.

British merchant bank Hambros reported a return to first-half profit.
Hambros reported pretax profits of 35.0 million pounds for the first half.
This profit compares to a 7.7 million pound loss for the same period in 1995.
Sir Chips Keswick is the chief executive of Hambros.
Regent Pacific Group is a Hong Kong investment manager that holds three percent of Hambros.
Regent Pacific Group has called for the breakup of Hambros to realize shareholder value.
Hambros' interim dividend was unchanged at 2.5 pence.
Bad debt provisions for Hambros were 5.9 million pounds for the period.
This is a decrease from 23.5 million pounds in the same period in 1995.
Keswick stated that the group was on track to replace low margin business with higher return business.

Robert Fleming announced increased pre-tax profits for the first half of the year.
Robert Fleming reported a 16 percent increase in pretax profit to 92.2 million pounds from 79.4 million pounds a year earlier.
A spokesman for Robert Fleming stated the results demonstrated the bank's ability to remain independent.
Robert Fleming has been considered a potential takeover target by larger foreign investment banks.
Chief executive John Manser described the profit increase as a 'very good start' and noted new businesses contributed to profitability.
Manser warned of challenges in the second half due to flat Asian markets and competitive pressures.
Robert Fleming's spokesman indicated the bank is now a more international operation and has improved its cost income ratio.
Robert Fleming faced challenges in the past year, including the loss of investment banking head Bill Harrison to BZW.
Jardine Fleming, a joint venture with Jardine Matheson, was subject to a regulatory probe resulting in fines and compensation of nearly $20 million.
Robert Fleming acknowledged that the issues at Jardine Fleming led to a marginally lower interim result than in 1995.

3i Group Plc reported a rise in first half net asset value (NAV) per share to 454 pence from 426 pence in the first half of last year.
3i Group Plc's profit before tax rose to 62.9 million pounds from 54.3 million pounds.
Ewen Macpherson, 3i's chief executive, stated that the company's performance was held back by continental Europe and the appreciation of sterling.
Macpherson noted that the British portfolio performed extremely well, with an 18 percent growth in revenue.
3i Group Plc invested 327 million pounds during the period, with 284 million pounds invested in Britain.
Macpherson indicated that the prospect of a general election in Britain by May 1997 created investment opportunities as some company founders decided to sell their holdings.
Macpherson mentioned that current pricing levels for small and medium-sized European companies were very attractive.
During the first half of the year, 3i Group Plc realized investments worth 122 million pounds in Britain and 36 million pounds in continental Europe.
3i Group Plc plans to expand in Europe by opening an office in Duesseldorf and additional offices in Hamburg, Munich, and Stuttgart.
3i Group Plc intends to open its first office in Southeast Asia, in Singapore, early in 1997.

Greycoat is a British property company.
Greycoat faced a merger proposal from Moorfield Estates.
Greycoat shareholders voted against a breakup resolution proposed by the UK Active Value Fund (UKAV).
95 percent of Greycoat shareholders who voted opposed the sale of the company's assets.
The vote against the breakup resolution represented 55 percent of Greycoat's share capital.
Greycoat's assets are valued at 500 million pounds ($811.6 million).
Greycoat shares closed at 163.5 pence.
UKAV is advised by Brian Myerson's Active Value Advisers.
UKAV abstained at the reconvened extraordinary general meeting.
Moorfield Estates proposed a merger that it believes could benefit Greycoat shareholders.

Members of the Transport and General Workers Union (T&G) at Tradeteam are to vote on strike action over proposed pay cuts.
The ballot of more than 1,000 workers at Tradeteam will start on December 9 and the result will be known on December 20.
Bass Plc stated there is no threat to the delivery of drinks to its customers during the Christmas period.
The T&G's ballot is proceeding after a legal injunction attempt by Tradeteam to halt it failed.
Tradeteam is a joint venture between Bass and NFC.
The T&G claims that management has been trying to cut wages by 100 stg per week and impose inferior working conditions.
The T&G stated that Tradeteam rejected attempts to establish national bargaining.
A Liverpool judge refused to grant an injunction to stop the ballot.
Bass Brewers Ltd made over 157 million pounds profit over the last year.
Tradeteam, which is 50.1 percent owned by NFC, denied that a trade dispute exists with the T&G.

Britain's Takeover Panel is a non-statutory body that oversees London's mergers and acquisitions market.
The panel has been campaigning against a European Union proposal on takeover bids in 1996.
The panel claims the EU proposal will lead to lawsuits and harm London's takeover regulation system.
CE Electric made a bid for Northern Electric, which has drawn scrutiny on the panel's role.
Northern Electric made a payment of 250,000 pounds to BZW, an advisor in the bid process.
BZW stated that the payment was discretionary and not linked to its purchase of Northern shares.
The panel extended the deadline for acceptances after being informed of the payment.
CE Electric achieved 50.13 percent support from Northern shareholders after the deadline extension.
Northern Electric expressed a desire to appeal the panel's decision regarding the bid.
Changes to the panel's operations may require government legislation or internal adjustments.

Britain's commercial property market is expected to improve in 1996.
Property experts do not anticipate a return to the boom of the 1980s.
David Hutchings of Healey & Baker predicts real rental growth of three percent in 1997.
Hutchings forecasts total returns of 15-17 percent for institutional quality portfolios in 1997.
The expected returns may exceed those of gilts and possibly equities.
Uncertainty ahead of a general election suggests a gradual upturn rather than a market boom.
There are improved signs of demand for office space in central London and retail developments.
A survey by the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) and Grimley found that 32 percent of firms expect to increase property holdings in the next six months.
The CBI/Grimley survey indicates that larger companies will lead growth in the commercial property market.
The survey predicts that growth will be strongest in the northwest of England.

Beijing's top negotiator with Taipei is Tang Shubei, vice-chairman of the Association for Relations Across the Taiwan Straits.
Tang Shubei stated that Taiwan's fears of being absorbed by China if it lifts the ban on direct trade and transport links are ridiculous.
Taiwan has banned direct air and shipping links with China since 1949.
Taiwan allows indirect links through Hong Kong or third countries.
Taiwanese businessmen have invested over $20 billion in China.
Many Taiwanese businessmen want direct transport links with China, but Taiwan authorities are hesitant to lift the ban.
Tang Shubei claimed that scrapping the ban would benefit both sides and that Taiwan would incur greater losses than China if it resisted direct links.
China introduced regulations in August to facilitate direct shipping links with Taiwan.
China first called on Taiwan to lift the ban 17 years ago.
Tang Shubei mentioned that the ban would effectively be lifted in mid-1997 when Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule.

Wang Dan has been charged with plotting to overthrow the government.
Wang Dan's mother, Wang Lingyun, plans to defend him against the capital charge.
Wang Lingyun is a 61-year-old researcher at a museum with no legal background.
Chinese laws permit family members to defend accused individuals.
A court spokeswoman confirmed the charge against Wang Dan but did not provide further details.
Wang Dan's trial date has not been confirmed, but it may occur as early as this week.
Wang Dan has been detained without charge since May 1995.
Wang Dan met his mother for the first time under police surveillance at a detention center in Beijing.
Wang Lingyun expressed concern for her son's health and stated that he is psychologically prepared for a heavy sentence.
Wang Dan has been accused of collaborating with overseas subversive forces, which Wang Lingyun disputes.

China sent a senior official to a reception at the Ukraine embassy on Friday.
The reception was held to mark Ukraine's independence day.
There was confusion over the guest list regarding who would represent Beijing.
Ukraine's ambassador expected Chinese Vice-Foreign Minister Tian Zengpei to attend.
The Chinese expected Vice-Foreign Minister Zhang Deguang to attend.
Zhang Deguang fell ill, and Vice-Foreign Minister Tang Jiaxuan attended instead.
Taiwan Vice President Lien Chan's visit to Ukraine angered Beijing.
Ukrainian Minister-Counsellor Leonid Leshchenko described the guest list confusion as a misunderstanding.
A Chinese Foreign Ministry protocol officer stated that Tian was abroad.
Tang Jiaxuan was filling in for Tian and was higher in rank than Zhang Deguang.

China demanded that the United States cancel plans to sell Stinger missiles and other weapons to Taiwan.
A Foreign Ministry spokesman stated that the U.S. should cancel the missile sale to prevent new damage to Sino-U.S. relations.
Beijing considers Taiwan a renegade province since the end of the civil war in 1949.
China opposes the sale of weapons to Taiwan.
The U.S. Defence Department notified Congress of plans to sell Stinger missiles and other weapons to Taiwan.
U.S. officials claimed the weapons were defensive and would not affect the military balance in the region.
Taiwan requested to buy 1,299 Stinger missiles, 74 guided missile launchers, and other military equipment for an estimated $420 million.
The principal contractors for the sale include Hughes Missile Systems Co., Boeing Missile and Space Systems Co., and AM General.
Sales must be made through the U.S. Defence Department, and Congress must be notified for potential veto.
Sino-U.S. relations have fluctuated due to various disputes, including human rights abuses and nuclear proliferation.

The mayor of Beijing, Li Qiyan, resigned on Tuesday.
Li Qiyan's resignation was expected following the downfall of his mentor, Chen Xitong.
The Beijing People's Congress approved Li Qiyan's resignation.
Li Qiyan will become secretary of the Labour Ministry's Communist Party committee.
Li Qiyan may eventually replace Li Boyong as labour minister.
Li Qiyan was forced to resign due to his close links to Chen Xitong.
Chen Xitong resigned as Beijing party boss in April 1995 after a corruption scandal.
Jia Qinglin was appointed as vice and acting mayor of Beijing.
Jia Qinglin was previously the party secretary of Fujian province.
He Guoqiang was appointed as the new governor of Fujian province.

China called on Taiwan to lift a ban on direct trade and transport links.
China stated that attempts by Taiwan to block these links would be futile.
The Xinhua news agency commented that obstructing trade and transport links is against the will of the people on both sides.
China introduced regulations to facilitate direct shipping links last week.
Taiwan has banned direct trade, transport, and mail links with China since 1949.
Indirect links between Taiwan and China have been allowed since the late 1980s through Hong Kong or a third country.
The commentary accused Taiwan authorities of creating obstacles to direct trade and transport links.
China regards Taiwan as a renegade province and has threatened invasion if Taiwan declares independence.
Many Taiwanese businessmen support direct trade and transport links with China.
Taiwan views the ban as its last bargaining chip in negotiations with China.

Two Chinese magazines are struggling for survival due to a campaign by China's propaganda officials to eliminate liberal influences from the media.
'Focus' magazine in Shenzhen has suspended publication for two issues after a Hong Kong newspaper reported on its cover story about the Cultural Revolution.
The Propaganda Department of the Communist Party disapproves of any commemoration of the Cultural Revolution.
A writer for 'Focus' stated that the suspension was a consequence of the Hong Kong newspaper report.
Li Mei, the publisher of 'Focus', claimed that the suspension was due to unrelated financial issues.
Other sources indicated that 'Focus' faced problems due to the Communist Party's crackdown on publications that deviate from state-approved content.
Propaganda officials stated that any publication that diverges from the party line will be suspended for restructuring.
The fate of the Beijing-based magazine 'Orient' is under discussion due to its publication of book reviews on Gu Zhun's works.
The Propaganda Department has prohibited debate on Gu Zhun's thoughts, as he was critical of totalitarianism and supported civil rights.
The fifth edition of 'Orient' was published in September under censorship, and its future editions are uncertain.

China has vowed to curb the influence of Buddhism in Tibet.
China stated that religion must bow to socialism.
Monks outnumbered students in Tibet.
More money was spent on monasteries than on Communist Party buildings in Tibet.
There were 1,787 temples in Tibet by early 1996.
Tibet had 46,000 monks and nuns, exceeding the number of high school students.
China has shut many temples in Tibet in recent years.
The Dalai Lama fled into exile in India in 1959 after an uprising against communist rule.
Beijing views the Dalai Lama as a political activist.
The Dalai Lama won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989 for his campaign for autonomy for Tibet.

A Chinese court will consider the appeal of dissident Wang Dan against his 11-year sentence for plotting to overthrow the government.
The Beijing Higher People's Court is expected to reject Wang Dan's appeal and uphold his conviction.
Appellate courts in China rarely overturn rulings made by lower courts.
Wang Dan's mother, Wang Lingyun, expressed doubt about the chances of an acquittal, stating there is no precedent.
Wang Dan's appeal is scheduled to be heard four days before the visit of U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher.
U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher is expected to raise human rights issues during his meetings with Chinese leaders.
Sino-U.S. relations have been strained over various issues, including human rights and trade.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Cui Tiankai stated that Wang Dan's trial does not affect Sino-U.S. relations.
Former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher expressed dismay over the harsh sentences imposed on Wang Dan and Wei Jingsheng.
Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson communicated his concerns about Wang Dan's imprisonment to Chinese Premier Li Peng.

A Tibetan nun named Ngawang Sangdrol has had her jail term doubled to 18 years.
Ngawang Sangdrol is 19 years old and has been jailed since she was 15.
Her sentence was doubled in July for refusing to accept Beijing's choice as the reincarnation of the Panchen Lama.
Ngawang Sangdrol is facing more time in jail than any other female political prisoner in Tibet.
She is due for release in the year 2010.
Officials in Lhasa denied knowledge of the report regarding her sentence.
The 10th Panchen Lama died in 1989, and Beijing has named a six-year-old boy as his reincarnation.
The Dalai Lama has named another six-year-old boy as the 11th Panchen Lama.
Beijing's choice is under state protection in the Chinese capital.
China denies the existence of political prisoners in Tibet.

China's breakaway Catholic Church has ordained about 50 graduates of a major seminary into the priesthood this year.
The new priests were the first group installed by the National Catholic Seminary since 1991.
The officially authorised seminary in Beijing did not accept new students for six years from 1986 due to a lack of funds and space.
The seminary receives 10,000 yuan ($1,200) a year from the government, which is one-sixth of its annual budget.
The seminary raises the remainder of its budget from donations.
Father Meng stated there is no shortage of youths who want to become priests.
Catholics in communist China can only worship openly if they belong to the state-sponsored Catholic Patriotic Association.
The Catholic Patriotic Association supervises the national seminary and does not recognize the Pope as the universal Catholic leader.
Human Rights Watch/Asia reported that Beijing has increased harassment of unauthorized Catholic and Protestant groups in recent years.
Bishop Zong Huaide of the state-backed church ordained five graduates of the seminary on Sunday.

China has retired its navy and air force commanders due to old age.
Admiral Zhang Lianzhong and Lieutenant General Yu Zhenwu, both 65, have stepped down as navy and air force commanders respectively.
Zhang was replaced by navy deputy commander Rear Admiral Shi Yunsheng, who is 56 years old.
Yu was succeeded by air force deputy commander Liu Shunyao, who is believed to be in his early 50s.
Communist Party boss Jiang Zemin approved the reshuffle in October as chairman of the party's Central Military Commission.
The source stated that Zhang and Yu retired due to old age and described the reshuffle as professionalisation of the military.
A Chinese analyst noted that the four vice-chairmen of the Central Military Commission are aged between 67 and 82 and still active.
Both new appointees, Shi and Liu, are believed to be proteges of Jiang.
Jiang ordered the promotions of Shi and Yu to deputy commanders in January 1995 and December 1994 respectively.
The People's Liberation Army (PLA) is the world's largest armed force with three million members and plans to reduce its size by 500,000.

A Chinese court has sentenced Zhang Zong'ai to five years in prison for subversion.
The Intermediate People's Court in Xi'an convicted Zhang of spreading counter-revolutionary propaganda and incitement.
Zhang Zong'ai has been detained since June and has appealed to the Shaanxi provincial Higher People's Court.
A spokesman for the Hong Kong-based Human Rights and Democracy in China Information Centre stated that the Chinese authorities aim to intimidate other dissidents.
Zhang Zong'ai was previously jailed for five years for demanding the impeachment of Premier Li Peng in relation to the Tiananmen Square protests in June 1989.
Zhang lost his position in the local lawmaking body, his teaching job, and his wife divorced him after his 1989 incarceration.
Zhang's sister, Zhang Xin, claimed he was innocent and had been wrongly accused.
Zhang's lawyer stated that the court found him guilty of attacking China's judiciary in an interview published in a Hong Kong newspaper.
Wang Dan, a former student leader of the 1989 democracy demonstrations, was sentenced to 11 years in prison for conspiring to subvert the government.
The court found Zhang guilty of signing a petition urging political tolerance but cleared him of wrongdoing regarding accepting money from an overseas group.

Rupert Murdoch predicted that News Corp Ltd would boost profits by 20 percent this year.
Murdoch stated that News Corp would win its legal battle with Ted Turner and Time Warner.
Murdoch visited Australia for News' annual meeting.
Murdoch expressed that he did not want to buy out John Fairfax Holdings Ltd.
News Corp publishes major tabloid newspapers in Sydney and Melbourne, as well as the Courier Mail and The Australian.
News Corp owns about five percent of Fairfax.
Murdoch is confident that News Corp will win its lawsuit against Turner and Time Warner.
Murdoch claimed that Time Warner's decision not to carry News' Fox News Service stifled competition.
Murdoch stated that News Corp is claiming US$1 billion in damages from Time Warner and Turner.
Turner described Murdoch's lawsuit as a 'frivolous piece of junk.'

News Corp Ltd announced plans to run its finances more conservatively.
Analysts welcomed News Corp's new financial strategy.
Rupert Murdoch is the chief executive and chairman of News Corp.
News Corp has over US$2.5 billion in cash after a recent bond issue.
Murdoch stated that News Corp aims to remain viable, profitable, strong, and liquid.
News Corp plans to finance its multi-billion dollar pay television network projects from cash flow.
Murdoch emphasized the need to maintain liquidity for new acquisitions.
Analysts noted that the new strategy contrasts with News Corp's previous large acquisitions and debt issues.
News Corp's earlier issue of preference shares to fund a buyout upset many investors.
Analysts believe Murdoch's approach indicates that any future acquisitions will be small.

Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd (ANZ) denied a newspaper report about investigating a A$24 billion merger with Britain's Standard Chartered Plc.
ANZ stated that it is not investigating or discussing a merger with Standard Chartered Bank.
ANZ issued a statement to the Australian Stock Exchange before the start of trade.
ANZ typically does not comment on rumors and speculation regarding mergers and acquisitions.
The Australian Financial Review reported that ANZ and Standard Chartered had engaged Goldman Sachs and Swiss Bank Corp for a feasibility study into a merger.
The merger was compared to the RTZ-CRA stock stapling, which created a dual-listed company and the world's biggest mining group.
The Financial Review suggested that such an alliance would make ANZ almost takeover-proof in Australia.
There are no cross-shareholdings between ANZ and Standard Chartered.
KPMG was employed to carry out due diligence on the proposed merger.
Analysts indicated that ANZ's share price could drop sharply due to the merger report.

Memtec Ltd attempted a US$280 million takeover of Gelman Sciences Inc.
Memtec chairman Denis Hanley stated that the failed takeover will not impact earnings or U.S. expansion plans.
A compensation clause in the original takeover deal protects Memtec's earnings for the year ending June 30, 1997.
Gelman Sciences agreed to be taken over by Memtec, which offered 1.05 Memtec American Depositary Receipts for each Gelman share.
The offer valued each Gelman share at approximately US$35.
Memtec's share price fell after the announcement of the takeover bid.
The agreement allowed Gelman to renegotiate or terminate the deal if Memtec's share price fell below US$30.
Gelman accepted a takeover bid from Pall Corp, valuing Gelman's shares at US$33 per share.
Memtec announced it would not increase its bid after the termination of the original merger agreement.
Memtec's shares increased by A$3.50 to A$41.50 following the end of the Gelman deal.

Geoff Tomlinson is the managing director of National Mutual Holdings Ltd.
Tomlinson stated that strong investment markets indicated group earnings for the 1996/97 year would likely align with July prospectus forecasts.
Tomlinson mentioned that the year had been favorable for their type of business.
He could not provide a formal profit forecast for the year ending September 30.
Tomlinson suggested that the assumptions in National Mutual's share offer document indicated the forecasts were likely to be met.
National Mutual forecasted a consolidated net profit after tax of A$198 million for the year ending September 30.
This forecast represented an increase from A$115.5 million in 1994/95.
The assumptions for the forecast included a 90 day bill rate of 7.5 percent, a 10-year bond rate of 8.75 percent, and a U.S. 10 year bond rate of 6.50 percent, all as of September 30.
The offer document stated that National Mutual's profit was not significantly sensitive to stock market assumptions.

Westpac Banking Corp Ltd announced a 19.5 percent rise in net profit for the 1995/96 year.
Westpac warned that fierce competition would flatten profits in the year ahead.
Westpac reported a net profit of A$1.132 billion for the year to September 30, 1996.
The profit increase was attributed to a sharp drop in bad debt charges.
Competition from non-bank mortgage originators is pressuring Westpac's margins.
Non-bank mortgage originators have captured 10 percent of the mortgage market from big banks.
Westpac plans to boost its mortgage origination program to compete against non-banks.
Westpac launched a securitised mortgage issue worth A$340 million.
Westpac's share price closed down 15 cents at A$7.05 after the profit announcement.
Westpac is the second major bank to forecast flat profits in the year ahead.

The Brunei Investment Agency (BIA) purchased a 13.4 percent stake in Macquarie Bank Ltd.
The purchase by BIA removed the links between Macquarie Bank and its British founder.
BIA paid Lloyds TSB Plc A$151.7 million (US$122.8 million) for the stake.
The purchase was made by BIA's Brunei Investment and Commercial Bank (BICB).
BICB became the largest individual shareholder in Macquarie Bank as a result of the purchase.
Macquarie Bank managing director Allan Moss stated that the bank had developed a good relationship with BIA.
Moss expressed confidence that BICB would be a constructive and long-term investor in Macquarie.
The purchase ended Hill Samuel's 27-year direct involvement in the Australian investment banking sector.
Hill Samuel established Macquarie Bank in 1969 and reduced its stake over the years.
Macquarie Bank has 1,800 staff and is listed on the Australian Stock Exchange.

A survey by BIS Shrapnel found that Australia's wealthy baby-boomers are disillusioned with bank services.
The survey indicated that loyalty is not rewarded by banks according to the respondents.
Those approaching retirement expressed dissatisfaction with their superannuation funds and are considering moving to other options.
The survey included 128 participants aged over 45 from 14 separate focus groups across Australia.
Respondents had assets worth over A$150,000, excluding their family homes.
Participants sought more individual treatment from knowledgeable staff in banking.
Geoff Ludowyke, the survey project leader, stated that those nearing retirement equate good service with personal contact.
The Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA) was identified as the least liked bank in the survey.
Respondents described CBA as slower, more unfriendly, more impersonal, and less modern than other banks.
Westpac Banking Corp Ltd was ranked as the next least liked bank after CBA.

Brambles Industries Ltd is based in Australia.
Brambles is considering acquisitions in the United States, Europe, and Asia in the current year.
John Fletcher is the chief executive of Brambles.
Brambles will only consider acquisitions in areas where it has Australian experience.
Brambles is looking to participate in the privatization of Australia's airports before June next year.
The vehicle for airport investment will be Brambles' joint venture company, Australian Airport Services, formed with Lend Lease Corp Ltd.
Brambles is looking at acquisitions in the Northern Hemisphere in industrial services, waste management, equipment rentals, and records management.
Brambles reported a 120.2 percent increase in net profit to A$215.1 million for the year ending June 30, 1996.
Before abnormals, net profit rose 15.8 percent to A$214.8 million.
Strong growth in earnings from Brambles' CHEP pallet business in the United States contributed to the results.

TNT Ltd reported an annual profit slump on Wednesday.
TNT Ltd plans to sell its troubled airline and implement other reforms to achieve profit growth in the current year.
TNT's net profit for the year to June 30 fell to A$9.84 million from A$40.01 million in 1994/95 and A$105.05 million in 1993/94.
David Mortimer stated that profits from Australia's Ansett Airlines and losses from Brazilian operations offset revenue growth in TNT's core operations.
Profits from TNT's core activities of domestic and international time-sensitive freight and logistics grew 48.7 percent to A$165.3 million in 1995/96.
TNT has moved to eliminate loss-making units and focus on profitable core activities.
TNT has closed its Australian LCL business and sold its operations in Brazil.
TNT plans to sell other unprofitable non-core businesses.
TNT announced plans to sell its stake in Ansett to Air New Zealand Ltd for A$325 million.
The remaining non-core activities of TNT include an airline leasing company, shipping operations, a mono-rail in Sydney, and some IT assets.

TNT Ltd reported an annual profit decline on Wednesday.
TNT Ltd plans to sell its troubled airline and implement reforms to achieve profit growth in the current year.
TNT's net profit for the year ending June 30 fell to A$9.84 million from A$40.01 million in 1994/95 and A$105.05 million in 1993/94.
David Mortimer stated that profits from Australia's Ansett Airlines and losses from Brazilian operations offset revenue growth in core operations.
Profits from TNT's core activities of domestic and international time-sensitive freight and logistics grew 48.7 percent to A$165.3 million in 1995/96.
TNT is focusing on profitable core activities and has moved to eliminate loss-making units.
TNT has closed its Australian LCL business and sold its operations in Brazil.
TNT plans to sell other unprofitable, non-core businesses.
TNT announced plans to sell its stake in Ansett to Air New Zealand Ltd for A$325 million.
The remaining non-core activities of TNT include an airline leasing company, shipping operations, a mono-rail in Sydney, and some IT assets.

News Corp Ltd must report a higher second quarter profit to achieve its 20 percent growth target for the 1996/97 year.
Analysts expect News Corp to report a second quarter net profit before abnormals of between A$450 million and A$490 million.
This would bring first half net profits to between A$735 million and A$775 million.
The first quarter net profit was A$285 million, and the first half profit would be up 17 percent from A$663 million in the first half of 1995/96.
Strong receipts from the movie 'Independence Day' and firm U.S. television revenue are expected to drive the stronger result.
The market is demanding a strong second quarter figure after previous below-expectation results.
The extent of any fall in News Corp shares will depend on how far earnings fall short of expectations.
News Corp's first half must be 15 to 20 percent better to achieve the forecast of a 20 percent improvement in profits.
Analysts expect revenues from Australian newspapers, magazines, and the Ansett airline operation to remain weak in the second quarter.
A presentation to analysts and investors on February 24 in Los Angeles is expected to influence the results positively.

Most banks in the U.S. Midwest are expected to post third quarter earnings gains of 10 percent or more.
The strong economy is generating loan growth, cost-cutting programs are showing results, and credit quality remains reasonably sound.
Michael Ancell, a banking analyst at Edward D. Jones, expects the banks he follows to have average earnings gains of 11 percent.
Analysts have been waiting to see deterioration in credit quality, especially in credit card loans.
Some banks, like First Chicago NBD, showed a higher charge-off rate in credit card receivables in the second quarter.
James Schutz, a banking analyst at Chicago Corp, stated that he does not see large increases in loan loss provisions.
Many banks have been aggressively cutting costs, which should help third quarter results.
Firstar Corp is pointed out as a bank that could benefit from an aggressive cost-cutting plan.
Northern Trust Corp and Norwest Corp are also expected to have strong gains due to generating fee revenue.
Thomas Maier, a banking analyst at EVEREN Securities, emphasized the importance of expense controls and revenue growth.

Mercantile Bancorp Inc announced it could pursue additional acquisitions while completing its $855 million merger with Mark Twain Bancshares Inc.
John Beirise is the group president of Mercantile in charge of mergers and acquisitions.
Beirise stated that not all of Mercantile will be involved in the acquisition of Mark Twain, allowing for potential acquisitions in other locations.
Mercantile has been an active acquirer and is skilled at assimilating mergers.
Mercantile has $18.2 billion in assets and currently has four mergers pending.
The Mark Twain deal is expected to close in the second quarter of 1997 and involves an exchange of shares valued at $49.62 per Mark Twain share.
The price of the Mark Twain deal is 2.8 times Mark Twain's book value.
Mark Twain reported a return on average assets of 1.82 percent in the third quarter, which is above average for Midwest banks.
Beirise stated that Mercantile was not considering its potential as a takeover target when making the deal to acquire Mark Twain.
Mercantile is the second largest bank holding company in Missouri, behind Boatmen's Bancshares Inc.

Corporate financing for a downtown Detroit sports stadium complex is in place.
Land acquisition for the stadium complex is nearly complete.
Mayor Dennis Archer stated that they are close to making the stadium complex happen.
Archer mentioned that property could be taken by condemnation or eminent domain if necessary.
Pending legislation in the Michigan Legislature could facilitate the condemnation process.
Archer indicated that the deadline for the Detroit Tigers and Detroit Lions to commit to the stadium complex is flexible.
Lions President William Clay Ford Jr. stated that the true deadline is Monday.
Wayne County voters will decide on Tuesday whether to approve a tax to raise $80 million for the complex.
Ford emphasized that a complete accounting of the land is necessary before going to the voters.
The owner of a parcel housing the Gem Theatre is a major holdout in the land acquisition process.

Dayton Hudson Corp. is the nation's fourth-largest retailer.
Dayton Hudson Corp. reported higher third-quarter results.
Analysts project a strong holiday shopping season for the industry.
Women's retail chains Ann Taylor and The Limited reported higher results.
Howard Eilenberg is an analyst at Johnson Redbook Service.
Eilenberg predicts a 5-to-5-1/2 percent increase in sales over the previous year.
Dayton Hudson reported a 164 percent increase in operating earnings for its third quarter ended Nov. 2.
Dayton Hudson's operating earnings were $116 million, or 49 cents a share.
A year earlier, Dayton Hudson earned $44 million, or 18 cents a share.
Saul Yaari is a retail analyst at Piper Jaffray.

Dutch bank ABN AMRO Holding NV agreed to pay $1.9 billion to acquire Standard Federal Bancorp.
Standard Federal Bancorp owns the seventh-largest savings bank in the United States and the largest in Michigan.
ABN AMRO is offering $59 a share for Standard Federal Bancorp, which has $15.5 billion in assets.
Standard Federal Bancorp is based in Troy, Michigan and owns Standard Federal Bank.
Standard Federal Bank operates about 180 bank branches and 11 home lending centers.
Standard Federal Bank also operates a wholesale mortgage banking business.
SFB stock fell by $1.625 to $56.375 after the acquisition offer was announced.
Tony Howard, an analyst at Olde Discount Corp, stated that some investors were disappointed with the acquisition price.
ABN AMRO plans to issue $750 million in preferred stock to help fund the acquisition.
ABN AMRO North America Inc. is the U.S. subsidiary through which the shares will be issued.

Retailers are expected to post solid sales gains for November.
Industry analysts predict sales at stores open at least a year will rise 2.5 percent to 4.0 percent in November.
Clothing is expected to be a strong contributor to sales in November.
Paul Harris Stores Inc. reported a 26 percent increase in same-store sales for November compared to the previous year.
Harry Ikenson, a retail analyst at Rodman & Renshaw Inc., believes most companies will meet or exceed their sales plans for November.
Analysts expect profit margins to improve due to tight inventory management and discounts not being higher than last year.
Dean Ramos at Dain Bosworth Inc. indicated that his sales index could rise one to two points above the 3.1 percent increase reported last year.
Holiday sales are critical for retailers, who typically earn a significant portion of their annual profits during this season.
Retail consumer spending rose 4.3 percent during the post-Thanksgiving weekend, according to TeleCheck Services.
TeleCheck reported an overall same-store sales increase of 2.1 percent.

$9.5 billion is the proposed acquisition price of Boatmen's Bancshares Inc. by NationsBank Corp.
Missouri banks were protected from outside buyers by state regulations until last year.
Michael Ancell is a banking industry analyst at Edward D. Jones & Co.
Ancell stated that NationsBank acquired a significant banking entity in the Midwest.
Mercantile Bancorp Inc. is a St. Louis-based bank holding company with $18.04 billion in assets.
Commerce Bancshares Inc. is based in Kansas City, Mo., and has $9.32 billion in assets.
James Weber is an analyst at A.G. Edwards & Sons.
Roosevelt Financial Group Inc. is a St. Louis-based thrift with $9.33 billion in assets.
First Bank System Inc., Norwest Corp., KeyCorp, Banc One Corp., and First Chicago NBD Corp. are potential buyers interested in Missouri banks.
Boatmen's Bancshares Inc. has a presence in nine states and $41 billion in assets.

Retailers were seeking a last minute boost for holiday sales the day before Christmas.
Industry analysts reported that sales were near or slightly below expectations for the holiday shopping season.
Sales came in below retailers' expectations last week, according to a survey by BTM/Schroders.
Analyst Michael Niemira expected December sales to rise by 4 percent to 4.5 percent.
Earlier expectations for December sales were a rise of 4.5 percent to 5.0 percent.
Shopping activity increased on Monday and Tuesday as shoppers rushed to find last-minute gifts.
Karen Farnham, assistant manager at Abercrombie & Fitch Co., noted that Monday was likely the busiest day.
Store manager Christina Vigo at Limited Inc. reported that last-minute shopping was hectic.
Saul Yaari, senior retailing analyst at Piper Jaffray Inc., predicted sales would be about 5 percent above last year's results.
Sales at department stores slowed in the last week, while discounters performed well.

Magna Group Inc plans to acquire Homeland Bankshares Corp.
Analysts believe the acquisition will not affect Homeland Bankshares Corp's potential to be acquired.
Steven Schroll, a banking industry analyst at Piper Jaffray, stated that the acquisition does not make Homeland Bankshares Corp less attractive as a takeover candidate.
Magna is considered one of several Missouri-based banks likely to be acquisition targets.
Joseph Stieven, a banking analyst at Stifel Nicolaus, indicated that the acquisition does not significantly change the company's takeover prospects.
Iowa has a limit on the total deposits a single banking company can hold.
Magna's acquisition of Homeland could complicate potential buyers' ability to acquire Magna due to Iowa's deposit cap.
Schroll believes the proposed deal will add to Magna's earnings in 1997.
Schroll estimates the deal could be 15 cents accretive or more.
Homeland has a high ratio of equity to assets at 10.79 percent in the second quarter.

U.S. retailers reported overall sales near plan for December.
Sales results varied widely by store and sector.
Department stores appeared to take market share from specialty stores.
Michael Niemira is an analyst with Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi Ltd.
Michael Niemira stated that major retailers continue to gain market share.
Sears, Roebuck and Co was one of the better performers according to analysts.
Sears reported a 9.5 percent rise in domestic same-store sales.
Sears chairman Arthur Martinez stated that gross margins are favorable for December and the fourth quarter.
Sears stock increased by 1-1/8 to 46-3/8.
Other gainers included Paul Harris Stores Inc, Kohl's Corp, Dayton Hudson Corp, and Saks Holdings Inc.

Caterpillar Inc chief financial officer Douglas Oberhelman stated that an increase in U.S. dealer new machine inventories at the end of 1996 was intentional.
Oberhelman indicated that the inventory levels were higher than the previous year by design.
Caterpillar reported record net income of $381 million or $1.99 a share for the fourth quarter of 1996.
The fourth quarter net income was an increase from $300 million or $1.53 a share a year ago.
The company's outlook for 1997 profit levels was that they would approximate those of 1996.
Oberhelman defended the company's view of slowing U.S. economic growth despite analysts' concerns.
Caterpillar's total capital expenditures were $642 million in 1996 and are expected to rise 10 to 15 percent in 1997.
Research and development spending is expected to rise 20 percent from the $410 million spent in 1996.
Caterpillar plans to continue introducing about 50 new or upgraded products a year through 1999.
Caterpillar is looking to expand in the power generation equipment market, which is valued at $5 billion.

Wallace Computer Services Inc. announced that its directors will recommend shareholders reject a bid by Wyser-Pratte & Co. Inc.
Wyser-Pratte holds 2.3 percent of Wallace's outstanding shares.
Wyser-Pratte has proposed three candidates for the board of Wallace Computer Services Inc.
Wyser-Pratte seeks to remove Wallace's poison pill takeover defense, which requires an 80 percent vote for certain mergers.
Wyser-Pratte filed its proposals with the Securities and Exchange Commission after Moore Corp. Ltd. abandoned a $1.3 billion acquisition campaign for Wallace.
Wallace's board will recommend shareholders vote against Wyser-Pratte's proposals at the annual meeting on November 6.
Wallace stated that Wyser-Pratte attempted to contact three directors nominated by Moore at last year's annual meeting.
Guy Wyser-Pratte, president of Wyser-Pratte, stated he would continue to push his proposals.
Wallace reported a profit of $19.2 million for the fourth quarter ended July 31, an increase from $15.8 million in the previous year.
Wallace's sales rose 8.2 percent to $214.5 million from $198.2 million.

Mercury Finance Co. found problems in its bookkeeping that caused it to overstate earnings by $90 million over four years.
The chief accountant of Mercury Finance Co., James Doyle, has apparently disappeared.
The irregularities in Mercury Finance Co.'s financial records appear to have come from unauthorized entries by its chief accounting officer.
A special committee of the board has been formed to investigate the issues with legal and accounting experts.
James Doyle was last seen at Mercury Finance Co. on January 23, the day the company reported fourth quarter results.
Mercury Finance Co. stated that it is in violation of some of its debt agreements and is negotiating with lenders.
As a result of the adjustments, shareholders' equity as of December 31, 1996, would be reduced from $353 million to $263 million.
Mercury Finance Co. announced that its 1996 net income would be restated to $56.7 million from $120.7 million.
BankBoston Corp. will await the results of the accounting investigation before proceeding with the sale of Fidelity Acceptance Corp.
Mercury Finance Co. stock was halted all day on the New York Stock Exchange.

Canada's big six banks have extensive branch networks.
The rise of the Internet and virtual banks challenges the dominance of Canada's big six banks.
Technological advancements are transforming Canada's traditional banking system.
New technology reduces the need for physical branch networks in banking.
Canada's consumer banking market is valued at $66.5 billion.
Matthew Barrett, chairman of Bank of Montreal, expressed concerns about the future of branch networks.
The big banks in Canada are investing in new distribution channels and branch upgrades.
ING Groep N.V. is the largest electronic challenger in Canada's banking market.
Royal Bank of Canada is the largest financial institution in Canada with $147 billion in assets.
ING plans to offer electronic banking services through ING Trust Co. of Canada.

Shares in Molson Cos. Ltd. decreased on Monday after its Molson Breweries unit lost the rights to brew Coors Light.
Coors Light is Canada's top-selling light beer.
An arbitration panel ruled that Molson relinquished its right to brew and sell Coors products in April 1993.
The ruling was based on Molson breaching its licensing agreement with Coors by allowing Miller Brewing Co. to acquire a stake without Coors' consent.
Molson class A stock closed down C$0.75 at C$20.15 on the Toronto Stock Exchange.
Molson's stock had previously dropped to C$19.50, near its 52-week low.
The panel ordered Molson to pay Coors all profits earned from selling Coors beer since 1993.
Coors brands produced by Molson account for 8 percent of its sales volume.
Coors Light commands a 5 to 5.5 percent share of the Canadian beer market.
Molson officials expressed willingness to negotiate a new licensing agreement.

Protesters gathered in Toronto on Friday to protest budget cuts by Ontario's Conservative government.
The protests disrupted subway and bus services in Toronto, affecting about one million commuters.
Marilyn Bolton, a spokesperson for the Toronto Transit Commission, stated that service was postponed due to picketing.
Unionized workers, civil servants, and social activists participated in the protests, which were part of the 'Days of Protest.'
