Commuter trains from Toronto's bedroom communities and service at Pearson Airport were not disrupted by the protests.
The Toronto Stock Exchange opened as usual despite expectations of disruption from the protests.
Protesters are opposing Premier Mike Harris' plans to cut spending by C$8 billion to eliminate a deficit.
The Conservative government has implemented various policies since 1995, including changes to labor laws and cuts to welfare and education budgets.
Sid Ryan, president of the Ontario division of the Canadian Union of Public Employees, expressed that the cuts are harming workers and increasing anger in Ontario.
Despite the protests, the Conservative government's popularity remains around 50 percent in opinion polls.

Toronto stocks ended weaker on Friday amid profit taking.
The TSE 300 Composite Index fell 7.51 points to close at 5591.31.
The trading volume was 90.4 million shares valued at C$1.47 billion.
Declining stocks outpaced advances 473 to 435, with 289 issues unchanged.
Ira Katzin, an investment adviser with RBC Dominion Securities, stated that profit-taking was the story of the day.
The TSE posted its 50th record close on Thursday and broke through the 5600 barrier.
The TSE reached an intraday high of 5606 before declining.
Toronto's nine weak sectors included losses in consumer products, base metals, communications, and pipelines.
The five strong sectors were led by financial services.
Bank stocks rose due to firmer North American bond markets and expectations for a Bank of Canada rate cut.

Toronto stocks reached new highs on Wednesday due to a rally in bank shares.
Foreign investors entered Canada's financial markets, attracted by falling interest rates and a recovering economy.
Shares in Canada's big six banks hit 52-week highs on the Toronto Stock Exchange.
The Toronto Stock Exchange closed at around 5749 after gaining 85 points.
The Canadian dollar reached its strongest level since October 30, 1995.
The Bank of Canada has cut interest rates 19 times since May 1995.
Canada's inflation rate is 1.2 percent, which is lower than the U.S. rate.
Several Canadian banks reduced residential mortgage rates to levels not seen in about thirty years.
Michael Gregory, an economist with Lehman Brothers, stated that foreign investors are increasingly interested in Canada.
Canada is in a better position to withstand U.S. rate hikes than in previous years, according to Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen.

Stock in Canada's big banks fell on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Tuesday.
CIBC Wood Gundy cut its ratings on four of the Big Six banks.
National Bank of Canada received the only buy recommendation among the Big Six banks.
CIBC Wood Gundy analyst Mark Maxwell stated that recommendations on Canadian bank stocks were lowered from three buys to one buy.
Toronto's bank index increased by 46 percent in 1996.
The average valuation multiple for the group of Canadian bank stocks is 1.7 times book value.
Toronto's financial services group dropped 145 points, or 2.7 percent, on Tuesday.
Bank of Montreal's stock fell C$1.55 to C$42.15 on 1.5 million shares.
Bank of Nova Scotia's stock dropped C$1.85 to C$44.50 on 995,000 shares.
Royal Bank of Canada's stock decreased by C$1.30 to C$46 on 2.9 million shares.

Quarterback Doug Flutie led the Toronto Argonauts to a 43-37 victory over the Edmonton Eskimos.
The victory secured the championship of the Canadian Football League.
The Argonauts won their first CFL championship since 1991.
Doug Flutie was named the Grey Cup's most valuable player.
Flutie completed 22 of 35 passes for 302 yards and scored a touchdown.
Flutie won the CFL's most outstanding player award after leading the Argonauts to a 15-3 season.
The CFL's new salary cap may prevent Toronto from paying Flutie's annual salary of $1 million Canadian.
The Grey Cup game was played in snowy conditions at Hamilton's Ivor Wynne Stadium.
The game was the second-highest scoring Grey Cup game.
The Ottawa Rough Riders franchise folded at the end of the regular season.

Toronto-Dominion Bank reported a 15 percent increase in earnings for 1996.
TD Bank's net income for the year ended October 31 was C$914 million, up from C$794 million in 1995.
TD Bank increased its quarterly dividend by C$0.03 to C$0.28 per share.
Bank of Montreal and Bank of Nova Scotia also reported record full-year earnings.
Bank of Nova Scotia raised its dividend by C$0.03 per share to C$0.37 per share.
TD Bank's performance was attributed to strong growth in other income, particularly in investment banking, brokerage, and mutual fund businesses.
The bank's loan loss provision decreased to C$152 million in 1996 from C$180 million in 1995.
Net impaired loans in the fourth quarter fell by C$95 million to C$344 million.
Net impaired loans as a percentage of total loans and acceptances was 0.4 percent at year end.
TD Bank's stock rose by 0.80 to 37.65 on the Toronto Stock Exchange.

The Canadian Football League is searching for a new leader after CFL commissioner Larry Smith resigned.
Larry Smith resigned following a chaotic, money-losing season.
Larry Smith will not seek a second term as commissioner when his contract expires on April 1, 1997.
Larry Smith stated that it is time for someone with new ideas and energy to lead the league.
Many fans are concerned about the survival of the CFL.
All but one of the nine CFL clubs lost money during the 1996 season.
The Ottawa Rough Riders franchise folded at the end of the regular season.
The future of the Montreal Alouettes is uncertain after a poor season.
The British Columbia Lions are in receivership.
Larry Smith was hired in 1992 after serving as an executive with a Canadian food company.

Three Canadian financial institutions launched North America's first city-wide, reusable smart card designed to replace cash in retail transactions.
The Exact card will be tested under a pilot program operated by Bank of Montreal, Toronto-Dominion Bank, and Canada Trust.
The project will take place in Kingston, Ontario, a city with a population of about 100,000 people.
About 600 Kingston merchants, including convenience stores, gas stations, and fast food outlets, signed up for the test project.
The consortium is advertising Exact as an alternative to cash, credit, and debit cards.
Canadians currently spend between C$40 billion and C$60 billion using small coins and bills.
Ron Hodge, vice president of card and direct services for TD Bank, stated that Exact reduces the need to carry small bills and coins.
Canadians carry an estimated 46.2 million debt and credit cards, with usage increasing by 43 percent in the past year.
Tim Hockey, vice president of core banking services for Canada Trust, mentioned that technology is changing the face of money.
Exact is based on smart card technology developed by Belgium-based Banksys.

Royal Bank of Canada and Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce are Canada's two largest banks.
Royal Bank of Canada reported a 12 percent increase in income to C$358 million ($261 million) for the three months ended July 31.
Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce reported a 24 percent increase in income to C$336 million ($245 million).
CIBC's earnings per share were C$1.50 ($1.09), exceeding analysts' forecasts of around C$1.43 ($1.04).
Royal Bank reported earnings per share of C$1.02 ($0.74), which met analysts' expectations.
The six major banks in Canada achieved a combined profit of C$5.17 billion ($3.7 billion) for the fiscal year ended Oct. 31.
Canadian consumers have expressed hostility towards soaring bank profits due to high service fees and tight lending policies.
CIBC stated it paid more than C$0.50 ($0.36) in taxes for every dollar earned so far this year.
CIBC's return on equity was 16.6 percent in the third quarter, up from 13.7 percent in the same quarter last year.
CIBC Wood Gundy's recent strategic moves have contributed to the bank's financial performance.

Ontario Finance Minister Ernie Eves stated that his budget cuts would not be as severe this year due to a stronger economy and an improving deficit outlook.
Eves reported that Ontario's 1996/97 deficit is now estimated at C$7.67 billion, a decrease of C$508 million from the original budget forecast.
Ontario is Canada's most populous province and industrial powerhouse.
The ruling Conservatives in Ontario previously indicated that an additional C$3 billion in spending cuts would be necessary to balance the budget by the turn of the century.
Since taking power in 1995, the Conservatives have identified approximately C$8 billion in cuts through the end of the decade.
Eves expressed that he does not feel compelled to find an additional C$3 billion in savings due to the improving economy.
The Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce predicted that Ontario's economy would grow by 3.1 percent this year and 2.3 percent in 1998.
Eves acknowledged that the province's deficit issue is not resolved and that he is still looking for cost efficiencies for the upcoming 1997/98 budget.
Government revenues increased by almost C$1.2 billion to C$47.8 billion for the year, primarily due to higher personal, corporate, and retail sales tax revenues.
Eves mentioned that the government's 30 percent tax cut has contributed to increased consumer confidence in Ontario.

Strong demand for light trucks will boost the Big Three U.S. automakers' combined profits to nearly $2 billion for the third quarter.
The third quarter profits will exceed year-ago results by a healthy margin.
Chrysler Corp. and Ford Motor Co. are expected to post strong gains from minivan and truck output.
General Motors Corp.'s earnings were held back by a significant increase in incentives.
In the third quarter of 1995, the three automakers earned $1.35 billion.
GM is expected to report third quarter net income of about $850 million, or $1.02 a share.
The results for GM include an after-tax gain of $250 million from the reversal of a decision to close its Wilmington, Del., plant.
In the year-ago period, GM earned $642 million, or 42 cents a share.
GM's worldwide car and truck production rose 11 percent in the third quarter over a year ago.
Ford's third quarter profits are expected to increase 78 percent to $637 million, or 51 cents a share.

Ford Motor Co. is in talks with the Detroit Lions to purchase naming rights to the football team's proposed new stadium in downtown Detroit.
Ford Chairman Alex Trotman stated that the deal is expected to be signed in the next few days.
The Lions are owned by Ford board members William Clay Ford and William Clay Ford Jr.
Trotman indicated that reports of Ford paying $30 million to $40 million for the naming rights are accurate.
Ford wants exclusive rights with the Ford name prominently featured on the new stadium.
Trotman mentioned that a specific name for the stadium has not yet been decided.
William Clay Ford Jr. and William Clay Ford abstained from board discussions regarding the stadium project.
The new stadium project is largely considered to be initiated by William Clay Ford Jr.
A contribution of $30 million to $40 million would assist in financing the $225 million domed stadium.
The proposed stadium would have a capacity of 65,000 seats and is planned to be built near the end of the decade.

Second-shift workers at General Motors Corp.'s Cadillac assembly plant will not report to work on Monday due to the Canadian Auto Workers strike.
Thousands more U.S. assembly employees may be laid off this week, according to GM.
The Cadillac plant will operate with only one shift on Monday and Tuesday.
The Cadillac plant is expected to halt production completely unless the strike is resolved.
The Cadillac plant employs more than 3,000 hourly workers represented by the United Auto Workers union.
The Cadillac plant depends on interior trim parts made at a strike-bound plant in Windsor, Ontario.
GM's Canadian workers began an escalating strike on October 3.
The strike shut down all of GM's operations in Canada by late on October 9.
GM and the union have been unable to reach an agreement for a new national labor contract for GM's 26,000 CAW members.
The union wants restrictions on outsourcing to protect its members' jobs, while GM seeks flexibility on parts purchases.

Ford Motor Co. reported a $472 million loss in Europe this week.
Ford faces challenges in cutting costs and improving its product line in a sluggish European market.
Ford executives announced plans to cut costs in Europe, including product, material, personnel, and plant costs.
An early retirement program is expected to eliminate more than 2,000 jobs in Europe.
Ford's initiatives will be announced within the next three months.
Ford previously eliminated about 13,000 jobs from its European operations in 1993.
Ford's $472 million loss in Europe is compared to a $320 million deficit from the previous year.
Analysts indicate that there are no quick fixes to Ford's problems in Europe.
Ford's production and parts suppliers are heavily concentrated in Germany, leading to high costs.
General Motors Corp. has a competitive advantage due to its more evenly spread assembly operations and suppliers in Europe.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) is investigating spontaneous air bag deployments in several General Motors Corp. cars.
NHTSA has received five reports of air bags deploying without a collision in 1996-model GM mid-size sedans.
The spontaneous deployments are attributed to corrosion in the air bag sensing and diagnostic module.
Water was spilled or leaked onto the floor of the vehicle in each reported case.
The investigation involves 395,994 cars, including the 1996 Chevrolet Lumina, Monte Carlo, Buick Regal, Pontiac Grand Prix, and Oldsmobile Cutlass Supreme.
Three of the five inappropriate air bag deployments resulted in injuries, but none resulted in death.
Four of the five cars were traveling between 10 and 40 mph when the air bags inflated.
NHTSA has reported that air bags have saved the lives of more than 1,136 adults since 1986.
NHTSA has stated that air bags have killed 28 children since 1990 due to inflation speeds of up to 200 mph.
NHTSA advises that all children under the age of 12 should ride in the back seats of cars and trucks equipped with dual front air bags.

Negotiators for General Motors Corp. and the United Auto Workers union resumed bargaining on Saturday.
The goal of the negotiations is to reach a new national labor agreement before a Sunday night strike deadline.
UAW President Stephen Yokich led the bargaining session at GM's Detroit headquarters.
The UAW canceled its contract with GM, which is set to expire at 11:59 p.m. EST Sunday.
This is the first time the UAW has threatened a strike in its 1996 negotiations with Detroit's Big Three automakers.
The negotiations have been characterized by a conciliatory tone and secretive discussions.
GM's 26,000 Canadian Auto Workers members returned to work after a three-week strike against GM's Canadian operations.
The U.S. negotiations are focused on job security and GM's desire to outsource some components work.
GM wants to modify the UAW contract pattern established by Ford Motor Co. and Chrysler Corp.
GM's chief negotiator, Gerald Knechtel, stated that the automaker is committed to reaching an agreement.

A midnight Sunday strike deadline for General Motors Corp expired without a walkout.
Negotiations between General Motors and the United Auto Workers continued into the early morning hours on Monday.
A GM spokesman stated that a more detailed statement would be provided later on Monday morning.
Norman Harp, a union committeeman for UAW Local 14, reported that workers were still on the job at GM's Toledo, Ohio, transmission plant.
Local UAW officials at other GM plants were instructed to stand by for further instructions.
The UAW cancelled its national contract covering 215,000 GM hourly workers one minute before midnight Sunday.
There was speculation that the UAW could strike selected plants instead of a national strike.
The Janesville, Wisconsin, plant and the Pontiac, Michigan, plant were identified as potential targets for a selective strike.
A selective strike would minimize the impact on the UAW's strike fund and reduce political fallout before the U.S. presidential election.
UAW officials stated that the two sides remain at odds over employment guarantees for 95 percent of the current UAW workforce.

General Motors Corp. and the United Auto Workers resumed contract negotiations on Wednesday.
Local walkouts continued in Wisconsin and Indiana during the negotiations.
About 2,750 members of United Auto Workers Local 23 struck GM's Indianapolis metal stamping plant.
4,800 workers walked off the job at GM's Janesville, Wisconsin, truck assembly plant.
UAW spokesman Reg McGhee stated that no other local strikes had started as of Wednesday morning.
UAW President Stephen Yokich indicated that local unions were on their own after the national contract with GM expired.
The strikes increased pressure on GM for a national agreement.
The UAW's 250-member National GM Council is scheduled to meet in Detroit on Saturday.
A major issue in the national talks is the future of 12 domestic parts plants that GM considers uncompetitive.
GM wants to exclude several plants from union demands for employment guarantees for 95 percent of UAW workers over the next three years.

Negotiators from General Motors Corp. and the United Auto Workers union were working toward a national contract deal.
A local strike at a metal stamping plant posed a threat to General Motors.
UAW officials reported that the two sides were closer to an agreement, but job guarantees and plant sales remained unresolved issues.
UAW President Stephen Yokich was meeting with the union's executive board in Detroit.
The executive board must approve any deal reached between General Motors and the UAW.
UAW spokesman Reg McGhee stated that there was some progress made in negotiations.
Local strikes in Indianapolis and Janesville, Wisconsin, could idle nearly 21,000 workers by Saturday.
GM truck plants in Moraine, Ohio, and Flint, Michigan, were expected to run out of parts from the Indianapolis stamping plant by late Thursday night.
Flint employs about 2,000 workers and builds crew-cab and heavy-duty full-size pickup trucks.
Moraine employs about 4,000 workers and builds Chevrolet Blazer and GMC Jimmy compact sport/utility vehicles.

General Motors Corp.'s board of directors may delay an increase in the company's quarterly common stock dividend if a contract deal with the United Auto Workers union is not reached by Monday.
GM's board is scheduled to meet on Monday to consider the automaker's fourth quarter dividend.
Analyst Ron Glantz from Dean Witter stated that an increase in the dividend would send the wrong message to the union.
Glantz indicated that unless a settlement is reached by Sunday, the board will not proceed with a dividend increase.
A dividend increase could jeopardize ongoing negotiations with the UAW as GM seeks concessions to cut costs and sell unprofitable parts plants.
The agreement being negotiated is expected to maintain job guarantees similar to those set by Ford Motor Co and Chrysler Corp, but may exclude some GM facilities.
Analysts believe GM is due for a dividend increase due to the company's improving cash position and stronger earnings.
The quarterly payout rate on GM's stock has been unchanged since February, when it was raised to $0.40 a share from $0.30.
Analyst Joseph Phillippi from Lehman Brothers noted that GM needs to increase its payout to improve its dividend yield, which is currently 2.98 percent.
Phillippi expects GM to raise its dividend by 50 percent, or $0.20 a share, in two increments once a contract is signed.

General Motors Corp. and the United Auto Workers union reached a tentative agreement for a new national labor contract.
The agreement was reached early on Saturday after months of contentious bargaining.
The deal covers 215,000 hourly UAW workers.
Local strikes in Indiana and Wisconsin will continue despite the new agreement.
UAW President Stephen Yokich indicated the possibility of additional strikes among GM's 123 UAW locals.
Yokich stated that the two locals that walked out have unresolved grievances.
About 250 local leaders from GM plants will meet in Chicago on November 6 to consider the agreement.
The details of the agreement were not released.
Gerald Knechtel, vice president of personnel, stated that the agreement fits within the pattern established at Ford Motor Co and Chrysler Corp.
The talks faced challenges over several plants that GM wanted to exclude from employment guarantees.

General Motors Corp reached an agreement to end a strike at an Indianapolis metal stamping plant.
The strike lasted five days and threatened GM's North American light truck production.
The strike idled more than 19,000 workers due to disputes at the Indianapolis and Janesville plants.
The Indianapolis strikers, numbering 2,750, could return to work after a ratification vote scheduled for Sunday morning.
GM's full-size pickup truck plant in Pontiac, Michigan, may shut down due to shortages of parts made in Indianapolis.
The new local labor agreement in Indianapolis was reached at approximately 6:15 p.m. EST on Saturday.
The national GM-UAW labor accord covers 215,000 U.S. hourly workers and addresses broad issues like wages and benefits.
Local agreements address plant-specific issues such as work rules and staffing levels.
UAW President Stephen Yokich indicated the possibility of more local strikes if negotiations do not progress.
President Bill Clinton expressed hope that the tentative agreement would be ratified and local issues resolved.

General Motors Corp. reached a tentative deal to end a strike at its truck plant in Janesville, Wis.
About 4,809 members of United Auto Workers Local 95 were scheduled to vote on the tentative labor agreement.
Production of Chevrolet Tahoe, Suburban, and GMC Yukon vehicles at the Janesville plant could resume if the deal is ratified.
All of GM's North American car and truck operations could be operating normally by Thursday.
GM had nearly 40,000 U.S. workers idled due to local UAW strikes and Canadian parts shortages.
The UAW threatened GM with additional local walkouts if negotiations with its locals are delayed.
The union's members walked off the job on October 29 over plant-specific issues.
GM agreed to hire 200 more workers and pay back wages to settle the Indianapolis strike.
GM truck plants in Shreveport, La., and Linden, N.J., will return to normal work schedules by Thursday.
The Wentzville, Mo., plants will keep 1,100 workers on temporary layoff for nearly two more weeks.

Rover and Vauxhall unveiled new investments at the British International Motor Show.
Rover is owned by Germany's BMW.
Rover plans to launch a new four-wheel drive vehicle called the 'baby Land Rover' in 1998.
The 'baby Land Rover' aims to compete with Japanese rivals in Britain and export markets.
Rover's investment program totals 3.0 billion pounds ($4.75 billion).
Rover will inject 3.5 billion pounds into the components industry, primarily benefiting British firms.
This investment will safeguard tens of thousands of jobs at Rover and its suppliers.
Vauxhall is owned by General Motors of the United States.
Vauxhall announced a 300 million pound investment to modernize its Ellesmere Port complex, securing 4,200 jobs.
The British motor market is experiencing sluggish sales, with growth mainly from company car fleets.

Wickes Plc is a Do-It-Yourself retailer that has faced accounting discrepancies for five years.
Wickes Plc announced plans for a one-off charge of around 10 million stg against its 1996 results.
The charge will relate to restructuring and investigation costs associated with accounting problems revealed in June.
Finance director Bill Hoskins stated that the total cost would be around 10 million stg.
Wickes Plc is considering a rights issue with a starting point of 30 million stg.
Chairman Michael von Brentano announced a 51 million stg write-off against shareholder funds due to profit overstatements.
There is an additional separate charge of 10 million stg related to property interests.
Wickes plans to explore options to improve its finances before approaching shareholders.
Details of the refinancing are expected to be revealed in December.
Wickes aims to achieve profitability by 1997 and plans to cut costs for transparent accounting.

AMEC Plc is a British building group.
AMEC Plc plans to issue details of its possible investment in Spie Batignolles by November.
Peter Mason is the chief executive of AMEC Plc.
AMEC Plc predicts that the investment deal will be completed by the end of the year.
Peter Mason stated that an initial stake in Spie Batignolles would likely lead to a larger controlling share in the future.
Spie Batignolles is a unit of the holding company Schneider SA.
The decision to float part of Spie Batignolles will depend on various factors, including negotiations and market conditions.
The deal has been under discussion for several months and is considered a good fit for AMEC.
The eventual combined group is expected to have 5.0 billion stg in sales.
The new deal will provide AMEC access to new markets in oil and gas and pharmaceuticals, as well as regions like Indonesia, South America, and South Africa.

Smiths Industries Plc announced a $30 million acquisition of Leland Electrosystems Inc.
Leland Electrosystems Inc. is a manufacturer of electrical power generators for military and civil aircraft.
Leland has a key position in the U.S. to supply the F18 military aircraft.
Leland has secured an order to supply 1,000 units of the new version of the F18 aircraft.
Russell Plumley, director of public affairs, stated that Leland's military aircraft contract involves substantial sums over a five to six year period.
The civil aviation side of Leland's business includes a contract to provide generators for the 777 commercial aircraft.
Smiths Industries Plc also services the F18 and 777 aircraft in other product areas.
The Leland acquisition is expected to enhance earnings in the first full year after the acquisition.
Smiths Industries Plc stated it would not implement job cuts or cost cutting as part of the acquisition.

Millennium Chemicals is a company owned by Hanson Plc.
Millennium Chemicals plans to be floated off in New York on October 1.
Millennium Chemicals intends to initiate a share buyback by the year 2000.
Millennium Chemicals has net debt levels around $2.0 billion.
William Landuyt is the chairman and chief executive of Millennium Chemicals.
Millennium Chemicals will implement a low-yielding dividend policy.
The planned dividend payout is around 60 cents a year or 15 cents a quarter.
Millennium Chemicals is focusing on growth rather than high dividend yields.
Investment plans include expansion in specialty products and regions such as Asia-Pacific and Western Australia.
The recent plant closure at SCM will have a neutral impact on trading profit.

Environmental warfare has emerged in the British construction industry.
Activists are targeting major corporations to impact their profit margins.
Some British companies refer to these actions as 'eco-terrorism.'
Companies such as Tarmac Plc, Costain Group Plc, and ARC have been targeted by activists.
Activist groups are perceived as organized and sophisticated rather than harmless.
David Harding, a spokesman for ARC, noted the use of mobile phones and the Internet by activists.
A road protester known as Steady Eddie stated that activists may engage in economic warfare.
Costain's contract for the Newbury bypass has led to violent protests and delays.
There have been incidents of bomb threats, staff intimidation, and picketing of executives' homes.
The Berkshire Wood Elves group is under police investigation for distributing leaflets on homemade explosives.

The Sea Launch satellite project has a budget of 350 million stg.
The project is backed by firms from the U.S., Russia, Norway, and Ukraine.
The first satellite is scheduled to be launched from a sea platform in June 1998.
Kvaerner is the project contractor and has a 20 percent stake in the project.
Kvaerner is overseeing the construction of the launch platform and control ship in Stavanger, Norway, and Goven, Scotland.
Boeing Commercial Space Co, RSC-Energia, and NPO-Yuzhnoye are also involved in the project.
Kvaerner is receiving a fee of 250 million stg to build the ship and platform launcher.
The Sea Launch project manager is Svein Johnsen.
Hughes Space & Communication International Inc has a contract for 10 launches.
Space Systems/Lorel has a contract for five launches.

Sea Launch is a project involving corporate partners from Russia, the United States, Norway, and Ukraine to develop space technology.
The total cost of the Sea Launch project is 350 million pounds ($583.2 million).
The project is funded by a consortium of four companies: Boeing Co. (40%), RSC-Energia of Russia (25%), Kvaerner of Norway (20%), and NPO-Yuzhnoye of Ukraine (15%).
Kvaerner is the prime contractor responsible for building the mobile seaborne rocket launch platform and the command ship.
The mobile launch platform is being constructed from an offshore oil rig that was rebuilt after being damaged in a 1988 explosion.
The platform is nearing completion in Stavanger, Norway, and the command ship is under construction in Govan, Scotland.
The first rocket launch is scheduled for June 1998 from a site in the Pacific Ocean.
Satellites and rockets will be assembled on the command ship before being transferred to the launch platform.
The command ship will control the rocket launch from a distance of two or three miles.
The Zenit rockets will be provided by Russia and can be assembled horizontally on the command ship.

The UK construction industry expects continued cutbacks in infrastructure spending in the upcoming budget.
Industry leaders predict minimal financial support from Chancellor Kenneth Clarke.
There are rumors that Chancellor Kenneth Clarke will further reduce the road budget this year.
Graham Watts, chief executive of the Construction Industry Council, stated that this budget may have severe cuts to accommodate pre-election tax cuts.
Builders are calling for stability in the housing market, including steady inflation and interest rates.
The Building Employers Federation opposes further reductions in mortgage interest tax relief.
The British Road Federation reported a 25 percent cut in the road budget over the last two years.
Mark Glover, a spokesman for the British Road Federation, expects an additional contraction of 200 million pounds in the road budget.
Spending on new roads and maintenance by the Highways Agency decreased from 2.04 billion pounds in 1994/95 to an expected 1.5 billion pounds in the current financial year.
The construction industry remains in recession due to cutbacks in spending and reduced state investment in rail and hospitals.

The Serious Fraud Office (SFO) launched an investigation into former bosses of Wickes Plc.
The investigation is related to accounting irregularities worth tens of millions of pounds.
The SFO is conducting the probe jointly with the British police fraud squad in London.
Investigators are expected to interview former chairman and chief executive Henry Sweetbaum, former finance director Trefor Llewellyn, and former buying and commercial directors.
No arrests or charges have been made, and no search warrants have been executed.
The SFO took on the case on November 20 but did not announce its involvement for operational reasons.
Wickes uncovered the accounting scam in June, which resulted in a 51 million stg overstatement of profits.
Wickes plans to restate profits next month and launch details of a refinancing rights issue of between 30 and 40 million pounds.
Wickes shares remain frozen at 69 pence per share.
Sweetbaum accepted ultimate responsibility for the accounting issues and agreed to repay his 1.2 million pounds in bonuses.

The British government referred a proposed merger of P&O and Stena Line to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission for investigation.
Ian Lang, president of the Board of Trade, requested the MMC to study the competition effects of the merger.
The merger was proposed to help P&O and Stena Line counter the market impact of Eurotunnel's Channel Tunnel.
Most Eurotunnel services were suspended following a serious fire last week.
P&O described the government's review of the merger as 'totally unnecessary'.
P&O's shares decreased by 6-1/2 pence to 589 1/2 pence following the news of the review.
P&O chairman Lord Sterling stated that the merger plans would be delayed for three months due to the MMC review.
P&O and Stena Line announced their merger plans in October in response to Eurotunnel's 40 percent market share.
The merger aims to reduce a combined fixed cost base of 280 million pounds by 75 million pounds.
Lord Sterling claimed that Eurotunnel's fire did not change the economic rationale for the merger.

Virgin Rail group is the rail division of Richard Branson's Virgin Group.
Virgin Rail announced plans to spend 250 million stg on new rolling stock.
Virgin Rail won the CrossCountry rail franchise.
Will Whitehorn is the director of Virgin Rail.
The order for new rolling stock will be placed next year, with delivery starting in 2002.
The government subsidy for the first year of the 15-year franchise will be 115 million pounds.
The 115 million subsidy has been reduced from the 1996/97 subsidy level of 127 million.
The subsidy will decrease over the 15-year term, with Virgin Rail making a 10 million payment to the government in the final year.
Virgin Rail plans to refurbish the HST 125 diesel trains and increase train miles by 14 percent.
CrossCountry had 108 million stg in passenger revenues in the year to March 31.

Computer Associates International Inc. agreed to pay about $1.2 billion for Cheyenne Software Inc.
Computer Associates will offer $30.50 in cash for each share of Cheyenne.
Cheyenne's stock increased by $7.625 to $30 on the American Stock Exchange.
Computer Associates' stock rose by 62.5 cents to $63.375 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Industry analysts expressed confusion over the high price paid by Computer Associates.
UBS Securities analyst Joseph Farley stated that the price is a departure from Computer Associates' standard practice.
Cheyenne reported revenues of $174.1 million for the fiscal year ending June 1996.
The acquisition has been unanimously approved by the boards of directors of both companies.
Cheyenne produces storage management, anti-virus, and communications software for client/server networks.
Computer Associates plans to fund the acquisition through cash balances and existing credit facilities.

Intel Corp stock increased in value due to its third quarter earnings report.
Intel's success positively impacted the stocks of personal computer manufacturers.
Intel's report did not significantly benefit other chipmakers.
Analysts expressed concerns about potential reductions in fourth quarter orders.
Intel stock rose to 111 after trading as high as 114-1/4.
Compaq Computer Corp stock increased to 73-3/8.
Dell Computer Corp stock rose to 86-1/8.
Gateway 2000 Inc stock increased to 55-3/8.
Chips reported earnings of $0.42 per share for its first quarter ended September 30.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index decreased by 1.69 points to 197.97.

Intel Corp stock rose by $3.50 to $111.125 on Tuesday.
Intel's quarterly earnings report exceeded Wall Street expectations.
Intel reported third-quarter profits of $1.3 billion, an increase from $931 million in the same quarter of 1995.
Wall Street had predicted Intel's profits to be $1.1 billion.
The earnings report positively impacted the stocks of personal computer makers that use Intel microprocessors.
Compaq Computer Corp. stock rose by $2 to $74.75.
Dell Computer Corp. stock increased by $3.50 to $88.375.
Gateway 2000 Inc. stock climbed by $3.375 to $56.75.
Analysts expressed concerns about the sustainability of Intel's order surge into the fourth quarter.
Intel's stock gains contributed to the Nasdaq index closing at a record high of 1,258.10.

Shares of leading U.S. technology companies were trading near all-time highs on Tuesday.
Quarterly earnings raised concerns about the growth of these companies.
Profit-taking occurred in the technology sector after a strong run-up in stock prices.
Microsoft Corp's stock was down 2-3/8 at 131-1/2 on Tuesday, despite beating third quarter earnings expectations.
International Business Machines Corp (IBM) slid 1-1/2 at 128-1/2 after reporting quarterly earnings above Wall Street consensus.
Intel Corp was trading 2-5/16 points lower at 105-7/16, continuing a decline from its record level of 114-1/4.
Some traders noted that despite healthy earnings, stocks were trading down.
Analysts expressed concern over the lack of follow-through on recent share gains.
IBM stock had recently traded at record highs, reaching above 135 on Monday.
Silicon Graphics Inc shares reported a net loss and were down to a new year-low of 19-7/8.

MCI Communications Corp. reached a 10-year deal with NextWave Telecom Inc.
The deal positions MCI among the top U.S. wireless communications providers.
Analysts believe MCI's investment in wireless remains cautious despite the deal.
MCI will function as a major reseller of wireless services instead of building its own network infrastructure.
Under the deal, MCI will offer wireless services to over 110 million potential customers in 63 U.S. cities.
MCI will purchase at least 10 billion minutes of capacity from NextWave over the next 10 years.
MCI will integrate its network with NextWave's network to provide seamless wireless services.
Whitey Bluestein, MCI's vice president for wireless strategy, stated the agreement establishes a nationwide PCS footprint for MCI.
The deal includes a competitive price per minute for wireless phone services.
NextWave was founded by Allen Salmasi, a former executive at Qualcomm Inc.

Bay Networks Inc shares increased on Wednesday after the company appointed a senior Intel Corp official as chairman and chief executive.
Analysts believe this appointment could provide Bay with stronger leadership.
Bay shares rose by 1-3/4 to 20-1/8 on Wednesday.
The shares were among the five most active on the NYSE.
Analyst Eric Blachno from Bear Stearns stated he will wait to see David House's strategies before supporting the stock.
Blachno downgraded Bay's stock to neutral from buy after the last earnings report, citing troubling signs in the company's switching business.
Bay's switching business has experienced revenue declines for the last two quarters.
Cisco Systems Inc and 3Com Corp have shown double-digit growth in revenues during the same period.
Bay Networks has been perceived as a laggard in the networking industry despite its reputation as a technology leader.
Leadership issues have been a concern for Bay Networks since its formation in 1994 from the merger of Wellfleet and Synoptics.

Iomega Corp. plans to apply its computer storage technology to handheld consumer electronics.
The reusable data storage system will be known as 'n-hand'.
The n-hand technology could be used in digital cameras, computer game devices, cellular phones, and handheld personal computers.
The n-hand technology could function as a removable 'digital film' in cameras.
Iomega's n-hand disks are expected to be priced at less than $10 for a 20-megabyte disk.
The n-hand disks are expected to be available by the second half of 1997.
The n-hand disks are about half the size of a business card.
Several industry analysts believe Iomega's technology could help propel digital cameras into the consumer mainstream.
A digital camera could store from 50 to 80 images on a single $10 n-hand disk, depending on image resolution.
Jim Porter stated that Iomega's technology could cut the cost of storing photographs by a factor of 20 times.

Chips stocks, particularly those of PC-related manufacturers, experienced gains on Tuesday.
A monthly industry report indicated strong demand in the North American semiconductor market.
Stocks of companies that manufacture programmable logic devices, including Altera Corp, Lattice Semiconductor Corp, and Xilinx Inc, also showed strength in early trading.
Nimal Vallipuram, a Bear Stearns chip analyst, stated that most of the upside is coming from the PC industry and does not indicate an industry turnaround.
The industry ratio of chip bookings to orders increased to 1.10 in October from 0.98 in September.
The increase in the ratio surprised analysts by its extent, despite being somewhat expected.
The report indicated general industry health but provided little insight into specific segments.
Commodity chipmakers, including Motorola Inc and Texas Instruments Inc, saw stock price increases.
Intel Corp, a major microprocessor manufacturer, also experienced a rise in stock price.
Mona Eraiba, a semiconductor analyst at Gruntal & Co, noted that the magnitude of the improvement was surprising but anticipated by Wall Street.

Intel Corp shares fell four points on Friday.
The decline in Intel shares is part of a three-day retreat.
The retreat was triggered by Advanced Micro Devices Inc's statement about its turnaround plan.
Analysts and money managers believe the decline in Intel is due to profit-taking.
Some momentum investors are shifting from Intel to AMD.
Intel stock has lost about six percent of its value since Wednesday.
Advanced Micro announced it is sampling its K6 chip, expected to ship in early 1997.
Intel closed at 115-7/8 on Friday with a trading volume of 15 million shares.
Intel is a key component of the Nasdaq Composite index.
The Nasdaq Composite Index closed at 1261.81, down 8.55.

Investors purchased semiconductor equipment stocks on Friday.
Analysts indicated that the cyclical downturn in chips has reached its bottom.
Applied Materials Inc expects its profit margins to remain higher than in previous market cycles.
Applied Materials shares increased by 4-3/4 points to 36-3/4 in early trading on heavy volume of 11 million shares.
Deutsche Morgan analyst Elliott Rogers raised Applied Materials' rating from hold to buy.
KLA Instruments Corp shares rose by 5-7/8 points to 39-1/8.
Tencor Instruments shares increased by 4-3/8 points to 25-5/8.
Lam Research Corp shares gained 4-3/8 points to 33-7/8.
Intel Corp shares rose by 2-1/8 points to 121.
Analyst Byron Walker noted that Applied Materials executives discussed potential stabilization of equipment order rates.

Small capitalization technology stocks experienced gains despite profit-taking in blue chip stocks on Monday.
Investors focused on lesser-known technology stocks, particularly in the Internet sector.
Scott Bleier is the chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd.
America Online Inc's stock rose by 4-1/8 to 39-1/2.
Adobe Systems Inc's stock increased by 2-1/4 to 41-3/4.
Informix Corp was the most actively traded issue on the Nasdaq, gaining 1-1/4 to 25.
Informix Corp's stock gain followed reports of its next-generation Universal Server database outperforming Oracle Corp.
Netscape Communications Corp's stock rose by 2-1/8 to 58.
CyberCash Inc's stock gained 2-7/8 to 28-1/8.
Paul Rabbit is the chief portfolio strategist at Oppenheimer.

General Electric Co Chairman John Welch expressed optimism about GE's prospects for the current year and beyond during a meeting with Wall Street analysts.
Welch stated he was comfortable with Wall Street's earnings estimates for the 1996 calendar year, which is $4.40 per share according to First Call consensus.
Analyst Russell Leavit reported that Welch expected earnings to increase by about 13 percent this year, aligning with expectations.
The meeting contributed to General Electric stock being listed among the NYSE most actives, with the stock rising 1-1/8 in early afternoon trading.
A GE spokesman declined to comment on Welch's remarks but noted the company was on track for a 'record year' in 1996 in terms of earnings.
After the meeting, CS First Boston analyst Martin Sankey maintained a strong buy rating on GE and raised his 1997 earnings estimate to $5.00 per share.
Leavit indicated that analysts were optimistic about GE's progress for the next year, particularly in the aircraft engine and power businesses, as well as the NBC broadcast unit.
Leavit kept his buy rating and earnings estimates of $4.40 for 1996 and $4.95 for 1997, which is above the First Call consensus.
A fund manager noted that most Wall Street analysts felt confident that the earnings estimates for this year and next year would be met.

Apple Computer Inc shares fell 17 percent on Monday.
Wall Street analysts expressed pessimism about Apple's short-term and long-term outlook.
Several brokerages recommended that investors sell Apple stock.
Apple's stock price decreased to 17-3/4, making it the most actively traded issue on Nasdaq with over 10 million shares traded.
Apple projected an operating loss of $100 to $150 million for the first quarter ending December 27.
The company attributed its financial issues to weak U.S. demand for its Performa consumer PC line and shortages of PowerBook notebook computers.
Apple reported a 10 percent decline in revenues for the December quarter compared to the September quarter, when revenues were $2.3 billion.
Analyst Kurt King stated that the situation reflects negatively on Apple's long-term position in the consumer market.
Concerns were raised about competition from new machines using Intel's multimedia chip technology and Microsoft Windows software.
There is uncertainty regarding Apple's future operating system and its ability to introduce a new system based on the NeXT system.

The Internet Society has backed away from a proposal to expand the number of addresses on the global computer network.
The Internet Society announced it would form a nine-member committee to study the issue instead of moving ahead with the proposal.
The proposal was unveiled in August to address disputes over desirable address names.
Don Heath is the president of the Internet Society.
Objections to the August proposal include technical networking issues and concerns about trademarks and intellectual property.
The new committee is expected to finish its work by early next year.
New names could be distributed four to six months after the committee's work is completed.
The committee may decide not to proceed with any address expansion, but this is considered unlikely by Heath.
Disputes over Internet names are increasing as more companies seek to market their products online.
Every site on the World Wide Web must have a unique address name.

U.S. laws governing the futures markets could be affected by the Supreme Court's interpretation of the word 'in'.
A legislative solution regarding the Commodity Exchange Act is anticipated.
The Commodity Exchange Act was amended in 1974 to regulate trading of futures contracts.
Futures exchanges claim a broad reading of the 1974 amendment would threaten their business.
Major banks argue a narrow reading of the amendment would require them to relocate operations outside the United States.
Congressional action on this issue is expected next year.
Howard Schneider, former Commodity Futures Trading Commission general counsel, believes legislation will ultimately address the issue.
The 1974 expansion of the Commodity Exchange Act included futures on non-agricultural commodities.
The Treasury Department suggested an amendment to exempt certain transactions from the Commodity Exchange Act.
The Treasury Amendment exempts transactions in foreign currency and government securities from the Commodity Exchange Act unless they involve sale for future delivery on a board of trade.

The Internet grew significantly in 2023, according to a survey by Louis Harris and Associates.
An estimated 35 million adults in the United States used the Internet in late September 2023.
This number increased from 27 million at the beginning of 2023.
Humphrey Taylor is the chairman of Louis Harris and Associates.
The number of adult Americans using computers for cyber-activities is increasing.
America Online Inc. and Compuserve Corp. had almost 41 million subscribers, the same level as in January 2023.
Online services faced increased competition from companies like AT&T Corp., which offer cheaper Internet-only access.
Home users reported spending an average of 2.8 hours online per week, down from three hours in April 2023.
Business and other users reported spending an average of 1.8 hours online per week, down from two hours in April 2023.
The poll found that more educated individuals are more likely to use computers and access the Internet.

The Internet could significantly benefit the U.S. economy if the federal government adopts free market policies in cyberspace.
A draft report from a group of President Clinton's top advisers recommends protecting the Internet from new taxes and censorship.
The interagency task force is led by senior presidential adviser Ira Magaziner.
The task force is preparing to issue a report of principles and policies for public comment after seven months of deliberation.
Magaziner stated that the report aims to outline what the government should not do as well as what it should do.
The growth of Internet commerce could enhance U.S. exports of various products and services.
U.S. exports of products such as movies, news, software, and consulting services totaled $40 billion in 1995.
Sales of goods and services online are projected to increase to $7 billion by the year 2000.
The draft report, titled 'A Framework for Global Electronic Commerce,' addresses issues including taxation, customs, privacy, and security.
The report suggests that the United States should advocate for the Internet to be designated a duty-free zone through the World Trade Organisation.

The Federal Reserve voted to allow banks to increase the percentage of revenue bank subsidiaries may earn from underwriting and dealing in securities from 10 percent to 25 percent.
The Fed Board of Governors voted unanimously on this change.
Bank subsidiaries had previously been limited to earning 10 percent of their revenue from these activities.
The Fed cited Swiss Bank Corp. for exceeding the 10 percent cap earlier this year.
The American Bankers Association managing director Larry LaRocca stated that the new rule is a boost for banks that underwrite securities.
Securities firms expressed dissatisfaction with the new rule, with Steve Judge from the Securities Industry Association comparing it to Santa Claus delivering gifts to only one house.
Bruce Thompson from Merrill Lynch and Co. expressed hope that the new rule would not reduce banks' support for Congressional action.
Rachel Robbins from J.P. Morgan & Co. stated that the new rule addresses only part of the need for complete financial reform.
The 1933 Glass-Steagall Act generally prohibits banks from engaging in non-bank activities but allows certain affiliations under section 20.
Currently, 41 bank 'Section 20' subsidiaries have permission to engage in underwriting.

U.S. banks will be able to increase their securities underwriting activities under a new rule adopted by the Federal Reserve.
The Federal Reserve voted unanimously to allow section 20 subsidiaries of banks to derive up to 25 percent of their revenues from underwriting and dealing in securities.
The new rule will take effect in 60 days.
Fed governors called for Congressional action to reform the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act and other laws separating banks from non-bank financial services industries.
Fed vice chair Alice Rivlin stated that the next move should be up to Congress regarding regulatory changes.
Governor Susan Phillips described the Fed's action as a constructive step and appropriate interpretation of existing legislation.
The Glass-Steagall Act prohibits banks from engaging in non-bank activity, but allows banks to affiliate with firms not primarily engaged in such areas under section 20.
The Fed currently authorizes 41 bank subsidiaries to deal and underwrite securities.
Robert Litan from the Brookings Institute stated that the Fed's action will increase pressure on Congress to repeal the Glass-Steagall Act.
Banking industry representatives expressed satisfaction with the Fed's decision, viewing it as a boost for banks involved in underwriting securities.

The Commerce Department will issue final rules on December 30 regarding the export of computer encoding products.
The proposal is unlikely to satisfy the software industry and privacy advocates who opposed a draft version.
Some changes were made in the final rules compared to the earlier draft, but the bulk of the proposal remains the same.
William Reinsch, the Commerce undersecretary, stated that some objections could not be addressed.
Previous rules from the Cold War severely limited the export of products containing encryption.
Under past rules, products could be exported using keys of up to 40 digital bits.
Longer encryption keys have become more common due to advancements in computer speed.
The demand for encryption-capable products is increasing globally due to the growth of the Internet and online commerce.
The new Commerce Department rules aim to balance U.S. competitiveness in the encryption market with law enforcement interests.
Products with key recovery features will be eligible for export after a one-time review under the new policy.

A study released by a coalition of Internet and computer companies claims that Internet users pose little threat to local telephone companies.
The coalition presented the report to counter previous studies by local phone companies that justified new access fees on Internet usage.
Local phone company studies claimed that Internet usage threatened to overwhelm the phone system.
Harris Miller, President of the Information Technology Association of America, stated that the Internet is not crashing the telephone network.
Miller claimed that the phone companies created a 'problem' to protect their own interests.
On December 24, the Federal Communications Commission tentatively decided not to impose access fees on Internet providers similar to those paid by long distance companies.
Lee Selwyn, one of the study's authors, stated that claims of phone network congestion from Internet traffic are greatly exaggerated.
Selwyn also claimed that ordinary consumers using the Internet pay the phone companies enough to cover the cost of increased use.
In 1995, consumers paid more than $1.4 billion for installation and use of six million second phone lines for Internet access.
Bell Atlantic spokesman Harry Mitchell disputed the study's conclusions, stating that the growing demand for phone lines impacts the capacity of the public telephone network.

A U.S. graduate student cracked a powerful computer encryption system.
The Commerce Department announced it would allow three companies to export a stronger encryption system.
Computer encryption programs were classified as munitions and stronger programs could not be exported until this year.
A new policy from the Clinton administration took effect on January 1, allowing companies to receive permission to export stronger programs.
Under Secretary of Commerce for Export Administration William Reinsch stated that the approvals were achieved without difficulty.
Companies must agree to incorporate features allowing the government to decode encrypted messages within two years to export stronger programs immediately.
The administration's policy has been criticized for not relaxing export limits enough.
Some companies feared that the two-year plan requirement would delay export approvals.
Reinsch indicated that quick approvals should encourage more applicants.
Encryption has become essential for protecting online communications and transactions.

The U.S. financial services industry will discuss bank reform proposals at a hearing on Tuesday before the House Banking Committee's subcommittee on financial institutions.
There is a general consensus in Congress and the industry to reconsider Depression-era laws that separate banking from other financial services.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin is considering a proposal to allow combinations between commercial and financial firms.
Savings institutions and insurance companies can already own or be owned by non-financial companies, while banks face stricter regulations.
A Treasury Department task force recommended that the upcoming bank reform proposal allow mixing of commerce and banking.
Rubin informed bankers at a private meeting that no decision has been made regarding the issue of mixing commerce and banking.
House Banking Committee chairman Jim Leach opposes the mixing of commerce and banking and warned that banks could be taken over by larger companies.
Insurance and savings groups will oppose restrictions on commercial and financial combinations at the hearing.
The mutual fund industry also opposes restrictions on commercial and financial combinations.
Small banks, represented by the Independent Bankers Association of America, support imposing legal barriers against commercial and financial combinations.

Internet access providers fear that Congress will negatively impact cyberspace.
Company representatives met with members of the Congressional Internet Caucus to discuss concerns about cyberspace legislation.
Tom Evslin, vice president of AT&T Corp.'s WorldNet Internet service, believes it is inevitable that bills will be introduced to legislate Internet content.
Evslin stated that preventing Congress from making mistakes regarding Internet legislation will be difficult.
Bill Schrader, president of Internet provider PSINet Inc., warned that careless legislation could harm the industry.
Members of Congress at the meeting pledged to protect the Internet.
Representative Rick White, co-chairman of the caucus, acknowledged the challenges ahead regarding various Internet issues.
White co-sponsored a bill to relax export restrictions on encryption features in computer hardware and software.
Senator Conrad Burns warned that government legislation will lag behind private sector developments.
Last year, Congress passed the Communications Decency Act, which was opposed by online companies and civil libertarians.

The Supreme Court will decide if a federal regulator properly allowed credit unions to expand their membership over the past 15 years.
This decision addresses a legal dispute between credit unions and banks.
Credit unions support the Supreme Court's reconsideration of a previous Appellate court decision that favored banks.
Bank representatives believe the Supreme Court's action is merely delaying the outcome.
Marc Schaefer, president of AT&T Family Federal Credit Union, stated that the 1934 Federal Credit Union Act was not intended to protect bank markets at the expense of consumers.
Schaefer claimed that consumers would benefit from competition between banks in the marketplace.
Donald Ogilvie, executive vice president of the American Bankers Association, argued that the facts and law support the banks' position.
Ogilvie expressed disappointment over the delay in enforcing a law he believes is clear.
The Supreme Court will hear arguments in the case during its upcoming term starting in October.
The case impacts approximately 3,600 federal credit unions serving 32 million customers.

Shares on most central and eastern European bourses gained ground this week.
Exchanges in Prague, Warsaw, Budapest, Bratislava, and Bucharest all rose.
Zagreb and Sofia traded mixed.
Ljubljana posted slight losses.
The Central European Share Index (CESI) firmed 66.11 points.
Czech share prices were mostly steady on the Prague Stock Exchange throughout the week.
The PX50 index edged up 3.6 points to close at 568.6 on Thursday.
SPT Telecom and Komercni Banka were leading trades on the Prague Stock Exchange.
SPT closed on Thursday at 3,340 crowns.
Polish shares rose for the sixth consecutive session on Thursday.

It's a Snip is competing to become the ninth horse to win the Pardubice steeplechase in consecutive years.
The Pardubice steeplechase has a history of 106 years.
Richard Dunwoody is the jockey for It's a Snip.
The Pardubice steeplechase is a four-and-a-quarter mile event (6.9 km).
The course includes a series of demanding obstacles.
The Pardubice has been compared to the Grand National at Aintree.
Race organisers have made the course easier in recent years.
The Taxis jump has been modified due to past protests and safety concerns.
A total of 21 horses have died in the Pardubice over the years.
Irish Stamp and Veleda II are the other two British horses competing.

Boris Becker, the third seed, won his match against Frederik Fetterlein with a score of 6-3 6-4 at the Czech Indoor Open.
Becker recently won the CA Trophy in Vienna.
Todd Martin, the fifth seed, defeated Cristiano Caratti 6-4 6-1 in his second round match.
Bohdan Ulihrach, the eighth seed, lost to Jiri Novak 6-4 6-2.
Becker experienced soreness in his hand during the match but managed to win in just over an hour.
Becker has faced recurring problems with a ligament injury since Wimbledon.
Becker is currently ranked sixth in the world and is competing for a spot in the ATP Tour Championships.
Wayne Ferreira, ranked second in Ostrava, is ahead of Becker by 46 points for the eighth spot in the ATP Tour Championships.
Martin's match against Caratti lasted 49 minutes.
Ulihrach previously defeated Daniel Vacek but struggled against Novak.

Tim Henman is the only seed in the $475,000 Czech Indoor Open semifinals.
Tim Henman defeated Wayne Ferreira with a score of 6-4 6-3.
David Prinosil defeated Todd Martin with a score of 7-6 7-6.
Martin Damm defeated Michael Stich with a score of 5-7 6-4 6-4.
Petr Korda won against Jiri Novak with a score of 6-1 6-0.
Tim Henman will play David Prinosil in the semifinals.
Wayne Ferreira is ranked seventh in the world.
Tim Henman is ranked 26th in the world.
Todd Martin is currently 199 points behind Wayne Ferreira in the ATP Tour championship race.
Martin, Stich, and Ferreira will compete in Stuttgart next week.

David Prinosil from Germany won the final of the $475,000 Czech Indoor Open against Czech Petr Korda with a score of 6-1 6-2.
Prinosil is 23 years old and was born near Olomouc, Czech Republic, before emigrating to Germany at the age of 14.
Prinosil dominated the match from the start, utilizing his powerful serve and precise groundstrokes.
Prinosil won the first set in 22 minutes by converting both break points he had.
In the second set, Korda attempted to take more risks but was unable to disrupt Prinosil's performance.
Prinosil achieved four consecutive service winners to win a crucial game in the fourth game of the second set.
Prinosil broke Korda's serve in the fifth and seventh games of the second set.
The match lasted a total of 50 minutes.
Prinosil expressed surprise at not losing a set throughout the tournament and stated he played exceptionally well.
Korda mentioned feeling drained from a previous match and noted that the short points limited his ability to control the match.

The Czech September trade deficit is expected to grow by between 13 and 15 billion crowns after a 14.7 billion crown monthly deficit in August.
A Reuters poll of Czech economists indicated the expected growth in the trade deficit.
Czech trade figures for the first nine months will be released by the Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) at 0900 local time on Thursday.
Most economists surveyed expect steady growth in the deficit and few surprises.
Boris Gomez, an analyst at ING Barings, stated that it is too early to talk about a period of stabilization in the deficit.
The nine-month trade gap is expected to be a record, following a January-August figure of 100.9 billion crowns.
The total shortfall for 1995 was 95.7 billion crowns.
The January-September 1995 trade deficit was 62.3 billion crowns.
Analysts agreed that a 13-15 billion September gap would align with prevailing trends and the estimated deficit of 150-160 billion crowns.
The trade balance has been negatively affected by a downturn in the economies of western Europe earlier in the year.

The Prague Stock Exchange experienced a significant one-day decline on Friday due to decreased foreign interest attributed to a lack of market transparency.
Four of the five largest issues on the PSE fell sharply during active trading.
The Reuters RPIX index dropped nearly three percent to 1,052.
Analysts have criticized the PSE for its lack of transparency and regulation.
Jan Sykora of Wood and Company stated that there is a total lack of interest in the market.
Miroslav Nosal of Patria Finance noted that a notable portion of foreign investors are dissatisfied with the current state of the Czech capital market.
The Czech Republic's Securities Act mandates the Securities Registry (SCP) to provide services related to securities transactions.
The SCP does not disclose transaction details, leading brokers to prefer its privacy and faster settlement process.
The average daily stock turnover on the PSE is $4-$6 million, compared to $15 million in Warsaw.
In April, the Czech parliament approved market reforms aimed at increasing transparency and accountability among companies and fund managers.

Investors are shifting from the Czech equity market to the debt market due to a lack of transparency and poor performance.
The official PX50 index of the Prague bourse has lost almost 18 percent in the past two months.
Analysts predict that the downward trend in the equity market will continue until after the New Year.
Michael Gartner, a debt analyst at ING Capital Markets, stated that the bond market is bullish and has a positive outlook.
Estimated daily bond turnover has increased to 900 million to one billion crowns, matching the turnover on the Prague stock exchange.
Alojz Lacko, a bond trader at Patria Finance, noted that the bond market is becoming more important for foreign investors due to reasonable prices.
Investors have complained about the equities market, where 70 percent of trading occurs off-market, affecting minority shareholder rights.
Bourse and Finance Ministry officials are planning to introduce tighter trading rules to address investor concerns.
Analysts believe that these regulatory changes may be too late to retain investors in the equity market.
Gartner highlighted that the bond market is transparent, liquid, and accessible to all types of investors.

Czechs showed low voter turnout for the newly-created Senate elections on Saturday.
The turnout for the elections was expected to be well under 40 percent.
This turnout is the lowest in the four parliamentary elections held since the fall of communism in 1989.
Opposition Social Democrat leader Milos Zeman expressed concern about the apathy towards the upper house.
Zeman predicted that turnout would improve in the second round of elections on November 22-23.
Preliminary data indicated that Klaus's Civic Democratic Party (ODS) was performing well despite low turnout.
In Plzen, turnout was reported at 36 percent, with an ODS candidate expected to face a Social Democrat in the second round.
In Most, turnout was reported at 26 percent, with the ODS candidate leading against a Social Democrat candidate.
The Senate elections were viewed as an indicator of the Czech Republic's political situation following inconclusive lower house polls.
Miroslav Sladek, leader of the far-right Republicans, criticized the Senate as a waste of resources.

Senate runoff elections on Friday and Saturday are expected to have little impact on Czech capital markets.
Investors are focusing on macroeconomic fundamentals rather than political influences.
Last weekend's first round of voting provided a mild boost to the Czech crown and the Prague Stock Exchange.
Analysts believe that unless the second round of voting results vary greatly, little further movement in the markets should be expected.
Jay King of Wood and Company stated that the elections will be a non-event from a foreign investor's perspective.
Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's Civic Democratic Party (ODS) received over 36.5 percent of the national vote in the first round.
The opposition Social Democrats (CSSD) received 20.3 percent of the vote.
Only 35 percent of the electorate participated in the elections.
The ODS won three outright Senate seats in the first round and had 76 candidates going into the runoff.
The CSSD had 48 candidates going into the runoff.

The Czech governing coalition led by Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus won 52 of 81 seats in the newly-created upper house of parliament.
The centre-left opposition Social Democrats won 25 seats in the same election.
The Senate is primarily an advisory body with limited legislative powers.
The election was the first test for Klaus since his coalition lost its lower house majority in June.
Analysts stated that the coalition's strong showing does not address ongoing issues in the capital market.
Charles Robinson of HILFE indicated that the market's reaction would initially be positive but would stabilize without significant changes.
The coalition's performance in the first round of voting increased domestic investor interest and pushed the market up.
Analysts believe that stock prices are unlikely to rise significantly in the near future due to prior expectations being factored in.
The Czech crown gained some value against its dollar/mark basket following the first round results.
Miroslav Nosal of Patria Finance stated that the final election results reflect the current political structure and will not lead to significant changes.

Czech shares increased on Monday after the coalition government's victory in the Senate elections.
Analysts attributed the rise in shares more to a technical correction than a change in investor sentiment.
The Prague Stock Exchange's PX50 index rose 0.86 percent due to gains in seven of the eight most-capitalised shares.
Brokers expressed limited optimism that the rally would last beyond a few days.
The centre-right government's performance was anticipated and already factored into the market prior to the elections.
Jay King from Wood and Company stated that the rally was technically-led and not fundamentally related to the Senate elections.
A local trader noted that the price increases were driven by year-end anticipation and were domestically motivated.
The minority coalition led by Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus secured 52 of 81 seats in the new upper house of parliament.
The centre-left opposition Social Democrats won 25 seats in the Senate elections.
Voter turnout was just over 30 percent, making it difficult for the coalition government to claim renewed voter support.

Markets in Eastern Europe experienced a downturn this week.
Stock exchanges in Bratislava, Bucharest, and Zagreb lost ground.
The Prague Stock Exchange remained stable, with the PX50 index increasing by 0.3 points to close at 510.4.
The centre-right governing coalition in the Czech Republic won Senate elections but did not positively impact the Prague Stock Exchange.
Investors are concerned about weak market regulation in the Czech Republic.
The Warsaw Stock Exchange remained flat, with no new signals for market direction.
Analysts believe the positive economic climate may help the Warsaw Stock Exchange rise above 14,000 points next week.
Comments from the central bank deputy head about potential interest rate increases created uncertainty in the Warsaw market.
Hungarian shares initially rose due to a government decision to increase energy prices but lost momentum midweek.
MOL, an oil and gas company, showed signs of weakness, raising concerns among dealers.

Shares in Cable & Wireless (C&W) advanced on Tuesday after news of a deal with NYNEX and Bell Canada International.
The deal creates Britain's largest cable operator by combining C&W's Mercury, Videotron, Bell Cablemedia, and NYNEX CableComms.
C&W shares peaked at 476.5 pence before closing up 25.5 at 466.5 pence.
Richard Brown is the chief executive of C&W and was appointed five months ago.
The deal follows the collapse of merger talks between C&W and British Telecommunications Plc earlier this year.
Analyst John Tysoe stated that the advantages of scope and size from the deal are irrefutable.
BT welcomed the consolidation in the sector but its shares closed down 4.5 at 353.5 pence.
The new merged company will provide integrated telecommunications, information, and entertainment services.
The merger will give C&W's Mercury access to 18 million business and domestic customers.
The number of homes targeted by the new company will be 2.47 million, surpassing Telewest's two million.

Cable & Wireless, NYNEX Corp, and Bell Canada International announced a merger of their British subsidiaries.
The merger includes C&W's Mercury, Videotron, Bell Cablemedia, and NYNEX CableComms.
Videotron is being acquired by Bell Cablemedia in a deal valued at approximately $1.09 billion.
Cable & Wireless is making a $338 million equity investment in Bell Cablemedia.
Cable & Wireless will own 52.6 percent of the new company, Cable & Wireless Communications.
NYNEX will own 18.5 percent and Bell Canada will own 14.2 percent of the new company.
The remaining 15 percent of the new company will be floated.
The new company will provide integrated telecommunications, information, and entertainment services.
Cable & Wireless Communications will serve around six million homes and businesses in Britain.
The company plans to list its shares in London and New York in about six months.

Lloyd's insurance market welcomed a U.S. district court ruling in its favor on Tuesday.
Lloyd's announced it would extend the deadline for acceptances of a 3.2 billion pound recovery plan.
Lloyd's chairman David Rowland stated the offer would remain open following the court's decision.
The district court in Baltimore, Maryland, overturned an injunction by U.S. Names regarding the recovery plan.
Insurance sources indicated the deadline would likely be extended for several days.
Lloyd's spokesman stated the ruling removed the last major legal obstacle to the recovery plan.
Lloyd's reported that over 82 percent of its 34,000 worldwide members had approved the recovery plan.
Only 53 percent of the 2,700 U.S. Names had approved the plan prior to the ruling.
A spokesman for the Merrett 418 Names Association described the successful appeal as beneficial for the recovery plan.
Lloyd's plans to reinsure its liabilities through a new company called Equitas.

Invesco announced a merger with AIM Management Group.
The combined entity will be named AMVESCO Plc.
AMVESCO Plc will manage approximately $150 billion.
The merger values AIM at around $1.6 billion.
Bob McCullough is Invesco's chief financial officer.
Charles Brady is Invesco's chairman and chief executive.
The merger is described as a merger of two companies, not a takeover.
Invesco will issue 290 million new shares to fund the merger.
AIM shareholders will own about 45 percent of the enlarged group.
The merger requires approval from both Invesco and AIM shareholders.

British property company Greycoat is facing pressure from rebel shareholders who want it broken up.
Moorfield Estates has proposed a merger approach to Greycoat.
Analysts believe Greycoat is not in a critical situation.
A proposal to sell Greycoat's assets will be presented to shareholders at a special meeting on Thursday.
The UK Active Value Fund, advised by Brian Myerson's Active Value Advisers, has put forward the asset sell-off proposal.
The UK Active Value Fund owns an 11 percent stake in Greycoat, which it acquired three years ago.
Brian Myerson's relationship with Greycoat's management has been problematic.
Moorfield Estates has made a proposal involving a share exchange offer for Greycoat.
Moorfield Estates aims to add value for shareholders through more active management of Greycoat's assets.
Analysts believe the Moorfield plan is unlikely to succeed, but there may be opportunities for Greycoat to acquire a more profitable company.

British merchant bank Hambros reported a return to first-half profit.
Hambros reported pretax profits of 35.0 million pounds for the first half of the year.
This profit was an improvement from a 7.7 million pound loss for the same period in 1995.
Sir Chips Keswick is the group chief executive of Hambros.
Regent Pacific Group is a Hong Kong investment manager that holds three percent of Hambros.
Regent Pacific Group has called for the breakup of Hambros to realize shareholder value.
Analysts noted that Regent's calls for Hambros to sell its Hambro Countrywide subsidiary were not discussed in their meeting with the company.
Hambros shares closed down 7.5 pence at 245 pence.
Analysts had predicted an interim dividend of 2.5 to 3.0 pence, but the dividend remained unchanged at 2.5 pence.
Hambros is considered one of the less attractive targets for takeover due to recent poor performance.

Robert Fleming announced increased pre-tax profits for the first half of the year.
The pre-tax profit for the first half of the year increased by 16 percent to 92.2 million pounds.
The previous year's pre-tax profit was 79.4 million pounds.
Chief executive John Manser stated that the profit increase showed new businesses were contributing to profitability.
Manser warned of difficult markets in the second half of the year.
An unnamed analyst suggested that the results were not outstanding given market conditions.
Robert Fleming lost investment banking head Bill Harrison in July.
In August, Jardine Fleming revealed a probe by British and Hong Kong regulators into irregular trades.
The probe resulted in fines and voluntary compensation of nearly $20 million to clients.
Regulators withdrew the authorization of Jardine Fleming's London-based fund company.

3i Group Plc reported an increase in its first half net asset value (NAV) per share.
The NAV per share rose to 454 pence from 426 pence for the same period the previous year.
Ewen Macpherson, 3i's chief executive, stated that the increase was partly held back by continental Europe and a strong pound.
Macpherson noted that the UK portfolio performed extremely well, with an 18 percent growth in revenue.
3i invested 327.3 million stg during the period, with 284.2 million stg invested in the UK.
Macpherson indicated that the prospect of a general election in the UK created investment opportunities.
3i realized investments of 122.2 million stg in the UK and 35.9 million stg in continental Europe.
The group plans to expand in Europe and will open an office in Dusseldorf, Germany in January.
3i intends to open additional offices in Hamburg, Munich, and Stuttgart.
The group will also open its first office in South East Asia, in Singapore, early in 1997.

British property group MEPC announced a 14 percent increase in pretax profits for the year.
MEPC's pretax profits rose to 140 million pounds from 122.6 million pounds the previous year.
A writedown on a Los Angeles shopping mall reduced MEPC's net asset value (NAV).
MEPC's net asset value fell to 450 pence per share from 457 pence per share.
MEPC shares were 11p lower at 441-1/2p by 1218 GMT.
The NAV was reported to be below market expectations.
Earnings per share rose nine percent to 22.9 pence.
The total dividend remained at 20 pence.
The NAV drop reflected a marginal fall in values in Britain and elsewhere.
MEPC's UK portfolio accounts for 70 percent of the group.

Ron Baker plans to bring a counter-claim in a lawsuit against him by Dutch bank ING Barings.
Baker's lawyer, Lindsay Hill, stated that the counter-claim will be heard together with the ING Barings case unless an arrangement is reached beforehand.
