ING Barings is suing Baker for 113,000 pounds, which includes a 100,000 pound loan and interest.
Barings collapsed in February 1995 due to losses of around $1.4 billion from unauthorized derivatives trades by Nick Leeson.
ING rescued Barings and formed ING Barings as its investment banking arm.
Nick Leeson is serving a six-and-a-half year jail sentence in Singapore for his role in the bank's downfall.
Writs have been filed by administrators of Barings against former auditors and former bosses, including Baker.
Baker's counter-claim will be for an unpaid bonus that he believes is due and outstanding.
Mary Walz, a former Barings executive, had her claim for an allegedly unpaid bonus rejected by a London industrial tribunal.
Hill stated that the tribunal's decision regarding Walz's case has no implications for Baker's case.

CE Electric is a U.S. energy group.
CE Electric made a hostile bid for Northern Electric Plc.
The Takeover Panel ruled against Northern Electric's appeal regarding the bid extension.
CE Electric's bid was valued at 782 million pounds, equivalent to 1.3 billion dollars.
The offer period for CE Electric's bid was extended to 1300 GMT on Tuesday.
CE Electric received acceptances totaling just over 50 percent needed for victory.
The original offer was meant to close last Friday but was extended after CE Electric's appeal.
The extension was granted due to concerns raised by CE Electric about share purchases by its advisers.
Northern Electric launched its own appeal against the extension of the deadline.
The Takeover Panel dismissed Northern Electric's appeal unanimously.

Pearson is a British media and leisure group.
Pearson has a 50 percent stake in Lazard Partners.
Lazard Partners owns three Lazard houses in London, Paris, and New York.
Marjorie Scardino became Pearson's chief executive last week.
There is speculation that Pearson may sell its stake in Lazard Partners.
A pre-emption agreement exists between Lazards and Pearson.
The pre-emption agreement allows Lazards to have first refusal on its shares if Pearson sells its stake.
Lazard has been a profitable venture for Pearson.
Pearson's 50 percent stake in Lazard Partners was negotiated during the 1980s.
Lazard holds 48 million shares of Pearson.

China stated that Japan is heading for confrontation due to its election platform that reiterates claims to disputed islands in the East China Sea.
China Daily commented that Japan is ignoring warnings and protests from China and is on the path to confrontation.
The Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) of Japan announced an election platform that reaffirms Tokyo's claim to the East China Sea islands, known as the Senkakus in Japan and Diaoyus in China and Taiwan.
China Daily suggested that it is not too late for Japan to stop its actions, which it described as a reckless gamble.
The newspaper urged Japan to take measures to prevent further escalation for the sake of the world and its future.
Approximately 300 Taiwanese and Hong Kong protesters challenged Japan's sovereignty claim by raising flags on the disputed islands.
Japan has requested China to help prevent further landings on the islands and has stated it will not recognize a lighthouse built by Japanese rightwingers.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang accused Japan of irresponsibility for encouraging landings by rightwing groups on the islands.
The dispute intensified after a Hong Kong activist drowned during a protest against Japan's sovereignty claim.
Japan's claim to the islands dates back to 1895, following its defeat of imperial China, while China has claimed sovereignty for centuries.

Wang Dan has been charged with plotting to overthrow the government.
Wang Lingyun, Wang Dan's mother, plans to defend him in court.
Wang Lingyun is a 61-year-old researcher at a museum with no legal background.
Chinese laws permit family members to defend accused individuals.
A court spokeswoman confirmed the charges against Wang Dan but did not provide further details.
Wang Dan's trial date has not been confirmed but may occur as early as this week.
Wang Lingyun claims the charge of collaborating with overseas subversive forces is unfounded.
Wang Dan took a correspondence course at the University of California, Berkeley.
Wang Dan was detained in May 1995 but was not formally arrested or charged until last week.
The charge against Wang Dan carries a maximum penalty of death and a minimum sentence of 10 years.

He Ping, a son-in-law of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, has resigned as director of the armament department of the People's Liberation Army.
He Ping is the husband of Deng Xiaoping's youngest daughter, Deng Rong.
He Ping resigned after his hopes for promotion were not realized.
He Ping wanted to become deputy chief of general staff but was offered the position of assistant chief of general staff instead.
The assistant chief of general staff is one rank below the deputy chief of general staff.
A replacement has been named to succeed He Ping as director of the armament department.
The refusal to promote He Ping is seen as a sign of Jiang Zemin's increasing power within the Communist Party.
Jiang Zemin is the chairman of the Central Military Commission.
Deng Xiaoping, who is 92 years old, no longer holds any office but remains influential.
Deng Xiaoping has not been seen in public since early 1994.

China stated that Taiwan is a pawn of hostile Western forces aimed at weakening the country.
The People's Daily, the official newspaper of the Communist Party, published a commentary on this topic.
The commentary was issued to mark the 25th anniversary of Taiwan's ousting from the United Nations.
Taiwan is accused of collaborating with anti-Chinese forces to regain admission to the United Nations.
The commentary claimed that some Western forces use the 'human rights card' and 'Tibet card' to limit China's development.
It suggested that the Taiwan issue is viewed by Western forces as a means to weaken and divide China.
In September, the U.S. House of Representatives approved a resolution supporting Taiwan's efforts to rejoin the United Nations.
China regards Taiwan as a rebel province and believes the issue was settled in 1971 when Beijing replaced Taipei at the United Nations.
The commentary criticized countries that support Taiwan's bid for U.N. admission as shortsighted.
China and its supporters blocked moves to consider U.N. membership for Taiwan for the fourth consecutive year.

Wang Dan is a prominent dissident in China.
Wang Dan faces charges of plotting to overthrow the government.
Wang Dan's trial is set to begin at the Beijing Intermediate People's Court.
Wang Dan's mother, Wang Lingyun, stated that he would plead not guilty.
Wang Lingyun expressed concern that her son may receive a harsh sentence despite his innocence.
Wang Dan has been in detention since May 1995.
Wang Dan could face a minimum of 10 years in prison and a maximum penalty of death.
The court has not provided details about Wang Dan's trial.
Wang Dan's family has found a lawyer to defend him after only one day to prepare.
Human Rights Watch reported that the chances of an acquittal for Wang Dan are slim.

Chinese dissident Wang Dan has appealed against his 11-year jail sentence for plotting to subvert the government.
Wang Dan's mother, Wang Lingyun, expressed little hope for an acquittal or a lighter sentence.
Wang Lingyun hopes U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher and German President Roman Herzog will address her son's situation during their upcoming meetings with Chinese leaders.
Wang Lingyun stated that Wang Dan should be acquitted because he is innocent.
Wang Lingyun acted as one of two defense lawyers in her son's case.
Court officials requested Wang Lingyun to submit a written defense for the appeal.
Family members may not be allowed to attend the appeals court trial for Wang Dan.
Experts on China's legal system believe the chances of the appeals court overturning the lower court's verdict are slim.
An official of the Beijing Higher People's Court confirmed that Wang Dan had filed his appeal.
The Beijing Number One Intermediate People's Court convicted and sentenced Wang Dan in less than four hours.

Wang Guangmei auctioned her private antique collection on Tuesday.
Wang stated she would use the proceeds to help impoverished mothers.
The auction took place at a hotel in Beijing.
Wang's collection included porcelain bowls, plates, and an ivory brush holder from the Qing and Song dynasties.
The collection fetched 566,000 yuan ($68,000) at auction.
Wang is the widow of former president Liu Shaoqi, who died in prison during the Cultural Revolution.
The Sungari auction house valued the antiques at up to 510,000 yuan ($61,000).
Some items in Wang's collection were part of her dowry from her wealthy father.
The collection was seized during the Cultural Revolution but was returned to Wang after her release from prison.
Wang expressed emotional ties to the collection but prioritized concerns for impoverished mothers.

China's exports increased in October due to sluggish domestic demand, faster payment of export tax rebates, and expanded credit to exporters.
Wang Jian, a researcher with the cabinet's State Planning Commission, stated that the upturn in exports is expected to continue through the first half of 1997.
Exports rose 23.3 percent to $15.22 billion in October compared to the previous year.
The International Business Daily reported that the increase in exports helped China achieve its largest monthly trade surplus of the year at $3.91 billion in October.
Wang Jian attributed the rise in exports to slow domestic demand and adjustments made by domestic enterprises to a cut in government-paid export tax rebates.
The government reduced the rebate on exports of industrial products from 14.0 percent to 9.0 percent on January 1, 1996.
Exports had declined in the first six months of 1996 due to rising wages and the strength of the renminbi.
The government has been increasing the payment of export rebates to stimulate exports.
Imports rose by three percent year-on-year to $11.31 billion in October.
In the first 10 months of this year, China's exports totaled $119.22 billion, while imports reached $107.21 billion, a rise of 5.5 percent from the previous year.

China's Supreme Court announced that a court has rejected the appeal of Zhou Beifang, upholding a suspended death sentence for bribery.
Zhou Beifang is 43 years old and was the former chairman of Hong Kong-listed affiliates of Capital Iron and Steel Corp (Shougang).
The appellate court showed leniency because Zhou expressed remorse and voluntarily returned ill-gotten wealth during the investigation.
Zhou was convicted of accepting bribes totaling 9.28 million Hong Kong dollars ($1.2 million) between June 1993 and April 1994.
Zhou was also found guilty of paying 1.2 million yuan ($144,600) in bribes to facilitate the relocation of his wife and daughter to the British colony.
Zhou is considered one of China's 'princelings', a term for the children of the ruling party elite.
Zhou's family has close ties to the family of Deng Xiaoping, a paramount leader of China.
Zhou's conviction is part of a highly-publicized anti-graft campaign launched by China last year.
The appellate court also rejected the appeal of co-defendant Chen Jian, who received a 15-year prison sentence for accepting bribes from Zhou.
Zhou Guanwu, Zhou Beifang's father, resigned as chairman and Communist Party secretary of Shougang in February 1995.

Chinese activists protested against American support for Japan's bid to become a permanent member of the U.N. Security Council.
The activists stated that Japan is not qualified to become a permanent member of the Security Council.
The letter opposing Japan's bid was signed by 15 activists.
The activists claimed that many Japanese politicians have been reluctant to apologize for war atrocities and have tried to whitewash history.
China claims that more than 35 million people were killed or wounded during Japan's invasion and occupation from the early 1930s to 1945.
The letter expressed strong protest against U.S. government support for Japan's bid.
Tong Zeng, a leader of the group, stated he would forward the letter to U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher.
The Chinese government has been reluctant to antagonize Japan due to a desire for more low-interest loans.
The United States has historically supported giving Japan and Germany permanent seats on the Security Council.
The U.N. Security Council currently consists of five permanent members and ten non-permanent members.

Chinese President Jiang Zemin stated that political differences should not interfere with trade and investment between China and Taiwan.
Jiang Zemin emphasized the complementary nature of the economies of China and Taiwan.
Jiang Zemin expressed a commitment to encouraging Taiwanese businessmen to invest in China.
Jiang Zemin assured that the legitimate rights of Taiwanese investors would be protected.
A delegation of nearly 80 Taiwanese business leaders and politicians visited Beijing.
Taiwan has banned direct trade, transport, and mail links with China since 1949.
Indirect trade and investment between Taiwan and China has been allowed since the late 1980s, typically through Hong Kong.
Jiang Zemin indicated that China aims to establish direct trade and transport links with Taiwan.
Beijing has increased pressure on Taiwan to lift the ban on direct links.
Kao Ching-yuan, head of the Taiwanese delegation, urged Beijing to resume talks with Taiwan.

A Chinese court rejected the appeal of Liu Nianchun against a labour camp term for writing petitions.
The Chaoyang District Court in Beijing stated that freedom of speech must not endanger state security.
The court's verdict indicated that Liu's 1995 petition contained attacks against the people's government.
The court ruled that Liu's petition exceeded the limits of the constitution and the law.
Liu argued that the constitution guaranteed his right to freedom of speech, but the court rejected this argument.
Liu's wife, Chu Hailan, plans to appeal the court's decision within 15 days.
Chu Hailan described the court ruling as unfair, not objective, and unjust.
Chu reported that she was sent to a labour camp to prevent her from meeting U.S. officials during a visit by Secretary of State Warren Christopher.
Liu Nianchun is currently serving a three-year term of re-education through labour and has been in detention for nearly one year.
Liu's petition called for the government to re-evaluate its crackdown on student demonstrators from the Tiananmen Square protests in 1989.

Kao Ching-yuan, a Taiwanese business leader, invited Wang Zhaoguo, director of the Chinese cabinet's Taiwan Affairs Office, to visit Taiwan.
Beijing has not confirmed whether it will accept the invitation from Kao Ching-yuan.
If Wang Zhaoguo accepts the invitation, he would be the most senior Chinese official to visit Taiwan since 1949.
Wang Zhaoguo expressed a willingness to visit Taiwan if given the opportunity, but did not make a definite commitment.
The Mainland Affairs Council in Taiwan stated it would welcome Wang's visit but emphasized that procedures must be followed.
The Taiwan Affairs Office did not comment on the remarks made by the Mainland Affairs Council spokesman.
Kao Ching-yuan is leading a delegation of nearly 80 Taiwanese businessmen, economists, and officials on a 12-day visit to Beijing.
Chinese President Jiang Zemin met with the Taiwanese delegation and assured them that political differences would not hinder trade and investment.
Kao raised concerns about tax and labor issues faced by Taiwanese investors in China during his meetings with Chinese officials.
Kao urged Beijing to resume talks with Taiwan, warning that political friction could undermine investor confidence.

Rupert Murdoch is the chairman and chief executive of News Corp Ltd.
Murdoch is visiting Australia for News' annual meeting next week.
Murdoch stated that News Corp aims to increase profits by 20 percent in 1996/97.
Murdoch ruled out a potential bid for John Fairfax Holdings Ltd.
Kerry Packer's Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd has attempted to sell its 15 percent stake in Fairfax over the last year.
News Corp owns approximately five percent of Fairfax.
Murdoch expressed confidence in winning a lawsuit against Ted Turner and Time Warner.
Turner described Murdoch's lawsuit against the merger of Turner Broadcasting System Inc and Time Warner as frivolous.
Murdoch indicated that the 20 percent profit increase is attainable if the American and British economies remain stable.
News Corp reported a net profit of A$1.02 billion for the year 1995/96.

Rupert Murdoch stated that The News Corp Ltd's first quarter performance was below expectations.
Murdoch expressed confidence in a 20 percent profit rise for the year 1996/97.
In the 1995/96 year, News Corp's net profit decreased to A$1.02 billion from A$1.37 billion in 1994/95.
Murdoch noted that revenues at the Fox U.S. television business started slowly in 1996/97 due to the Atlanta Olympic Games.
He indicated that Australian newspaper revenues would be flat in 1996/97.
Murdoch reported that News Corp's British newspapers were performing well, with The Sunday Times' circulation increasing.
He announced that News Corp had US$2.5 billion in cash after recent U.S. bond issues.
Murdoch stated that News Corp planned to fund future expansion from cash flow where possible.
He mentioned that News Corp would float its British digital media technology company, Digital Media Services, and sell 20 percent of it.
Murdoch indicated that News' Asian satellite pay television operation, STAR TV, was performing well.

Niugini Mining Ltd owns 17.15 percent of the shares in Papua New Guinea's Lihir Gold Ltd.
Niugini Mining Ltd is exploring ways to return Lihir shares to its shareholders.
Ian Goudie is the chief executive of Niugini Mining Ltd.
A straightforward return of the shares to shareholders cannot be approved until late 1998 due to Lihir mine's current debt arrangements.
Niugini Mining Ltd is considering other structures to return the shares before late 1998.
The return of Lihir shares is one of several ways to unlock the true value of the Lihir stake.
The true value of Niugini Mining Ltd's Lihir stake is not reflected in its current share price.
Niugini Mining Ltd's assets can be viewed in two parts: the Lihir stake and other smaller mining assets.
Separating the two parts of Niugini Mining Ltd's assets could appear to have more value to shareholders.

Rupert Murdoch's News Corp Ltd is likely to benefit from the planned US$20 billion merger of MCI Communications Corp and British Telecommunications Plc.
News Corp has a partnership with MCI that may strengthen due to the merger.
The merger will create the world's second largest telecommunications group.
Analysts believe the merger will stabilize News Corp's partnership with MCI.
Concerns had arisen about MCI potentially selling its nine percent stake in News Corp.
The merger reduces the risk of MCI selling its stake in News Corp for at least 12 months.
MCI and News Corp announced a broad alliance in May 1995, with MCI acquiring a nine percent stake in News Corp.
MCI's stake in ASkyB will be reduced from 50 percent to 20 percent.
MCI Chief Executive Bert Roberts stated that no major new launches are expected from the venture with News Corp.
Roberts indicated that MCI is unlikely to take up its option to increase its stake in News Corp.

Simsmetal Ltd is an Australian-based metals recycler.
Simsmetal Ltd expects lower net profit for 1996/97 compared to 1995/96.
Simsmetal Ltd's managing director is John Crabb.
Scrap metal prices have decreased to their lowest levels in almost four years.
Simsmetal Ltd anticipates difficult trading conditions due to weak demand in Europe and Asia.
Simsmetal Ltd's net profit for the first quarter of 1996/97 fell 34 percent to A$8.28 million.
Simsmetal Ltd's profit for 1995/96 was A$46.7 million, which was 23 percent lower than the previous year.
Simsmetal Ltd is in talks to acquire a large British scrap metal business.
Simsmetal Ltd ended the first quarter with approximately A$62 million in cash.
Simsmetal Ltd plans to use either cash or unused borrowing lines for the acquisition.

Westpac Banking Corp Ltd is Australia's second largest bank.
Westpac announced a 19.5 percent rise in net profit for the 1995/96 year.
Westpac warned that fierce competition would flatten profits in the year ahead.
Westpac reported a net profit of A$1.132 billion for the year to September 30, 1996.
Bad debt charges fell to A$121 million in 1995/96 from A$330 million in 1994/95.
The drop in bad debt charges contributed about A$200 million to the 12 percent rise in pre-tax and abnormals profit.
Competition from non-bank mortgage originators is pressuring Westpac's margins.
Mortgage originators have taken over 10 percent of the mortgage market from big banks, including Westpac.
Westpac launched an issue of securitised mortgages worth A$340 million.
Westpac plans to multiply the size of securitised mortgage issues in the current year.

An inquiry into Australia's financial system has been established by the government and is headed by Stan Wallis.
The inquiry's interim discussion paper, released on Wednesday, leaves open the option of mergers among Australia's big banks and foreign takeovers of local banks.
The inquiry outlines various options for reform without stating its own preferences.
The key aim of any reforms should be to increase the efficiency of Australia's banks to compete globally.
The inquiry states that new technology will transform the financial sector.
Big banks, such as National Australia Bank Ltd, have lobbied for relaxed merger rules, arguing that such mergers are necessary for global competition.
The former Labor government implemented a policy that prevents mergers or foreign takeovers of Australia's four largest banks and its two largest insurance and superannuation groups.
The current conservative coalition government will maintain the 'six pillars' policy until it reviews the Wallis inquiry's recommendations, expected by the end of March 1997.
The inquiry seeks to identify means to increase the efficiency of the Australian financial system without compromising its safety and performance.
The inquiry asks whether competition and innovation could be stimulated by widening access to traditional banking activities.

The Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) rate cut on Wednesday is expected to squeeze bank margins.
Major banks have previously delayed passing on official rate cuts to variable rate home loan customers by around seven weeks.
Major banks have begun lowering variable and fixed deposit rates immediately after rate cuts, temporarily widening their margins.
The delay in passing on the recent rate cut has been shortened to about five and a half weeks.
Analysts attribute the contraction in delays to increasing competition from non-bank mortgage lenders and regional banks.
ABN AMRO Hoare Govett banking analyst Michael Pulman stated that competition is putting more pressure on margins.
Aussie Home Loans announced it would cut its variable rate to 7.49 percent from 7.99 percent for existing customers starting January 28.
National Australia Bank Ltd plans to cut its variable mortgage rate to 8.25 percent from 8.75 percent for existing borrowers starting January 23.
Westpac Banking Corp's delay in passing on the rate cut has dropped to 37 days.
St George Bank Ltd reduced the time to pass on the rate cut for its major variable rate product to 20 days from 55 days.

Almost 300 students and workers from Kiribati were aboard the MV Maasmond.
The MV Maasmond is a 1,000-tonne charter ship.
The ship lost power due to a fire in the engine room.
The Royal New Zealand Airforce Orion rescue plane located the MV Maasmond drifting about 800 kilometers east of Tarawa.
The MV Maasmond had 290 passengers on board.
The ship has enough food and water for five days.
The MV Maasmond partially restored its electric power but could not start its engine.
The ship's charterer is Kiribati businessman Waysang Kumkee.
The MV Maasmond was chartered to carry passengers and cargo to Christmas Island from Tarawa.
The cargo included rice and tinned food.

Lend Lease Corp and Modern Home Co announced a joint venture to build a markets complex in Northern Bangkok.
The project will cover 160 hectares and cost A$1 billion (US$778 million).
The complex aims to create a new industrial, commercial, and residential hub in Northern Bangkok.
Stage one of the project is 60 percent complete and projected to cost A$700 million.
Stage one is processing 15,000 tonnes of produce a day and has parking for 25,000 vehicles.
The complex, known as the Thai Markets project, will be located on the main northern road from Bangkok, about 20 km from the airport.
The project will include food processing facilities for packaging and processing produce for export.
The second and third stages will cost A$300 million and include factories, retail outlets, and homes.
Lend Lease's Asian unit will contribute up to A$100 million for a 10 percent stake in the joint venture.
The project is expected to take four years to complete and is supported by the Bank for Agriculture and Agricultural Cooperatives and the Thai Ministry of Commerce.

Goodman Fielder Ltd is expected to report a slightly higher annual net profit before abnormals early on Thursday.
Firmer margins in some areas are expected to be offset by higher grain costs.
A Sydney analyst forecasts a pre-abnormals net profit of just under A$100 million.
The median forecast in BZW Australia's Barceps survey is for a A$100.0 million pre-abnormals net profit for the year to June 30, 1996.
Forecasts for pre-abnormals net profit range from A$97.0 million to A$102.3 million.
Goodman Fielder posted a profit of A$97.3 million in 1994/95.
Another Sydney analyst estimates extra grain costs of about A$60 million for the second half of 1996.
Analysts expect the cost of grain to ease back later in calendar 1996.
The higher grain costs were likely offset by lower packaging and palm oil costs in the second half of 1995/96.
Goodman chief executive David Hearn stated that the pre-abnormal profit would be around A$100 million.

Rupert Murdoch's News Corp reported a lower than expected profit for the first half of 1996/97.
News Corp remains confident of a 20 percent profit boost for the full year.
Net profits before abnormals increased by 10.3 percent to A$731 million (US$555 million).
The reported profit was below analyst forecasts of A$735 million to A$775 million.
News' shares fell 16 cents to A$6.60 after the result, but closed at A$6.76.
News Corp had previously stated it expected strong movie and television revenues to increase profits by at least 20 percent in 1996/97.
News Corp officials indicated they are still on track for the 20 percent growth.
Operating income from News' Fox Filmed Entertainment unit increased to A$202 million for the first half of 1996/97.
British newspaper profits rose 18 percent in the first half, with gains in circulation revenues at The Sun, The Times, and The Sunday Times.
All of News Corp's newspapers maintained their dominant position in their respective markets despite cover price increases.

Caterpillar Inc. reported record third-quarter profits of $310 million, an increase of 45 percent from $213 million a year ago.
Sales increased to $4.03 billion from $3.73 billion in the same period.
Earnings per share rose 50 percent to $1.61 from $1.07.
The results exceeded Wall Street expectations, leading to a $2.50 increase in Caterpillar stock to $76.625 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Analysts had forecast profits of $1.34 a share, according to First Call.
For the first nine months of 1997, sales were $12.06 billion, up from $11.86 billion a year ago.
Profit for the first nine months surged to $980 million from $836 million.
Caterpillar Chief Financial Officer Douglas Oberhelman stated that most of the earnings gain was due to improved operations.
Profit margins rose to 25 percent in the quarter from 19 percent a year ago.
Higher machine sales in the United States accounted for most of a 5 percent increase in sales volume in the quarter.

Mercantile Bancorp Inc is a potential target in the Missouri bank merger wave after its planned combination with Mark Twain Bancshares Inc.
Michael Ancell, an analyst at Edward D. Jones & Co, stated that Mercantile is still a buyout candidate.
Mercantile Bancorp Inc is the largest bank holding company in Missouri after Boatmen's Bancshares Inc.
Analysts view Mercantile as attractive to banks seeking to establish a presence in the lower Midwest.
NationsBank Corp agreed to buy Boatmen's Bancshares Inc for $9.5 billion in August.
The deal for Boatmen's Bancshares Inc was valued at 2.7 times book value.
Mercantile's deal values Mark Twain Bancshares Inc at about 2.8 times book value.
The pooling of interests deal is worth $49.62 per share to Mark Twain shareholders.
The combined total assets of the St. Louis-based bank holding companies would be $21.3 billion.
James Schutz, a banking analyst at Chicago Corp, described the transaction as pricey and noted Mark Twain is a profitable franchise.

Olympic Financial Ltd stated it could reach a deal to sell the company by October.
Warren Kantor is the chairman of Olympic's executive committee.
Kantor mentioned that the investment banker Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette is considering strategic alternatives for the company.
Olympic received an indication of interest from a potential buyer.
Kantor noted that others have expressed interest in the company since the announcement.
The first contact from a potential buyer came from a company with investment grade credit.
Olympic's credit is not investment grade.
Kantor stated that Olympic needs capital to expand technology as the business grows.
Olympic's loans serviced increased to $3 billion at the end of June from $1.5 billion a year ago.
Kantor indicated that Olympic aims for Classic loans to constitute 50 percent of its portfolio by the end of the year.

McDonnell Douglas Corp. announced it would consider mergers and acquisitions but not a restructuring.
The Defence Department eliminated McDonnell Douglas from the competition to build a new generation fighter jet.
The new generation fighter jet program could be worth $200 billion or more.
Chief Executive Officer Harry Stonecipher stated that the company continues to look at mergers and acquisitions.
The Pentagon awarded contracts to Boeing and Lockheed Martin Corp. to develop prototype fighter jets.
McDonnell Douglas is the nation's second-largest defence contractor.
Industry analysts suggested that McDonnell Douglas may need to restructure or seek a merger after the Pentagon's decision.
McDonnell Douglas had preliminary merger discussions with Boeing Co. earlier this year.
Stonecipher expressed that he does not think Boeing would be a potential acquisition target for McDonnell Douglas.
British and U.S. forces plan to buy 3,000 new generation fighter jets, with initial delivery scheduled for 2008.

Shoppers lined up outside stores on Friday, some arriving before dawn.
The day after Thanksgiving is traditionally one of the busiest days for retailers.
The day after Thanksgiving marks the unofficial start of the holiday shopping season.
Analysts expect sales gains of about 5 percent over last year's weak sales growth.
There are five fewer days between Thanksgiving and Christmas this year.
Allen Sinai, chief economist at Primark Decision Economics, forecasts sales growth of 4.5 percent for November and December.
Roni Campos lined up outside Wal-Mart at first Colony Mall in Sugarland, Texas, at 6:30 a.m.
Stephanie Foster began her shopping at 5 a.m. at Mervyns California and noted a line outside Target of at least 200 people.
Rosalee DiGregorio was one of the first customers at Target and mentioned they had 40 Nintendo consoles in stock.
Tracy Mullin, president of the National Retail Federation, stated that Barbie dolls, especially Holiday Barbie, are expected to be hot sellers.

Freight hauler Yellow Corp. announced it could cut 1 percent to 2 percent of its workforce as part of a restructuring of Yellow Freight System.
Yellow Corp. is based in Overland Park, Kansas.
The company has offered early retirement to 153 employees who are 55 and older.
Yellow Corp. will announce layoffs in the first quarter.
The company will take an unspecified charge to fourth quarter earnings to cover expenses related to early retirement, severance, and reorganization costs.
Each geographic unit of Yellow Freight will have a group vice president who reports to Yellow Freight President Bill Zollars.
Five officers at the central office will also report to Bill Zollars.
Bill Zollars stated that the company is decentralizing responsibility to be more responsive to customer needs.
Employees have until January 15 to decide on early retirement.
The number of layoffs will depend on early retirement decisions and the company's needs during reorganization.

Firstar Corp announced it expects to fall short of analysts' fourth-quarter earnings estimates.
Firstar Corp cited temporary factors for the expected shortfall, including a modest decline in commercial loans outstanding.
Firstar Corp has $19.9 billion in assets.
Firstar Corp expects fourth-quarter earnings of about $0.95 a share, which is $0.08 short of the consensus and unchanged from a year ago.
Firstar Corp is implementing a program to trim costs and enhance revenues.
Analysts are uncertain if the decline in commercial loans outstanding will be reversed.
Firstar's investor relations spokesman Joe Messinger stated the decline in loans is due to the focus on restructuring.
Firstar expects credit card charge-offs to remain higher than its historic levels in the quarter.
Firstar's 10-Q filing indicated expected credit card charge-offs to rise to 4.5-5.0 percent in the fourth and first quarters.
If Firstar meets its $0.95 a share estimate, 1996 earnings would be $3.34 a share, compared to $3.00 a share a year ago.

Retailers may be disappointed with post-Christmas sales due to snow and holiday exhaustion.
John Konarski is the vice president at the International Council of Shopping Centers.
The International Council of Shopping Centers surveys 85 large regional malls across the country.
Konarski believes many people completed their shopping before Christmas.
Konarski expects holiday season sales to increase by 4 percent to 6 percent from the previous year.
Tracy Mullin is the president of the National Retail Federation.
Mullin expects holiday sales to rise about 5 percent from last year.
Sales performance this year is better than last year's weak results of 2.5 percent to 3 percent.
Jay Meltzer is the managing director of LJR Redbook Research.
Meltzer noted that sales slowed moderately compared to last year.

Chrysler Corp. and Ford Motor Co. introduced new sport utility vehicle models at the North American International Auto Show.
The Lincoln Navigator and Dodge Durango were introduced a day after General Motors Corp.'s unit unveiled an upscale version of the Yukon sport utility vehicle.
Subaru of America Inc. debuted a new sport utility vehicle based on a passenger car chassis.
Sport utility vehicle sales in the United States exceeded two million in 1996.
Sport utility vehicles are the fastest-growing automotive segment.
Porsche AG plans to enter the sport utility vehicle market by the turn of the century.
Diane Swonk, deputy chief economist at First Chicago NBD Corp., stated that sport utility vehicles are replacing old station wagons and impacting the luxury car market.
The Lincoln Navigator includes leather seating surfaces, walnut wood accents, and second-row bucket seats.
The Lincoln Navigator is expected to be priced in the mid-$40,000 range and aimed at affluent empty nesters or high-profile active families.
The Lincoln Navigator is expected to sell 20,000 units annually and features a 5.4-litre V8 engine with an 8,000-pound towing capacity.

First Chicago NBD Corp reported that rising bankruptcy filings contributed to an increase in credit card charge offs in the fourth quarter.
Charge offs rose to 6.7 percent of managed receivables in the fourth quarter, compared to 5.9 percent a year ago.
Robert Rosholt, chief financial officer, stated that the increase in charge offs was due to a resurgence of bankruptcy filings, an increase in contractual charge offs, and flat average loan volume in the third quarter.
Credit card fee revenue rose 28 percent from a year ago to $259 million, adjusting for securitization.
Analysts noted that the charge-off rate was high, indicating that the credit card operation may not be as profitable as at other institutions.
Some analysts mentioned that the bank has tightened credit standards in the past year and expressed less concern about the charge-off rate.
Market-driven revenues were $83 million in the fourth quarter, up from $40 million in the previous quarter but down from the bank's average of $100 million per quarter.
Trading profits were $12 million in the fourth quarter, compared to a $12 million loss in the third quarter.
Return on common equity was 17.5 percent in the quarter, up from 15.4 percent a year ago.
Return on assets was 1.46 percent, up from 1.02 percent a year ago.

Caterpillar Inc reported record earnings of $381 million, or $1.99 a share, for the fourth quarter of 1996.
The earnings for the fourth quarter of 1996 were above the $1.53 a share reported in 1995 and the consensus estimate of $1.88 a share.
Caterpillar's stock price decreased by 1-1/8 to 77-3/8 on the day of the earnings report.
Caterpillar expects U.S. gross domestic product growth of about two percent in 1997, which is slower than in 1996.
Thomas Burns Jr., an analyst at NatWest Securities Corp, believes the U.S. economy will improve and does not expect a decline in housing starts.
Burns is more optimistic about European growth than Caterpillar, stating there is a turn up on the way in Europe.
Caterpillar's outlook suggests that bullish factors will be offset by delays in infrastructure products due to fiscal restraint in Europe.
Lisa Shalett, an analyst at Sanford C. Bernstein, noted that one-time currency factors contributed to the earnings exceeding estimates.
Burns estimates Caterpillar's earnings per share will increase to $7.70 in 1997, while Blair Brumley from Dain Bosworth Inc forecasts $8.00 per share.
Brumley stated that share repurchases, gains in the engine business, and price increases from new products should boost earnings.

Mercury Finance Co. found problems in its bookkeeping that caused it to overstate earnings by $90 million over four years.
The chief accountant of Mercury Finance Co., James Doyle, has apparently disappeared.
The irregularities in Mercury Finance Co.'s financial records were attributed to unauthorized entries by its chief accounting officer.
A special committee of the board has been formed to investigate the issues with legal and accounting experts.
James Doyle was last seen at Mercury Finance Co. on January 23, the day the company reported fourth quarter results.
Mercury Finance Co. stated that its planned acquisition of Fidelity Acceptance Corp. may be jeopardized due to the accounting problems.
As a result of the adjustments, shareholders' equity as of December 31, 1996, would be reduced from $353 million to $263 million.
Mercury Finance Co. is in violation of some of its debt agreements and is negotiating with lenders.
Mercury Finance Co. reported that its financial condition remains strong and would support continuing operations and expansion plans.
Moody's Investors Service cut its rating on Mercury Finance Co.'s short-term borrowings.

Mercury Finance Co is facing a liquidity crisis that may lead to bankruptcy protection.
The company is unable to raise new commercial paper to repay maturing debt.
Mercury Finance Co could not pay $17 million in commercial paper due on Friday.
The company has another $100 million in commercial paper due on February 6.
Standard & Poor's Corp lowered Mercury's commercial paper to a default rating.
Mercury Finance Co is facing shareholder lawsuits due to a restatement of net income by about $90 million.
The company's market capitalization decreased by approximately $2.2 billion on Friday.
Mercury Finance Co had about $1 billion in loans receivable at the end of October 1996.

Canada's six biggest banks are expected to report third-quarter earnings on Tuesday.
Analysts predict a third consecutive record year for these banks.
Improved interest rates, higher investment banking revenues, and better loan quality are expected to drive profits.
Earnings for the Big Six banks are projected to be 15 percent to 20 percent higher than the same quarter last year.
Bank of Montreal and Bank of Nova Scotia will report earnings on Tuesday.
Toronto-Dominion Bank and National Bank of Canada will report earnings on Thursday.
Royal Bank of Canada and Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce are scheduled to report results on September 5.
Analysts expect stronger securities earnings despite a recent downturn in financial markets.
The banks are anticipated to benefit from lower loan losses as the industry recovers from past issues in commercial real estate.
Bank stocks have remained strong performers despite a correction in stocks earlier this summer.

Toronto is Canada's biggest city and financial capital.
Protests are planned in Toronto against budget cuts by Ontario's Conservative government.
The protests are referred to as the 'Days of Protest' and are expected to be the largest labour protest in Canada since the Winnipeg General Strike in 1919.
Organisers aim to close businesses and disrupt services, including underground trains and Pearson Airport.
Toronto has a population of 2.2 million people.
Thousands of unionized workers, civil servants, and activists will participate in the protests.
Alan Tonks, chairman of Metro Toronto, warned residents to prepare for inconvenience and frustration during the protests.
The Ontario government plans to cut spending by C$8 billion to eliminate a deficit.
Premier Mike Harris has been referred to as 'Newt of the North' in reference to Newt Gingrich.
Transit officials obtained a partial injunction against picketing at subway stations.

Protesters gathered in Toronto on Friday to protest budget cuts by Ontario's Conservative government.
The protests disrupted subway and bus services in Toronto, affecting about one million commuters.
Marilyn Bolton, a spokeswoman for the Toronto Transit Commission, stated that service was postponed due to picketing.
Unionized workers, civil servants, and social activists participated in the protests on the first day of the 'Days of Protest.'
Commuter trains from Toronto's bedroom communities and service at Pearson Airport were not disrupted by the protests.
The Toronto Stock Exchange opened as usual despite expectations of disruption from the protests.
Premier Mike Harris plans to cut spending by C$8 billion to eliminate a deficit.
The Conservative government has made significant changes since taking power in 1995, including revamping labor laws and cutting welfare payments.
Sid Ryan, president of the Ontario division of the Canadian Union of Public Employees, expressed that the cuts are harming workers.
Despite the protests, the Conservative government's popularity remains around 50 percent in opinion polls.

The Montreal Canadiens are a franchise in the National Hockey League.
Molson Cos. Ltd. is the owner of the Montreal Canadiens.
There were rumors of a sale of the Canadiens on Friday.
A consortium led by Serge Savard was reportedly assembling a bid for the Canadiens.
The Canadiens have won 24 Stanley Cup championships since 1916.
Molson Chief Executive Norman Seagram stated that neither the hockey club nor the Molson Centre are for sale.
Analysts speculated that the Canadiens and the arena could be worth up to C$400 million.
Serge Savard is a Hall of Famer who played for the Canadiens from 1967 to 1981.
Savard was fired by the Canadiens last year after serving as general manager for 13 years.
Molson Breweries owns 40 percent of Canada's largest brewer.

Veronika Hirsch was hired by Fidelity Investments to lead its efforts in the Canadian market.
Hirsch has been removed from her fund due to an investigation by Canadian regulators.
Hirsch joined Fidelity three months prior to her removal.
Hirsch is involved in a controversy regarding personal trades made before joining Fidelity.
Hirsch's investments in Oliver Gold Corp. attracted the attention of the British Columbia Securities Commission.
Fidelity ousted Hirsch from her portfolio and stated her status was 'under discussion.'
Fidelity offered clients the option to withdraw their money without penalty.
The fund managed by Hirsch grew to C$190 million in assets since its launch on September 23.
Fidelity's head office in Boston declined to comment on the situation.
Hirsch purchased 65,000 special warrants of Oliver Gold while working at AGF Management Ltd.

T.A. Associates Inc. launched a C$767 million bid for Altamira Management Ltd.
T.A. Associates is offering C$38 per share for Altamira.
Manufacturers Life Insurance Co. Ltd. has made a bid of C$32 per share for Altamira.
Two major Altamira shareholders control 41.5 percent of the company and are preparing to block Manulife's takeover bid.
The legal action by the shareholders was postponed to negotiate a settlement.
T.A. Associates is one of the largest private equity investors in the United States.
Andrews McLane is the managing director of T.A. Associates.
Manulife owns 30.5 percent of Altamira and has support from 40 Altamira fund managers and employees.
Almiria Capital Corp. owns another 30.5 percent of Altamira and opposes the bid from T.A. Associates.
A joint statement indicated that all parties intend for Altamira to continue its business in the ordinary course.

Canada's Big Six banks are expected to report record profits for the third consecutive year.
The combined profit of Canada's Big Six banks is projected to exceed C$6 billion for the year ending October 31.
This profit figure surpasses the previous record of C$5.2 billion in 1995.
The increase in profits is attributed to higher investment banking and fee revenues, as well as lower loan losses.
Analyst Roy Palmer from TD Securities Inc. predicts that earnings growth will slow in 1997.
Analysts expect fourth-quarter profit gains for the banks to be between 15 percent and 17 percent.
The Toronto Stock Exchange's financial services group reached a 52-week high of 5541.40.
Canadian bank stocks have gained popularity among foreign investors due to declining interest rates and a recovering economy.
CIBC Wood Gundy lowered its recommendations on most Canadian banks earlier this month.
Bank of Montreal is expected to report a fourth-quarter profit of C$1.06 per share.

Canada's Big Six banks are projected to achieve a record C$6 billion annual profit.
Bank of Montreal and Bank of Nova Scotia reported earnings exceeding C$1 billion.
Toronto-Dominion Bank did not reach C$1 billion but had a record year.
Royal Bank of Canada and Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce will report their earnings next week.
Roy Palmer, a banking analyst with TD Securities Inc., predicts record earnings for the upcoming reports.
National Bank of Canada will also report its earnings next Thursday.
Bank of Montreal, Scotiabank, and TD reported double-digit increases in net income.
The earnings reported so far align with analysts' forecasts.
RBC Dominion Securities Ltd, the investment arm of Royal Bank, posted a record profit.
Royal Bank's earnings increased to C$154.3 million for the year ending Sept. 30.

Profits at Canada's six big banks topped C$6 billion ($4.4 billion) in 1996.
The profits surpassed last year's record of C$5.2 billion ($3.8 billion).
Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce and National Bank of Canada completed the earnings season on Thursday.
The six banks reported a combined profit of C$6.26 billion ($4.6 billion) for fiscal 1996, which ended on October 31.
The banks experienced a third consecutive year of record profits amid public dissatisfaction over service charges and credit card rates.
Bank officials stated that millions of Canadians owned bank shares through mutual funds and pension plans.
Shareholders of four of the six banks received increased dividends this year.
CIBC chairman Al Flood stated that the bank's activities contribute to jobs, investment, tax revenue, dividend payments, and foreign income for Canada's economy.
CIBC reported a net income of C$1.36 billion ($1 billion) in fiscal 1996, up from C$1.01 billion ($743 million) in 1995.
CIBC increased its quarterly dividend by C5 cents (3.6 cents) to C50 cents (37 cents).

The CBC cut almost 1,000 jobs on Wednesday as part of an overhaul.
The Canadian Broadcasting Corp. faced a C$414 million reduction in government subsidies.
The CBC announced plans to scrap 2,400 jobs through layoffs, voluntary departures, and the elimination of vacant positions.
The CBC set a target of 800 job cuts in 1998.
Jim Byrd, vice-president of CBC English television, stated that the next few months would be tough but suggested that the worst may be over financially.
The CBC provides television and radio services in English and French.
The Canadian government previously contributed almost two-thirds of the CBC budget.
CBC unions claimed that the job cuts would result in an inferior product for Canadian taxpayers.
Radio Canada International is set to close next March due to a lack of government funding.
CBC President Perrin Beatty mentioned the possibility of using on-air fund-raising drives and corporate sponsorships to offset shrinking federal subsidies.

Canada's annual mutual fund season is marked by high-powered advertising campaigns.
Canadians are expected to invest billions into registered retirement savings plans (RRSPs) this season.
Interest rates are at 40-year lows and stock prices are very high.
John Wiltshire is the vice-president of marketing for Investors Group, which manages C$25 billion in assets.
RRSPs were introduced in Canada in the late 1950s to help individuals save for retirement.
Investors can deduct RRSP contributions from their taxes for the previous year's income.
Canadians have over C$211 billion invested in mutual funds, an increase from 1990.
An estimated C$23 billion is expected to be added to mutual funds this year.
Fund companies anticipate a shift of C$250 billion from guaranteed investment certificates and term deposits into mutual funds.
Canadian broadcast rules prevent companies from making performance claims in advertisements.

Canada announced plans to lift restrictions on foreign banks to increase competition in the banking sector.
Draft legislation to allow foreign banks to open branches in Canada will be ready before the end of 1997.
Doug Peters, secretary of state for financial institutions, stated that a federal election may delay the bill's passage until next year.
Peters claimed that branching would encourage new banks to enter the Canadian market and provide existing foreign banks with more competitive opportunities.
Foreign bankers have expressed concerns that Canada is behind its Group of Seven trading partners in opening its banking sector to foreign competition.
Current regulations require foreign banks to operate as separately capitalized subsidiaries in Canada.
The cost of operating a subsidiary has led to a decrease in the number of foreign banks in Canada from about 60 in the 1980s to 43.
Alfred Buhler, chairman of Bank of America Canada, stated that a freer market would make Canada more attractive to foreign banks.
ING Groep N.V. plans to launch a telephone banking operation in Canada with an initial investment of $50 million.
Citicorp and Wells Fargo and Co. are also planning to offer banking services to Canadian consumers and small businesses.

General Motors Corp. is facing potential losses as a strike against its Canadian operations enters its second week.
GM Chairman Jack Smith stated his commitment to maintaining competitiveness.
26,000 Canadian Auto Workers members are set to strike GM plants at midnight Wednesday.
The strike is expected to lead to parts shortages and assembly plant shutdowns in the United States.
G. Richard Wagoner, president of GM's North American Operations, indicated that U.S. plants can operate for a limited time before a shutdown occurs.
Jack Smith described some union demands regarding outsourcing as unacceptable.
Smith stated that certain issues must be resolved to maintain GM's competitiveness.
GM is considered the least efficient U.S. automaker and needs to sell certain parts plants due to high wage structures.
GM has $13 billion in cash and a fully funded pension plan, positioning it to handle the strike.
GM filed a shelf registration statement with the Securities and Exchange Commission to sell up to $1.3 billion in debt securities.

The president of the Canadian Auto Workers is Basil 'Buzz' Hargrove.
A strike against General Motors Corp has been ongoing for 10 days.
Hargrove stated that the United Auto Workers are facing similar issues in reaching a labor agreement with GM.
GM is resisting the U.S. pattern agreement established at Ford Motor Co and Chrysler Corp.
The U.S. pattern agreement guarantees employment levels at 95 percent of the companies' current hourly workforces.
The provision aims to limit the automakers' ability to outsource work.
Hargrove expressed a desire for UAW President Stephen Yokich to reach a settlement.
GM has agreed to the principle of limiting outsourcing in the U.S. but does not want to meet the 95 percent employment guarantee.
Negotiations between the UAW and GM have been low key during the Canadian strike.
The CAW strike began on October 3, and all 26,000 GM workers represented by the union were on the picket line by midnight on Wednesday.

Chrysler Corp. reported a 92 percent increase in third-quarter profits.
Chrysler earned $680 million, or 93 cents a share, in the July-September period.
Chrysler set records for both net income and earnings per share for the third quarter.
A year earlier, Chrysler earned $354 million, or 45 cents a share.
Chrysler's third-quarter performance was described as outstanding by Chairman Robert Eaton.
Chrysler's strong performance was fueled by record-setting demand for its products.
Chrysler incurred an after-tax charge of $55 million, or 7 cents a share, for an early retirement program.
About 531 salaried employees opted for the early retirement program during the quarter.
Excluding the charge, Chrysler earned $735 million, or $1 a share, from operations.
Analysts had expected Chrysler to earn about $520 million, or 71 cents a share.

Lear Corp. agreed to buy the instrument panel and trim parts unit of Borealis Holding AB.
Lear signed a memorandum of understanding to acquire Borealis Industrier AB for undisclosed terms.
Borealis Industrier is based in Gothenburg, Sweden and manufactures various components for the European car and truck industry.
Borealis Industrier had sales of about $230 million in 1995 and owns five plants in Sweden employing about 1,800 people.
Primary customers of Borealis Industrier include AB Volvo, Saab Automobile AB, and Scania AB.
Borealis Holding is owned by Neste Oy and Statoil AS.
The completion of the transaction is subject to approval by the Swedish competition authority and other conditions.
The acquisition supports Lear's strategy to provide total automotive interior systems.
Lear previously purchased Masland Corp. for $384 million and Automotive Industries Inc. for $626 million.
Lear's stock was unchanged at $38 a share on the New York Stock Exchange.

The United Auto Workers union set a Sunday night deadline for a strike against General Motors Corp.
UAW President Stephen Yokich stated that union negotiators were not optimistic about reaching a new contract by the deadline.
The UAW will terminate its extended 1993 contract with GM if no agreement is reached by the deadline.
The UAW typically does not work without a contract.
UAW members have been advised to continue working unless notified otherwise by their local union.
The UAW bargaining team will continue efforts to achieve a new agreement before the contract expiration.
General Motors recently settled a 20-day strike with the Canadian Auto Workers union.
Negotiations between the UAW and GM are at odds over employment guarantees and GM's desire for flexibility in outsourcing parts work.
Ford Motor Co. and Chrysler Corp. have agreed to guarantee jobs for 95 percent of their current workforces over the next three years.
GM's chief negotiator stated that they are committed to an agreement that balances employee needs with GM's competitiveness.

Negotiators for General Motors Corp. and the United Auto Workers adjourned their talks on Saturday evening.
There are less than 30 hours remaining before a midnight Sunday strike deadline.
UAW President Stephen Yokich is leading the bargaining efforts.
The union announced it will cancel its contract with GM at 11:59 p.m. EST Sunday.
GM spokesman Charles Licari did not comment on whether the adjournment indicated poor progress in the talks.
The negotiations are for a new national labor agreement covering GM's 215,000 UAW workers.
This is the first time the UAW has threatened a strike in its 1996 negotiations with Detroit's Big Three automakers.
The UAW's negotiations have been characterized by a conciliatory tone and secretive discussions.
GM's 26,000 Canadian Auto Workers members returned to work after a three-week strike against GM's Canadian operations.
The U.S. talks are focused on job security and GM's desire to outsource certain work.

General Motors Corp. workers are currently working without a contract.
United Auto Workers President Stephen Yokich has not called a strike against General Motors.
Negotiations for a new national labor contract covering GM's 215,000 UAW hourly workers were recessed after a midnight strike deadline passed.
Yokich stated that some negotiators would resume talks later in the day.
Yokich emphasized that agreements can only be settled at the bargaining table.
The UAW plans to hold a meeting with plant-level leaders in Detroit on Saturday regarding the negotiations.
Yokich indicated that some local unions at GM may resort to walkouts if their demands are not met in separate negotiations.
The local negotiations have become a sticking point for the national negotiations, with only a few local unions having signed agreements with GM.
Local agreements typically address plant-specific issues, while the national contract covers broader issues such as wages and benefits.
GM Vice President of Personnel Gerald Knechtel stated that the talks have been constructive and significant progress has been made.

The United Auto Workers union initiated two local strikes against General Motors Corp.'s truck operations.
Approximately 2,750 members of UAW Local 23 struck at GM's Indianapolis metal stamping plant.
About 4,800 workers struck at GM's Janesville, Wisconsin, truck assembly plant.
Negotiations at GM's Detroit headquarters were scheduled to resume Wednesday morning after pausing Tuesday night.
GM spokesman Jerry Holmes stated that the automaker had no formal response to the walkouts.
The Janesville plant produces Chevrolet Tahoe, Suburban, and GMC Yukon sport utility vehicles.
The Indianapolis plant supplies sheet-metal stampings to nine of GM's North American truck assembly plants.
UAW President Stephen Yokich indicated that local strikes were a possibility after negotiations failed.
Ron Gettelfinger, UAW regional director, confirmed he called the Indianapolis strike to address local issues.
UAW Local 95 in Janesville stated that their strike was due to unresolved local issues after 44 bargaining sessions.

A strike at General Motors Corp.'s Indianapolis metal stamping plant is expected to cause two GM truck assembly plants to shut down.
The two truck plants will run out of parts from Indianapolis late Thursday night during their second production shifts.
A plant in Fort Wayne, Indiana, shut down on Wednesday night and laid off about 2,250 of its 2,600 workers.
The Fort Wayne plant halted production of GM's Chevrolet and GMC pickup trucks.
The plants that will be affected receive parts from Indianapolis and include locations in Pontiac, Flint, Michigan; Oshawa, Ontario; Linden, New Jersey; Shreveport, Louisiana; Moraine, Ohio; and Silao, Mexico.
The strike involves 2,750 workers at Indianapolis and 4,800 workers in Janesville, Wisconsin.
GM and the UAW are engaged in a bargaining session to negotiate a new national labor contract for 215,000 GM hourly workers.
The bargaining session is reported to be the longest so far between the union and GM.
The shutdown of the Janesville plant could cost GM $50 million a week in pre-tax profits.
GM makes an average of $9,000 in variable profits on each truck produced.

The United Auto Workers (UAW) cancelled a meeting of its National GM Council that was scheduled for Saturday.
The National GM Council consists of about 250 plant-level leaders at GM locals across the country.
The council was expected to vote on a tentative agreement covering GM's 215,000 UAW workers.
UAW spokesman Reg McGhee did not provide a reason for the cancellation.
The council will meet on Wednesday, Nov. 6, in Chicago if the union reaches an agreement with GM.
An official close to the talks stated that the meeting was cancelled because the union did not reach a deal in time.
GM spokesman Gerry Holmes indicated that the parties were working to resolve final issues.
The cancellation of the meeting was viewed as a negative sign for the GM contract talks.
The two sides have been negotiating over the total number of hourly workers GM will guarantee over the next three years.
GM is expected to match the wage package offered by Ford Motor Co. and Chrysler Corp.

General Motors Corp. and the United Auto Workers union reached a tentative deal for a labour contract.
The labour contract is intended to preserve jobs but did not stop local strikes in Wisconsin and Indiana.
The national agreement covers wages, benefits, and job security for GM's 215,000 hourly UAW workers.
Contentious plant-specific issues remain unresolved at most of GM's 123 locals.
UAW President Stephen Yokich announced the pact at a news conference.
President Clinton expressed hope that the tentative agreement will be ratified and local issues resolved.
Approximately 2,750 workers struck at GM's Indianapolis metal stamping plant.
About 4,800 workers struck at GM's Janesville, Wisconsin, truck assembly plant.
The strikes were due to local grievances, including demands for more workers.
The strike at Indianapolis disrupted supplies to nine GM North American truck plants.

Workers at a General Motors Corp. metal stamping plant in Indianapolis returned to work after ratifying a deal to end a five-day strike.
The strike at the Indianapolis plant threatened to paralyze most of GM's light truck production.
A similar settlement was not reached at GM's Janesville, Wis., truck assembly plant, where a strike by 4,800 workers entered its sixth day.
The Janesville plant builds GM's Chevrolet Tahoe, Suburban, and GMC Yukon sport/utility vehicles.
The deal for 2,750 workers in Indianapolis includes the hiring of 200 new workers.
The deal maintains seniority rules for skilled trades workers and provides back pay for workers to settle grievances.
UAW regional director Ron Gettlefinger expressed regret over the strike and hoped other GM plants would heed the seriousness of local agreements.
The Indianapolis strike disrupted shipments of parts to nine of GM's North American light truck plants.
Parts shortages caused by the strike led GM to shut down truck plants in Fort Wayne, Ind., Shreveport, La., Moraine, Ohio, and Linden, N.J.
Including the strikers at Janesville and Indianapolis, over 19,000 workers were idled, in addition to 18,858 GM workers on layoff due to parts shortages from a previous strike.

General Motors Corp. can reduce its workforce under a United Auto Workers pact.
The GM agreement differs significantly from contracts with Ford Motor Co. and Chrysler Corp.
The GM agreement includes tougher restrictions on using outside companies for parts.
The contract aims to curb job losses to lower-cost outside suppliers.
About 250 plant-level leaders approved the GM pact unanimously.
GM's 215,000 rank-and-file UAW members are expected to ratify the pact by Nov. 17.
Most local officials expressed satisfaction with the GM pact.
The contract requires GM to maintain employment at 95 percent of current levels with exceptions.
The pact allows GM to stop replacing retiring workers when efficiency gains are made.
GM can adjust workforces in larger geographic groupings than Ford and Chrysler.

Ford Motor Company Ltd is the U.K. arm of the U.S. carmaker Ford.
Ford U.K. stated that the British sales outlook for 1997 appears flat.
Ian McAllister is the chairman and managing director of Ford U.K.
McAllister attributed sluggish interest among UK consumers to weak sentiment.
Consumers in the UK have become cautious due to negative experiences from the recession.
An end to consumer worries and a resolution of recessionary effects are needed for the private car market to improve.
Industry analysts noted that growth in the UK car market has been driven by company purchases rather than individual consumers.
McAllister indicated that company fleet sales will be a priority for Ford in the coming year.
Ford plans to reduce its involvement in the heavily discounted rental market.
McAllister acknowledged that slight growth in the European car market in 1996 was influenced by government incentives and heavy discounting.

Nissan Motor Co is expected to decide on building a new medium-sized vehicle for the European market in spring 1997.
Ian Gibson is the managing director of Nissan Motor UK and vice-president of Nissan Europe.
Gibson will present his plan to the Nissan board in Tokyo next spring.
The investment size, design details, and production for the new vehicle are not yet finalized.
It is uncertain whether the plan to build the new vehicle will proceed.
The new car will be positioned between the Micra and the Primera models.
The new vehicle will be based on the Almeira model, which is manufactured in Japan and shipped to Europe.
If the new car is built in Europe, its design and development will be specifically for the European market.
If approved, the decision would involve moving up to 100,000 units of production capacity from Japan to Europe.
Gibson estimated the minimum cost of developing the new model at 200 million GBP, with industry costs ranging from one to three billion GBP.

Wolseley Plc is expected to report slightly lower year pretax profits next Tuesday.
Wolseley Plc is expected to report a rise in its dividend payout.
Wolseley issued a profit warning earlier this year, stating that year profits for the period to July 31 would not match 1995.
Wolseley is expected to perform better than rivals Redland Plc and RMC Group Plc.
Analysts forecast Wolseley's year profits to range from 230 million stg to 240 million, with an average prediction of 234.9 million.
Wolseley's profits last year were 245.4 million.
The expected dividend payout for Wolseley is between 10.3 pence and 10.5 pence, with an average prediction of 10.3 pence.
Wolseley's revenues are reported to stem 50 percent from the U.S. market.
The UK market is described as difficult, and France is described as dreadful.
Market watchers are looking for evidence of changes in Wolseley's group strategy following a recent change in top management.

Cowie Group is Britain's second biggest bus company.
Cowie Group was approached by a defence vehicle manufacturer about forming a leasing joint venture.
The joint venture would target clients including the Ministry of Defence.
Cowie Group stated that the approach was made this year.
Cowie Group is open to considering new options for business.
Cowie Group downplayed a report by The Times about buying and leasing battle tanks.
Cowie Group acknowledged receiving an approach for a leasing venture for military transportation equipment.
Robert Blower, a spokesman for Cowie, confirmed the approach from a UK defence equipment supplier.
Cowie Group would need shareholder approval for any move into military vehicles.
Cowie Group has won a contract for forklift trucks with the Ministry of Defence.

All four Hanson companies are due to be spun off as part of the demerger process.
Hanson companies received takeover approaches for part or all of their units in the chemicals, tobacco, building, and energy sectors.
William Landuyt is the chairman and chief executive of Millennium Chemicals and a Hanson group board member.
Landuyt stated that there has been interest for every business in Hanson.
The expressions of interest included possible offers for whole divisions and individual companies within the four divisions.
Landuyt's company, Millennium, had sales of more than two billion stg and 588 million stg in operating profit in 1995.
Millennium received approaches for all three of its units: Quantum, SCM, and Glidco.
The board of Millennium decided against pursuing any of the takeover approaches.
Landuyt defended Millennium's decision to incorporate a 'poison pill' clause to protect it from hostile takeovers.
The poison pill clause means that a company gaining a 15 percent stake in Millennium would see those shares become worthless.

Imperial Tobacco Plc recently split from Hanson Plc.
Imperial Tobacco Plc admitted that Hanson Plc received a takeover approach before the demerger.
Hanson Plc rejected the takeover approach because the price was too low.
Gareth Davis is the chief executive of Imperial Tobacco Plc.
Gareth Davis stated that a phone call was made to Grosvenor Place, which is Hanson Plc's headquarters.
Gareth Davis described the prices discussed during the takeover approach as 'silly'.
The interested party in the takeover approach was a tobacco firm.
Gareth Davis did not comment on speculation regarding B.A.T. Industries Plc as a potential buyer.

Taylor Woodrow is Britain's biggest builder.
In 1996, Taylor Woodrow celebrated its 75th anniversary.
Taylor Woodrow's shares outpaced the market in 1996 after a decline in 1995.
Colin Parsons is the chairman of Taylor Woodrow.
Taylor Woodrow's profits increased by 81 percent to 25.4 million pounds in 1996.
Taylor Woodrow's shares reached a high of 183 pence in September 1996.
As of the time of the report, Taylor Woodrow's shares were at 156 pence.
Taylor Woodrow's shares outperformed the Financial Times All Share index by 30 percent.
Taylor Woodrow's shares outperformed the building and construction sector by 18 percent.
Taylor Woodrow experienced a share price low of 53 pence in July 1991.

Eurotunnel faced financial pressure due to a fire that damaged a main tunnel.
The fire resulted in no running services and affected consumer confidence.
Eurotunnel recently restructured nine billion pounds ($15 billion) of debt to avoid bankruptcy.
One of Eurotunnel's two rail tunnels remains shut pending a safety review.
Analysts noted a modest fall in Eurotunnel shares following the fire.
Eurotunnel warned of reduced services for weeks due to repair work.
The cost of repairs may exceed initial estimates, potentially reaching millions of pounds.
Eurotunnel is losing revenues at a rate of one million pounds a day while the tunnel is shut.
Eurotunnel's spokesman stated that repair costs should be covered by insurance.
Eurotunnel had approximately 45 percent of the cross-Channel ferry market before the fire.

Christian Salvesen announced plans to demerge its Aggreko business and make a 150 million pound special payout.
The announcement came after Christian Salvesen rejected a 1.1 billion hostile bid from Hays Plc.
Chris Masters is the chief executive of Christian Salvesen.
Masters stated that the demerger offers better shareholder value than the rejected bid from Hays Plc.
The demerger of Aggreko is part of a six-year restructuring process that has improved the company's results.
Christian Salvesen reported first-half pretax profits of 51.6 million pounds, up from 45.0 million pounds.
Sales for the same period increased to 383.1 million pounds from 345.9 million pounds.
The company plans to pay special dividends totaling 150 million pounds and an ordinary dividend of 3.8 pence per share.
An enhanced dividend of 17 pence will be paid at a cost of about 50 million pounds.
A foreign income dividend of approximately 100 million pounds is expected to be paid before the end of March 1997.

The Serious Fraud Office (SFO) has launched an investigation into former bosses of Wickes Plc.
The investigation is related to accounting irregularities worth tens of millions of pounds.
The SFO is conducting the probe jointly with the British police fraud squad in London.
Investigators are expected to interview former chairman and chief executive Henry Sweetbaum, former finance director Trefor Llewellyn, and former buying and commercial directors.
No arrests or charges have been made, and no search warrants have been executed.
The SFO took on the case on November 20 but did not announce its involvement for operational reasons.
Wickes uncovered the accounting scam in June, which led to a 51 million pound overstatement of profits.
Wickes plans to restate profits next month and is preparing a refinancing rights issue of between 30 and 40 million pounds.
Wickes shares remain frozen at 69 pence per share.
Henry Sweetbaum has agreed to repay his 1.2 million pounds in bonuses, and Trefor Llewellyn has agreed to repay his bonus of 485,000 pounds.

Stagecoach Plc is a bus to rail operator.
Stagecoach Plc's share price has doubled in under a year.
Stagecoach Plc reported record profits of 47 million stg.
Keith Cochrane is the finance director of Stagecoach Plc.
Keith Cochrane stated that Stagecoach Plc expects ongoing progress in its second half dividend.
Stagecoach Plc raised its interim payout by 43 percent to three pence.
The first dividend reflected a profit of 15 million stg from the sale of its stake in Strathclyde Buses.

Richard Branson's Virgin Group secured a British rail franchise on Friday.
Virgin Group plans to invest an additional 250 million pounds on new trains and increased services.
Virgin Group won control of the CrossCountry service, which serves over 130 stations and is based in Birmingham.
Virgin Group has 842 staff and earned passenger revenues of 108 million pounds in the year to March.
The government subsidy for the first year of the 15-year franchise will be 112.9 million pounds.
The initial subsidy has been reduced from 127 million pounds in 1996/97 and will average 36.4 million pounds over the franchise term.
Virgin Rail plans to buy a new fleet as part of its bid, with orders to be placed next year and first deliveries expected in 2002.
Virgin will refurbish HST 125 diesel trains and aims to increase train miles by 14 percent between May 1998 and 2002.
The services will be rebranded under the Virgin name and will cover destinations in England, Scotland, and Wales.
Virgin Rail is on the shortlist for the West Coast rail franchise and has submitted a bid for the Thameslink service in London.

Semiconductor stocks have been underperforming on Wall Street for the past year.
Analysts believe semiconductor stocks are likely to become strong performers again.
There are signs that double-digit growth is returning to the semiconductor sector.
North American sales and bookings data for September are expected to be released on Tuesday afternoon.
The upcoming data is anticipated to confirm that the semiconductor industry has reached a cyclical bottom.
Analysts expect a rebound in profits for the semiconductor industry, possibly starting in the fourth quarter.
Montgomery analyst John Joseph stated that chip sales should reaccelerate from this point.

Intel Corp. stock rose by $3.50 to $111.125 on Tuesday.
Intel's quarterly earnings report exceeded Wall Street expectations.
Intel reported third-quarter profits of $1.3 billion, an increase from $931 million in the same quarter of 1995.
Wall Street had predicted Intel's profits to be $1.1 billion.
The earnings report positively impacted the stocks of personal computer makers that use Intel microprocessors.
Compaq Computer Corp. stock rose by $2 to $74.75.
Dell Computer Corp. stock increased by $3.50 to $88.375.
Gateway 2000 Inc. stock climbed by $3.375 to $56.75.
Analysts expressed concerns about the sustainability of Intel's order surge into the fourth quarter.
Intel's stock gains contributed to the Nasdaq index closing at 1,258.10, a record high.

Computer Associates International Inc. is expected to unveil a new Internet division on Monday.
The new division aims to help businesses avoid the need to seek multiple vendors for Web site setup and management.
Computer Associates manages Web sites for large corporate customers.
The company plans to sign up hundreds of thousands of small businesses for its service, regardless of their computer ownership.
Neighborhood businesses will contract with Computer Associates to establish an Internet presence.
Customers will be able to access a shop's Web site to place orders.
Companies currently face challenges in establishing an Internet presence due to the need for various vendors for hardware, software, and consulting services.
Computer Associates' one-stop Internet service aims to handle technical responsibilities for customers.
The company is the world's top mainframe software supplier and the second largest independent software firm after Microsoft.
The launch of the new business unit is part of several announcements at the CA World conference in New Orleans.

MCI Communications Corp. reached a 10-year deal with NextWave Telecom Inc.
The deal positions MCI among the top U.S. wireless communications providers.
MCI will connect its network to a system planned by NextWave for wireless personal communications services.
The agreement allows MCI to offer service to over 110 million individuals in 63 areas, including 29 of the top 50 markets.
MCI will purchase at least 10 billion minutes of capacity from NextWave over the 10 years.
The terms of the deal were not disclosed.
Personal communications services allow customers to send voice and data transmissions over wireless telephones.
NextWave was the largest bidder in the U.S. Federal Communications Commission's auctions for 'C-band' wireless radio spectrum.
NextWave plans to sell stock to the public.
MCI aims to expand into the market for wireless personal communications services through this deal.

In the third quarter of 1996, International Data Corp. reported a 12 percent growth in U.S. PC shipments compared to the previous year.
International Data Corp. described this growth as the slowest pace in five years.
Dataquest reported a 16.3 percent increase in worldwide PC shipments during the same period.
The differing conclusions from the two firms reflect IDC's focus on the U.S. market and Dataquest's emphasis on global shipments.
Dataquest PC analyst Kimball Brown stated that concerns about slowing PC growth are exaggerated.
IDC analyst Eric Lewis noted that PC vendors are being cautious due to previous excess inventory issues.
Compaq Computer Corp. led in PC shipments both worldwide and in the United States during the third quarter.
Apple Computer Inc. and the combined companies of Packard Bell Inc. and NEC Corp. experienced declines in shipments compared to the previous year.
